8de821a5e7f4ca67: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia Rapid Transit Corporation Sdn Bhd (MRT Corp) has awarded a RM2.69 billion contract for a key cross-sea section of the Penang LRT Mutiara Line.
This paves the way for a direct rail link between Penang Island and the mainland.
The Civil Main Contract 2 (CMC2) package was awarded to a joint venture comprising China Communications Construction Company, TRC Construction and Ufuk Semarak.
MRT Corp said the contract covers designing and constructing a 5.5km extension from Macallum to Penang Sentral.
This includes a 3.05km sea-crossing bridge with navigational spans for vessels accessing the ports of Prai and Butterworth.

The extension will connect Penang Island with Seberang Perai and link the Mutiara Line to Penang Sentral, the state's main multimodal transport hub, allowing passengers to interchange with KTM rail services, ferries and buses.
MRT Corp said the journey between Komtar and Penang Sentral is expected to take about eight minutes.
The award comes as construction of the broader Mutiara Line reaches 16 per cent completion, with work remaining on schedule.
MRT Corp chief executive officer Datuk Mohd Zarif Hashim said the CMC2 award marked an important step in extending the project's benefits to communities on both sides of the Penang Strait.

"This extension reflects the vision of Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who recognised from the outset that an investment of this magnitude must benefit communities on both sides of the strait."
Mohd Zarif said MRT Corp's responsibility was to deliver not only the infrastructure but also the long-term benefits promised by the project.
The company said a comprehensive traffic management plan is being implemented with relevant authorities to maintain traffic flow, safeguard the public and minimise disruption from construction works.
The Mutiara Line is among the country's major urban rail investments and is expected to support Penang's economic growth while improving connectivity and accessibility across the state.

923ef888b48c503d: LOS ANGELES: California Governor Gavin Newsom said on Thursday he would commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates currently condemned to execution in his state, the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, declaring that he believes capital punishment to be morally wrong.

The announcement, in a three-page letter addressed to "all Californians", came as Newsom, a Democrat who is expected to seek his party's presidential nomination in 2028, neared the end of his second and final four-year term as governor.

Newsom, who previously served as mayor of San Francisco and lieutenant governor, declared a moratorium on executions in March 2019, about two months after first taking office as governor. California last put a prisoner to death in 2006, when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor.
Capital punishment remains on the books in California as a sentencing option unless repealed by voters or the legislature, and could be restored to practice by future governors.
Voters last upheld the death penalty in 2016, rejecting a referendum to abolish executions while approving another measure designed to reform and speed up the process.
Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office would continue to "evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigour, care and restraint these decisions demand".

Under Newsom's sweeping grant of clemency, the death sentences of all 548 condemned prisoners will be commuted to life in prison without eligibility for parole. Under the state's constitution, California's Supreme Court must review clemency granted to any offender twice convicted of a felony.
Matter of conscience
The governor said he was "acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing".
He acknowledged that death row inmates were convicted of causing "indescribable suffering", and that "many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die".
"But as governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," Newsom wrote. "These offenders will die in prison, but not by our hand."
The US debate over capital punishment intensified recently after Tennessee's failed execution of condemned killer Christa Pike, who survived two attempts to inject her with lethal drugs on Sept 30.
Pike, whom witnesses heard gasping, crying, whimpering and breathing loudly through much of the botched procedure, was hospitalised afterwards and sent back to prison on Oct 10.

The death penalty received further scrutiny after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the planned firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas on Nov 5, 2009.
President Donald Trump later ruled out a livestream of the execution, but Hasan is still scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec 3.
Newsom's announcement came as executions were scheduled in three other states, one of which was carried out on Wednesday in Indiana, with two others expected later in the day in Alabama and Florida.
At odds with public opinion

Still, Newsom's action on the death penalty gives him a signature legacy on a highly contentious social issue as he lays the groundwork for what is expected to be a bid for the White House in two years.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted weeks after the botched execution in Tennessee found 55 per cent of Americans supported the death penalty for people convicted of the most serious crimes, down from 63 per cent in 2017, while 31 per cent said they opposed capital punishment altogether.
In the same poll, a third of respondents said they believed the government should try a second time to put a condemned criminal to death if a first execution attempt failed.

About 15 countries still actively execute people, according to the human rights group Amnesty International. The death penalty remains on the books in 27 US states, although executions are concentrated in a handful of those states, and more than 20 states have abolished capital punishment altogether.
California's cohort of condemned inmates accounts for more than a fourth of nearly 2,000 prisoners on death row nationwide, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.

Newsom's death penalty stance contrasts sharply with that of Trump, who resumed US government executions following a 20-year gap near the end of his first White House term, putting 13 federal prisoners to death by lethal injection in his final few months in office.

Although the clemency act has no bearing on federal cases, Bill Essayli, a Trump-appointed US prosecutor in Los Angeles, decried Newsom's move as "a major blow to Californians and the families of victims murdered in horrific circumstances".
Newsom signalled he was considering a mass commutation in an Oct 1 podcast conversation with death penalty opponent Bryan Stevenson.
"I have to prepare for my own consciousness, my rocking chair test," Newsom said. "Do I commute the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere?"
Stevenson encouraged him to do so.

Death penalty opponents raise the possibility of wrongly executing an innocent person, note racial and socioeconomic disparities in the application of capital punishment, and argue there is no convincing evidence that it deters murder more effectively than life imprisonment without parole.
Supporters argue that capital punishment provides just punishment for the most serious crimes, deters would-be offenders and ensures murderers cannot kill again.

851804b0cb7c8a9f: KUALA LUMPUR: Bank Negara Malaysia may have held interest rates steady but the door remains open for a rate hike as early as the first quarter of 2027.

Economists said the central bank has little immediate reason to tighten policy, with Malaysia recording the lowest inflation rate in Asean and the ringgit holding broadly steady against the US dollar year-to-date.

Generous petrol subsidies have also helped shield consumers from the energy shock, while the 2027 Budget emphasis on fiscal discipline has reduced the need to raise rates pre-emptively despite a string of pro-consumer measures.

Still, they expect a hike in the overnight policy rate (OPR) to 3.0 per cent in January as resilient economic growth and a modest pick-up in inflation strengthen the case for monetary policy normalisation.
Bank Negara maintained the OPR at 2.75 per cent at its final Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting of 2026 on Thursday.
The central bank said the latest indicators pointed to continued resilience in global growth, supported by strong global technology investment and stable labour markets.
Recent indicators showed sustained economic growth momentum in the third quarter of 2026, it added.
The central bank expects economic growth to exceed five per cent this year. The economy grew 5.3 per cent in the third quarter.
"Growth was underpinned by strong export performance amid sustained domestic demand. The solid growth momentum is expected to bring 2026 growth to above five per cent," it said in a statement.
HSBC senior Asean economist Yun Liu said Bank Negara appears to have gained more room to wait for the right moment before acting.

Stable inflation, a resilient ringgit and tighter fiscal management have given the central bank greater flexibility than many of its regional peers, whose currencies have come under sharper depreciation pressure.
"We continue to expect Bank Negara to raise the OPR by 25 basis points in the first quarter of 2027, taking it back to 3.0 per cent.
"The move is likely to be a pre-emptive step to get ahead of potentially stronger inflationary pressures next year, rather than the beginning of an aggressive tightening cycle," Yun said.
Unlike some regional central banks, Yun said Malaysia's next rate move is more likely to be a one-off policy normalisation than the start of a sustained series of hikes.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said Bank Negara's "status quo" decision reflected its optimism over Malaysia's economic outlook, with growth expected to remain healthy despite external uncertainties.
The balance of risks to the economy appeared broadly balanced, although inflationary pressures could warrant monetary policy normalisation in 2027, he added.
"We believe the 25 basis point hike could happen as early as January next year when the MPC meeting cycle commences in 2027," he told Business Times.
Afzanizam said monetary policy normalisation is apt to ensure interest rates send appropriate signals to the economy and encourage capital allocation towards more productive activities.
He said keeping interest rates too low when economic growth is above trend and inflation remains elevated could encourage speculative activities.
He also said Malaysia's economic resilience had remained evident despite fuel supply disruptions arising from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Afzanizam attributed this partly to Petroliam Nasional Bhd's ability to secure alternative fuel supplies outside the Strait of Hormuz through its extensive international business network.
He said the government's fiscal capacity to accommodate a higher fuel subsidy bill of RM40 billion had also helped cushion the impact on the economy.
The use of MyKad for targeted fuel subsidies had helped reduce leakages, allowing savings to be channelled back to Malaysians, he added.
Universiti Teknologi Mara senior lecturer Dr Mohamad Idham Md Razak said maintaining the OPR was appropriate given resilient domestic demand and relatively contained inflation.
He said there was no immediate need to tighten monetary policy as the current rate continued to provide stability for households and businesses while supporting consumption and investment.

"Stronger GDP growth does not automatically justify an interest rate increase, particularly when growth is supported by exports, investment and sustained domestic demand rather than excessive borrowing or overheating," he said.
Idham said any future adjustment to the OPR should be gradual and guided by inflation trends, wage developments, credit growth and domestic economic conditions rather than GDP growth alone.
He added that Bank Negara should distinguish between temporary supply-side inflation and persistent demand-driven pressures before considering monetary tightening.
"Supply-driven inflation requires targeted fiscal and supply-side measures, while sustained demand-driven inflation may warrant monetary tightening," he said.
Idham said the central bank should closely monitor whether higher costs were being passed on to consumers and becoming embedded in broader prices and wages.
He said the priority should be to prevent persistent inflation from eroding household purchasing power without unnecessarily weakening economic growth.
The MPC's first meeting in 2027 is scheduled for Jan 21.

ed4cb36e3269d56d: CELEBRATING happy occasions at work is far more important than many business owners and leaders realise. It is not simply about organising a lunch, cutting a cake, sharing a meal or having an occasional get-together. It is about creating a culture where people feel valued, appreciated and connected to the organisation they work for.

Every workplace has its challenges. Deadlines need to be met, targets achieved, expectations managed and problems resolved. The daily demands of work can be relentless, and employees can easily become consumed by routines and responsibilities. In such an environment, it is important to create moments that allow people to pause, enjoy themselves and celebrate the positives.
These moments matter.

As business owners, we sometimes forget that the emotional connection we have with our businesses is not necessarily shared by the people who work for us. We have invested our money, time, energy and often a significant part of our lives into building something. Naturally, we feel personally invested in its success. Our employees, however, may see it primarily as their place of work and a means of earning a living.

There is nothing wrong with that distinction. It is simply a reality of the employer-employee relationship. However, it also means that leaders must make a conscious effort to build a sense of belonging and shared purpose within their teams.
Celebrating happy occasions is one of the simplest and most effective ways of doing so.

It does not always have to be a major achievement or a significant milestone. Birthdays, anniversaries, festive occasions, personal achievements, new beginnings and even the completion of a particularly demanding period of work provide opportunities to bring people together. Sometimes, there does not even need to be a specific reason. A spontaneous team lunch or an afternoon of relaxation can be just as meaningful.
The underlying message is what matters: we recognise you, we appreciate you, and we enjoy having you as part of our team.

People want to feel that they matter. They want to know that their contribution is recognised and that they are more than just another employee on the payroll. When an organisation takes the time to celebrate its people, it communicates appreciation in a way that goes beyond salaries, benefits and formal performance reviews.

Importantly, these occasions also help build relationships beyond the confines of daily work. Employees get to interact with colleagues in a more relaxed environment, discover common interests and develop friendships. Hierarchies become less pronounced, conversations become more natural and people begin to see one another as individuals rather than simply colleagues performing different functions.

This is particularly important for building stronger teams. Good working relationships are rarely built exclusively through meetings, instructions and performance targets. They develop through shared experiences, mutual respect and the opportunity to connect on a more human level.

There is also a psychological benefit to celebrating positive occasions. Work can sometimes become repetitive, demanding and stressful. When people are constantly focused on what needs to be done next, they can lose sight of what has already been accomplished. Celebrations provide an opportunity to acknowledge progress, reinforce positive experiences and remind everyone that their efforts are contributing towards something worthwhile.

In fact, celebrating small victories can be just as important as recognising major achievements. Waiting until the end of the year or until a significant business milestone to show appreciation means missing countless opportunities to lift morale along the way.
Consistency is key.

Leaders should not treat team celebrations as an occasional public relations exercise or something to be introduced only when business is performing particularly well. They should become part of the organisation's culture. Even during challenging periods, finding affordable and thoughtful ways to bring people together can make a difference.

Of course, celebrations do not need to be extravagant. It is not about how much money is spent, the venue chosen or the elaborate arrangements made. It is about the thought, effort and sincerity behind the gesture. A simple meal shared together can sometimes achieve far more than an expensive corporate event.

There is another important consideration. When employees see their leaders making an effort to celebrate with them, they are reminded that leadership is not solely about giving instructions, demanding results and correcting mistakes. It is also about creating an environment where people feel comfortable, respected and motivated.

This does not mean compromising standards or blurring professional boundaries. Accountability, discipline and performance remain essential. However, a workplace can demand excellence while still being enjoyable, encouraging and supportive. In fact, the two should complement each other.

Business owners and leaders must understand that morale is not something that can be switched on when productivity begins to decline. It requires continuous attention. It is built through everyday interactions, genuine appreciation, open communication and, importantly, shared moments of happiness.

When people enjoy coming to work, feel connected to their colleagues and believe their contributions are appreciated, they are more likely to approach their responsibilities with enthusiasm and commitment. While celebrations alone cannot guarantee better performance or employee retention, they help create the conditions in which stronger engagement and teamwork can flourish.
Ultimately, people may forget the details of a particular working day, a difficult meeting or a demanding deadline. However, they are more likely to remember how an organisation made them feel.

As leaders, we spend considerable time thinking about how to improve our businesses, increase productivity and achieve better results. We should spend just as much time thinking about the people who make those results possible.
Celebrate the happy occasions. Acknowledge the little victories. Share a meal, have a laugh and create memories together.
Because building a successful organisation is not just about getting people to work together. It is about giving them reasons to enjoy being part of the journey.
And sometimes, the best investment a leader can make in team morale is simply taking the time to celebrate life with the people who help build the business.

5df0016aedc58be2: KUALA LUMPUR: Energy stocks took a beating on Bursa Malaysia on Thursday after crude oil prices slipped below US$100 a barrel for the first time in six weeks, amid growing expectations that the United States-Iran conflict could ease.
The sell-off dragged the Bursa Malaysia Energy Index down 21.45 points, or 2.59 per cent, to 806.47 from Wednesday's close of 827.92, even as the broader market rallied.
Of the 35 energy stocks listed on Bursa's Main Market, 17 ended lower, 11 were unchanged and only seven advanced.
Hengyuan Refining Company Bhd was among the hardest hit, plunging 57 sen, or 15.75 per cent, to RM3.05 as investors reassessed the outlook for oil prices and refining margins.

The sharp decline came after an extraordinary rally that had seen Hengyuan's shares more than quadruple this year, making the refiner one of the biggest beneficiaries of the oil price surge amid the US-Iran conflict.
Refiners such as Hengyuan can benefit from rising oil prices through inventory gains, although their profitability also depends on the difference between crude oil costs and refined fuel prices.
Its rival, Petron Malaysia Refining & Marketing Bhd, also declined, shedding nine sen, or 2.77 per cent, to RM3.16.
Other energy counters were not spared.
Enra Group Bhd tumbled eight sen, or 10.13 per cent, to 71 sen, while Hibiscus Petroleum Bhd lost 15 sen, or 7.28 per cent, to RM1.91.
Vantris Energy Bhd slipped 1.5 sen, or 5.56 per cent, to 25.5 sen.
Energy stocks bucked the broader market rally, with the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI rising 19.30 points, or 1.19 per cent, to 1,635.86 on improving global sentiment and easing geopolitical tensions.
Brent crude futures for January delivery had plunged 8.7 per cent to US$94.62 a barrel on Wednesday, their lowest level since Aug 31, as expectations grew that the US-Iran conflict could ease.
At press time on Thursday, Brent had recovered slightly, rising 0.53 per cent to US$95.12 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude slipped 0.25 per cent to US$87.90.
The retreat in oil prices followed the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections, which saw the party secure majorities in both chambers of Congress.
The outcome raised expectations that President Donald Trump's administration could face greater political pressure to bring the conflict with Iran to an end.
Investors have since begun reassessing the geopolitical risk premium built into crude prices, as the prospect of easing tensions reduces fears of supply disruptions in the Middle East.
The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections also weighed on technology stocks, amid concerns over tighter regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre-related companies.
Back home, the Bursa Malaysia Technology Index fell 3.17 points, or 4.27 per cent, to 71.14, making it the worst-performing sectoral index of the day.
The decline mirrored a sell-off in US AI and data centre-related stocks, as investors braced for greater regulatory scrutiny and potential changes to technology tax incentives.
Reports suggested investors were bracing for tighter regulatory oversight, possible rollbacks of technology tax incentives and greater antitrust scrutiny under a Democrat-controlled Congress.
Such measures could potentially slow the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, weighing on sentiment towards technology-related counters.

405210191184d203: LEVERKUSEN: AC Milan's Europa League hopes suffered a blow after they slumped to a 2-0 home defeat by Ferencvaros on Thursday, while Olympique de Marseille secured their first win of the campaign with a 1-0 victory at Bayer Leverkusen and Juventus beat AZ Alkmaar 2-1.
Milan slipped to their third defeat in four European matches and remain outside the playoff places.
The Hungarian side are tied on 12 points with Benfica and Bournemouth. Benfica, 3-1 winners over Lech Poznan, lead the standings on goal difference. Milan are a lowly 28th with three points.

Lenny Joseph put Ferencvaros ahead in the 52nd minute when he capitalised on a misplaced pass from goalkeeper Lorenzo Torriani and rolled the ball into an empty net before doubling the visitors' advantage 14 minutes later.
Ferencvaros held firm despite substitute Bamidele Yusuf being sent off in the 77th minute to preserve their clean sheet and all but extinguish Milan's late hopes of a comeback.
"I won't give up on this competition. As long as we're not mathematically out of it, we'll keep fighting in this competition, just as we do in the others," Milan coach Ruben Amorim said.
In Germany, Marseille earned their first three points of the competition thanks to a stunning solo effort from Amine Gouiri after a largely uneventful contest against Leverkusen.
The forward broke the deadlock in the 77th minute, collecting the ball near halfway before surging past defenders and firing a right-footed shot into the net.
Juventus prevailed 2-1 at AZ Alkmaar, with Teun Koopmeiners opening the scoring against a team captained by his brother Peer in the 19th minute.
The Dutch midfielder swept home a first-time finish after Randal Kolo Muani beat his marker down the right and cut the ball back to the edge of the area.

Kolo Muani doubled Juventus's lead eight minutes before halftime, punishing an error forced by the visitors' high press before cutting inside and drilling a low shot into the far corner. Mexx Meerdink pulled one back late on but AZ could not find an equaliser.
Juventus are fifth, level on 10 points with Union Saint Gilloise and Olympiacos.
Elsewhere, Daichi Kamada struck deep into stoppage time to rescue a 1-1 draw for Crystal Palace against Hoffenheim at Selhurst Park, cancelling out Alexander Prass's early opener for the German side.
Palace earned a point despite being reduced to 10 men after Adam Wharton was sent off in the 77th minute.
Bournemouth maintained their perfect record with a fourth consecutive win, coming from behind to beat Sparta Prague 3-1 away after the hosts were reduced to 10 men following Tobias Guddal's red card.
Ebrima Singhateh gave Sparta the lead before second-half goals from Tyler Adams, Evanilson and Rayan completed the comeback for the Premier League side.

3b45aebdfa0fa034: GENEVA: Countries announced US$405.8 million in new pledges Thursday towards supporting schooling for millions of crisis-affected children, the UN fund for education in emergencies said.
Education Cannot Wait (ECW) hailed the "remarkable start" towards its goal of raising US$600 million for its work over the next four years, at a time when global aid funding faces dramatic cuts.
Together with financial resources secured prior to Thursday's pledging conference, the fund said US$541.6 million had been promised, securing 90% of its target.
ECW estimates that 258 million school-aged children and teens are affected by conflicts and climate-related disasters around the world, including 93 million who are completely out of school.

"Education is not a privilege. It's not an act of kindness. It is a fundamental right every child, when born, should have," Sigrid Kaag, chair of ECW's high-level steering group, told Thursday's event.

Germany's pledge of 100 million euros (US$113 million) was the largest, followed by Britain's of 80 million pounds (US$108 million), and Norway at 600 million kroner (US$65 million), according to an ECW overview.
ECW builds schools, buys educational materials, provides daily meals and offers psychological support, among other services.
Since its founding a decade ago, it says it has reached more than 16 million crisis-affected children and trained nearly 300,000 teachers.
And it plans to reach another 10 million children during the 2027-2030 period -- half of them girls and including one million with disabilities, it said.
For children in crisis situations, education must not be "a luxury", ECW director Maysa Jalbout told Thursday's conference.
"It's oxygen... It bridges from the horrors of today to the promise of tomorrow."
bdbeddaf1213caa1: PETALING JAYA: Analysts believe PKR should let DAP contest the Batu Lintang seat in the upcoming Sarawak state election, saying the latter party enjoys greater support from the Chinese-majority electorate there.
Universiti Malaysia Sarawak’s Dick Lembang Dugun said PKR’s state chapter was almost non-existent, whereas DAP remains an outspoken party in the Bornean state’s political landscape.
“PKR is toothless today in speaking on Sarawakian issues and rights,” he told FMT.
“I believe it would be the right decision for DAP to contest Batu Lintang. Sarawak DAP is seen as being more functional compared with PKR in today's political environment in Sarawak.”
In the 2021 Sarawak polls, PKR contested 28 seats but failed to win a single one. Twenty-two of its candidates even lost their election deposits.
James Chin of the University of Tasmania said DAP has an advantage in Batu Lintang, thanks to its greater appeal among Chinese voters, who make up the majority in the constituency.
“Historically, DAP was successful in Batu Lintang, and Chinese voters, who comprise more than 80% of voters there, have shown they are more likely to vote for DAP rather than PKR,” he added.
Established in 1991, Batu Lintang used to be a stronghold of the Sarawak United Peoples’ Party (SUPP), a Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) component.
DAP wrested the seat in 2006, marking the opposition's first victory there, before making way for PKR's See Chee How, who comfortably retained it in 2011.

See won the seat again for PKR in 2016, but was sacked by the party in 2020 for going against the leadership. In 2021, he managed to defend the seat on a Parti Sarawak Bersatu (PSB) ticket, albeit with a very slim majority of 93 votes.
See secured 4,420 votes to SUPP’s Sih Hua Tong’s 4,327, while the PKR candidate, Cherishe Ng, only garnered 1,823 ballots.
See’s chances worse under SUPP
Amid speculation that See could be fielded by SUPP in the upcoming polls, Chin and Dugun both believe the three-term assemblyman’s chances could be worse as a GPS candidate.

Chin said voters in Batu Lintang have always been pro-opposition, citing the results of past state elections, including the 2021 polls which saw PSB—then an opposition party—emerge victorious despite a split in opposition votes.
In 2021, opposition votes were mostly split between PSB, PKR and Parti Bumi Kenyalang, which managed to secure 1,570 votes—a mere several hundred less than PKR.
“That shows how opposition-leaning voters in that seat are. So by joining the state government through SUPP, See has actually affected his chances,” said Chin.
Dugun said hardcore opposition supporters may show their unhappiness with See’s decision to join SUPP and contest as a GPS candidate, and may vote against him.
He said DAP must push the right narratives in its campaign to win over Chinese voters, adding that the party was more than capable of managing the issue.

“The Chinese tend to think that there must be a strong opposition in the state assembly to act as a check and balance. They know that the dominance of one coalition or party in government is unhealthy.”
Strong candidate will give DAP ‘very good’ chance

Acknowledging the advantage of See’s three-term incumbency, Chin said DAP would need to field a strong, prominent candidate to give itself the best chance of regaining Batu Lintang for Pakatan Harapan.

“If it puts up Sarawak DAP chairman Chong Chieng Jen or two-term Bandar Kuching MP Dr Kelvin Yii, or even Chong’s aide Michael Kong, who has been around for quite long, then they stand a very good chance,” he said.
9d28cf3de2c847f0: PETALING JAYA: Penganalisis berpendapat PKR wajar memberi laluan kepada DAP untuk bertanding di kerusi Batu Lintang pada PRN Sarawak akan datang, memandangkan parti itu mempunyai sokongan lebih besar dalam kalangan pengundi majoriti Cina di kawasan berkenaan.

“Dari segi sejarah, DAP pernah berjaya di Batu Lintang dan pengundi Cina, yang merangkumi lebih 80% daripada keseluruhan pengundi di situ, menunjukkan kecenderungan lebih tinggi untuk mengundi DAP berbanding PKR,” katanya.

See sekali lagi memenangi kerusi itu untuk PKR pada 2016, tetapi dipecat daripada parti pada 2020 kerana menentang kepimpinan. Pada 2021, beliau berjaya mempertahankan kerusi itu atas tiket Parti Sarawak Bersatu (PSB), meskipun dengan majoriti tipis hanya 93 undi.
See memperoleh 4,420 undi berbanding calon SUPP, Sih Hua Tong, yang mendapat 4,327 undi, manakala calon PKR, Cherishe Ng, hanya meraih 1,823 undi.
Peluang See lebih tipis jika bersama SUPP

Di sebalik spekulasi bahawa See mungkin diketengahkan oleh SUPP pada PRN akan datang, Chin dan Dugun berpandangan peluang bekas Adun tiga penggal itu mungkin lebih tipis jika bertanding sebagai calon GPS.

Pada 2021, undi pembangkang kebanyakannya berpecah antara PSB, PKR dan Parti Bumi Kenyalang, yang berjaya memperoleh 1,570 undi, hanya beberapa ratus undi kurang berbanding PKR.
“Ini menunjukkan pengundi di kerusi itu cenderung menyokong pembangkang. Jadi, dengan menyertai kerajaan negeri menerusi SUPP, See sebenarnya telah menjejaskan peluang kemenangannya,” kata Chin.
Dugun berkata, penyokong tegar pembangkang mungkin melahirkan rasa tidak puas hati terhadap keputusan See menyertai SUPP dan bertanding sebagai calon GPS, malah mungkin mengundinya.
Beliau berkata, DAP perlu mengetengahkan naratif yang tepat sepanjang kempen untuk meraih sokongan pengundi Cina, sambil menambah bahawa parti itu sememangnya berkemampuan menangani isu berkenaan.

“Pengundi Cina cenderung berpendapat bahawa perlu ada pembangkang yang kuat dalam Dewan Undangan Negeri (DUN) untuk berperanan sebagai semak dan imbang. Mereka tahu dominasi satu gabungan atau parti dalam kerajaan adalah tidak sihat.”
Calon berwibawa beri peluang ‘sangat cerah’ kepada DAP

Mengakui kelebihan See sebagai penyandang selama tiga penggal, Chin berkata DAP perlu mengetengahkan calon yang kuat dan dikenali ramai bagi memberikan peluang terbaik kepada Pakatan Harapan (PH) untuk merampas semula kerusi Batu Lintang.

“Jika DAP meletakkan pengerusinya di Sarawak, Chong Chieng Jen, atau Ahli Parlimen Bandar Kuching dua penggal, Dr Kelvin Yii, mahupun pembantu Chong, Michael Kong, yang sudah lama berkecimpung dalam politik, parti itu mempunyai peluang yang sangat cerah,” katanya.
99789fff746e209d: IPOH: For P Ravi, preparing for Deepavali involves more than decorating the house and getting ready to welcome guests. It also means getting into the car and driving more than 200km from Kuala Lumpur in search of the snacks his family has come to associate with the festival.

For the past six years, the 56-year-old has made Kampung Kacang Putih in Buntong, Ipoh, one of his regular pre-Deepavali stops - usually arriving about a week before the celebration to stock up on favourites such as murukku and tapioca chips.
“I leave Kuala Lumpur at around 7.30am and it takes more than two hours to get here,” he said. “It is not a burden because this place has been my family’s choice for the past six years.”

Ravi, who was born in Melaka, usually spends between RM500 and RM1,000 at several shops in the area. Much of what he buys eventually ends up on the table for guests, while some is packed up for relatives, neighbours and colleagues.

For his family, that sharing has become as important as the snacks themselves. “It has become a family tradition every time we celebrate Deepavali, as a way of strengthening ties with colleagues and neighbours,” he said.

K Gaayathri, 30, also makes it a point to buy her festive snacks in Buntong. The KL resident said the sheer variety available there has made the area a dependable stop whenever the Festival of Lights approaches.
For her, serving kacang putih to visitors is simply part of the celebration. “Deepavali just does not feel complete without such snacks being served to guests,” she said.

That sentiment helps explain why Kampung Kacang Putih becomes especially lively in the weeks before the festival. At DNS Kacang Putih, manager S Sathis Kumar said preparations begin about two weeks before Deepavali to cope with the seasonal rush.
Demand, he said, can rise by around 60% compared with ordinary periods, with customers coming from different communities and all parts of the country.
“Among the products that are in high demand are spicy mixed murukku, kuih loyang, round murukku, kuih batu, as well as various types of sweets and ladoo,” he said.

Buntong’s connection with kacang putih stretches back around 60 years, and many of the businesses in the area have been passed down through generations. What began as a local speciality has since become familiar to Malaysians well beyond Ipoh, particularly during festive seasons.

The selection reflects that long history. Alongside better-known favourites such as murukku and tapioca chips are pakoda, sivel, dal, aulu, poori, Sri Lankan pakoda, omom, kadalai and kacang susu - giving visitors plenty to choose from before heading home.
For Ravi, however, the attraction is not simply the variety or price: after six years of making the same journey, the drive to Buntong has become woven into his family’s Deepavali preparations.
Indeed, the snacks they bring home are part of the pleasure of opening the door, setting the table, and sharing the celebration with others.

f49af9c11655c170: ABU DHABI: Rory McIlroy incurred a two-stroke penalty at the end of his opening round at the Abu Dhabi Championship on Thursday for a rules infringement, with Italy's Francesco Laporta storming into the lead.
Officials ruled that McIlroy improved his lie on the 12th hole when he appeared to press down grass behind his ball with his club before chipping at Yas Links.

He initially made a double bogey on the par-four hole, but that later became an eight as he posted a two-under 70, leaving him eight shots off the pace set by Laporta in his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title.
"There's no intent. I play by the rules," said McIlroy. "I try to do everything that I can to never end up in these positions."
"But just by looking at the video, like it doesn't look very good," he added. "Obviously that wasn't my intent. I'm just trying to get a feel for the lie.

"I guess the technical term for the rule is if you press down on the piece (of grass). I don't feel like I pressed down. But at the same time, I don't want the perception of, like, people thinking like I got away with something either.
"So I'm happy to take a 2-shot penalty and move on and move into tomorrow."
Laporta fired a bogey-free 62 featuring eight birdies and an eagle to open up a three-shot lead over Jon Rahm, Bernd Wiesberger and Sam Bairstow.
Rahm, making his tournament debut after agreeing a departure from LIV Golf last month, had not played since September following the birth of his daughter.
The 36-year-old Laporta is seeking his first European Tour win while also bidding to climb into the 50-player field for the season-ending Tour Championship next week in Dubai.
"Everything was just going like a video game, like just hitting shots straight and making some putts and just giving myself opportunities," said Laporta. "I'm very happy about that."
Current Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra matched McIlroy with an opening 70, while second-placed Patrick Reed struggled and finished two over par for the day.
376698c8e493c0de: LAGOS: A Nigerian court Thursday declared invalid the nomination of Atiku Abubakar as the presidential candidate for the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC), just two months before the country's elections.

The party, which accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of involvement in the lawsuit, will appeal, its spokesman said -- but the ruling creates legal headaches for Abubakar and uncertainty for voters with the Jan 16 vote around the corner.
The ADC, one of the main opposition parties trying to oust President Bola Tinubu, has been mired in lawsuits around its leadership, which have now ensnared its 2027 nominee.

Thursday's decision is "another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition and deny Nigerians the right to choose their leaders in the forthcoming general elections", ADC spokesman Bolaji Abdullahi said in a statement.
Earlier this year, the federal government backed a separate lawsuit over the ADC's eligibility to contest the 2027 vote in Africa's most populous country.
Tinubu spokesman Daniel Bwala told AFP the APC "is not involved at all" in the suit over the party's leadership that sparked Thursday's decision.
Nigerian media reported that the federal high court in Abuja overturned the current leadership of the ADC by David Mark, who has been fighting with Nafiu Bala Gombe leading the party.
In ruling against Mark, the nomination of Abubakar -- made while he was at the party's helm -- has also been tossed, Nigerian media reported.
'Excessive' litigation marred 2023 poll
The decision was handed down a day after Abubakar launched his campaign with a rally in Sokoto state.
"The timing of this judgment is no coincidence," Abubakar said in a statement.
He did not address the ruling at a rally in northwestern Kebbi state later that day.

Sadiq Ibrahim Dasin, the ADC's chairman in Abubakar's home state of Adamawa, told AFP that the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) "has not raised a finger on the qualification of any of our candidates".
"We should continue with the campaign," he said.
INEC did not respond to a request for comment.
During Nigeria's 2023 poll, EU election observers said "excessive pre-election litigation exposed pervasive intraparty conflicts".

"Among at least 1,200 court cases, some were perceived as politicised, others too technical, while some overlapped with the polls," the observation mission's report said, warning the suits risked "undermining trust in the democratic process".
Also Thursday, the party of Peter Obi, the other major opposition candidate, claimed its meetings were being disrupted by the APC, citing multiple last-minute hotel cancellations in Abuja.
"This is not democracy," Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress said in a statement.
Bwala denied the accusations, saying "hotels in Abuja are privately owned".

If Abubakar cannot run, that would leave the election without any major candidate from the north -- a potentially disruptive development in a country where regional representation is a politically sensitive issue.
"The judiciary, to some extent, is allowing themselves to be used by the politicians, the ruling party," said Abubakar supporter Sunday Joseph, speaking to AFP in Adamawa state.
"They are afraid of Atiku," he said, using the candidate's first name, as he is often referred to by supporters.
Abubakar came second in the 2023 presidential contest.
Obi, who called Thursday's ruling against Abubakar "shocking", finished third.

Abubakar, on his seventh go at leading Nigeria, promised "to make sure that security is restored in every part of this country" at a rally Wednesday in restive Sokoto state, which is under pressure from both jihadists and non-ideological criminal gangs.
He also promised to reinstate fuel subsidies as voters grind through a brutal cost of living crisis following economic reforms passed under Tinubu.

2bfe2d045069bfad: SAO PAULO: Lewis Hamilton will celebrate the 400th Formula One start of a glittering career at this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with rivals hailing the seven-time world champion's longevity, speed and enduring hunger for success.

The 41-year-old Briton, Formula One's most successful driver with a record 106 race wins and 105 pole positions, reaches the milestone still competing at the front and showing little sign of slowing down.
"It's kind of crazy. I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," Hamilton told reporters on Thursday.

"I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week (in Mexico). I still have the pace, I still have the speed, I still have the dedication, which is most important, and the focus."

Hamilton is third in the drivers' championship, two points behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen. He claimed his record-extending 105th pole position in Mexico last week but finished second after a clash with Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc.
Hamilton made his Formula One debut with McLaren in 2007 and won his first championship a year later.

He secured six more titles with Mercedes between 2014 and 2020 before joining Ferrari last season. Only Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso, 45, has made more grand prix starts, with the double world champion closing in on 450 races.

While Hamilton said the round number itself was not especially meaningful to him, he acknowledged the significance of reaching it in Brazil, a country where he enjoys enormous popularity and was made an honorary citizen in 2022.
"For me, that number is kind of irrelevant. But it's beautiful to be able to have that here in Brazil," he said.

McLaren's Lando Norris said Hamilton's career remained a benchmark for younger drivers hoping to build similar longevity, while adding performances this season had dispelled any doubts about his competitiveness.
"I think it's a pretty incredible achievement for him to fight for this long. He's a good inspiration for many of us," said the 2025 world champion.
"When I look at Lewis, he makes me not very happy to have only won one championship.

"But that's in a good way that I can look at him and see him and his age, his form, and makes me believe more than ever that I could fight for many, many more years, and that's something I look forward to doing."
Audi's Nico Hulkenberg also praised Hamilton's determination to continue competing despite having already surpassed nearly every major record in the sport.
"He could have easily retired many times and said, 'that's enough'," Hulkenberg, 39, said. "Fair play and respect to him that he still puts in the work, still wants this, and still does this."
cac1966d2368512b: A couple of billion for the thoughts of United’s Politburo at half-time in the Roma match on Tuesday.
Two-nil down. Roof leaking. Ritual demonstrations.
Tennis balls on the pitch at the start. It looked like ‘game, set and match’ for Michael Carrick.
And unsavoury songs about the owners throughout. Big Jim was in his tax haven but heard enough not to stand for Mayor of Manchester any time soon.
We wonder: were phone calls made? Did someone get the nod? Would the trigger be pulled at the whistle or after Sunday’s match with Villa?
Then a soft penalty. A calamitous encroachment. A retake and a glimmer. Then an Italian air-shot. And finally, a winner.
Was the equaliser THE moment? Would Roma defender Leonardo Balerdi’s name echo through United’s future like Mark Robins has in their past?
(Robins poked home the scruffy goal that is said to have saved Sir Alex Ferguson from the sack in 1990.)
United got out of jail then and now we wonder if this could be the unlikeliest of turning points?
After all, football history is full of them.
But there are already two reality checks: wonderkid JJ Gabriel is going to Real Madrid and Unai Emery is staying with Villa.
The Spaniard had, according to sources, been the choice to succeed Carrick, and matters came to a head as the teams meet on Sunday.
Uncanny coincidence? Fate taking a hand? Or the fixture list again revealing its wicked sense of humour?
Whatever, it forced Villa’s owners to move quickly to reward the man who has transformed their club with a whopping new contract.
So, it seems that the second-half comeback won’t save Carrick’s job, but merely provide a short stay of execution.
Could the presence of a Glazer – Edward, the lesser-spotted brother to the rare birds, Avram and Joel – mean the family is getting involved in football matters?
As the vitriol about the owners, with Ratcliffe getting his share, plumbs new depths, many observers recall him saying that if he had to take what the Glazers do, he would walk out.
Well, in recent weeks, the terms for his departure have been met.
He may not have been serious, but for all his stone-hearted culling of staff, he doesn’t possess the Glazers’ ‘Hazmat suit’ of distance.
But quitting now would leave unfinished business, and his reputation in tatters.
And who on earth would want to buy it? Besides the billion and a half debt, both the team and the stadium need that much spending on them.
Carrick gave Old Trafford’s atmosphere credit for the comeback. But the famous old stadium still has to be fixed.
Tax exile Ratcliffe wants to build a new one for his legacy – with taxpayers’ money, of course.
Plans have stalled as the team has sunk.
And fixing the latter has become more urgent.
After Emery, next on the list are Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann.
For instant impact, you’d go for Conte who does turn teams around quickly.
Not many have won titles in both England (one with Chelsea) and Italy (five), and he gave it a shot at Spurs.
He also wants the job. On the two countries’ respective finances, he says: “In Italy we shoot with pistols, in England they have bazookas.” He wants a bazooka.
Whether Ratcliffe or the Glazers would give him one is doubtful. Some writers have said he wouldn’t survive his first press conference.

But if United feel they want some fire after Carrick’s icy unflappability, they would follow an old Italian proverb, ‘Fat Pope, Thin Pope’ – about maintaining a balance between a liberal and a conservative.
United have not done that with their managers post-Fergie. Nagelsmann would be a strange choice, but young German bosses are in vogue with Fabian Hürzeler impressing at Brighton.
He would bring a bit of style in keeping with United’s reputation for flair.
But he never quite lived up to his sensational early success with Hoffenheim, either with Bayern Munich or the national team.
And he would be a rookie in the EPL, whereas Howe is a veteran.
However, the Englishman, who might be considered a safer bet, has a reputation for building from the back – a sensible method but not the ‘attack, attack, attack’ that fans demand.
Whoever takes over, assuming Carrick doesn’t engineer another comeback win at Villa, will have a list of signings for the January transfer window.
In terms of need, United could be the biggest spenders but will Ratcliffe – if he’s still there – cough up?
He’ll have to agree to busting his own budget or he won’t be getting anyone worth his salt. Players are needed all over the park except midfield.
United will get a look at how to build a club on Sunday when they visit Villa Park. A revamped young side will be gunning for them and the manager they wanted will be plotting their demise
Emery has found his perfect team and wants to build a dynasty there.
A 3-0 defeat at Barcelona was a reminder of how far they still need to travel.
But at least the new North Stand is taking shape, unlike the ‘ground under repair’ that is Old Trafford.
Progress all around. More than enough for Emery to turn down the poisoned chalice of United.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect the views of FMT.
8424b8cbc8e88fa1: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
One connection, works every time, needs no retries

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
fe701c18583be8bf: TORONTO: LIV Golf, which shook up world golf in 2022, will liquidate after losing big-name players and the financing it needed to stay alive, the breakaway circuit said on Thursday.
Throughout the wind-down process, LIV Golf said it would remain open to, and continue to consider any offers from third parties that could get more value from its assets.

"In light of the current circumstances, we believe shifting toward an orderly wind-down is the most responsible path forward for the League at this time," Gene Davis and Jon Zinman of LIV Golf board’s special committee said in a press release.
The future of LIV Golf had been in question after the circuit lost financial support from Saudi Arabia'sdeep-pocketed Public Investment Fund beyond the now-completed 2026 season.

LIV Golf had secured US$300 million of potential financing from BC Partners to allow the staging of tournaments in 2027 but the plan was scrapped after a number of notable players opted not to commit to the league.

“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," a BC Partners spokesperson said.
"While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders."
Bitter legal battles

Leading golfers, such as former world number one Jon Rahm, announced their departures from LIV Golf after it filed for bankruptcy protection in September. Rahm is planning to play on the Europe-based DP World Tour in 2027. The US-based PGA Tour has banned LIV Golf players for one year from their last appearance on the rebel circuit.

LIV Golf sent shockwaves through the sport when it burst onto the scene in June 2022 with a mix of star power and past-their-prime veterans who signed lucrative contracts to appear in tournaments with no cuts and guaranteed paydays.

The PGA Tour refused to let members compete in LIV Golf events, and suspended defecting golfers who included major champions such as Bryson DeChambeau, Dustin Johnson, Brooks Koepka and Phil Mickelson.
That meant golf's biggest names did not compete against each other outside of the four majors that are governed by separate bodies.

Those suspensions triggered a wave of bitter legal battles, including an antitrust lawsuit in which DeChambeau, Mickelson and others accused the PGA Tour of using monopoly power to penalise independent contractors.
Critics decried LIV Golf as a vehicle for Saudi Arabia to improve its reputation and deflect criticism of its human rights record. The ​Saudi government denies accusations of human rights abuses.

American golfer Peter Malnati, who served as a player director on the PGA Tour Policy Board from 2023-25, learned about LIV's plan for liquidation during his media availability after completing his opening round at a PGA Tour event in Mexico.
"I'm not an economics major, I'm not even business savvy ... but it didn't take too much to see that that wasn't a viable economic model." Malnati told reporters.
"If their goal was truly to be additive to the golf space, they went about it in a strange way. If their goal was to be disruptive, they did a heck of a job."
'Round of a lifetime'
In June 2023, the PGA Tour and the Saudi fund again stunned the world of golf by announcing a framework to form one unified commercial entity and end the litigation.
As talks stalled, the PGA Tour even enlisted Donald Trump in the hope the US president, an avid golfer whose courses have hosted multiple LIV events, could broker a deal.

The PGA Tour ultimately rejected the Saudi fund's US$1.5 billion investment proposal, which was contingent on LIV Golf remaining intact and PIF governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan serving as co-chair of the PGA Tour Enterprises board.
In late April, after pouring more than US$5 billion into LIV Golf, the Saudi fund said the circuit no longer fitted its investment strategy, and it would pull funding after the 2026 season.

"Building a global platform designed to bring new, younger, and more diverse fans to the sport of golf has been the round of a lifetime for all of us," LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil said on Thursday. "LIV Golf was fun, demanding, inspiring, at times challenging — but always rewarding."
4b14548d2bcab5e5: WASHINGTON: The US on Thursday imposed sanctions targeting Cuba's oil and electronics sectors, as well as the daughter of the head of the island's largest military-controlled business conglomerate, the state department said.
The new wave of sanctions includes, for the first time, two Chinese companies, accused of supplying Cuba's military with electronics and other security equipment.

"Cuba's ruling elite hoards the island's energy and shipping resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, fuel shortages, and a stagnant economy," said the state department in a statement.

Since January, Washington has launched a devastating set of new sanctions and an oil blockade against Cuba, crippling the island nation's economy and leading to widespread blackouts and shortages of necessities.

US president Donald Trump has hinted at launching a military intervention to overthrow the island's Communist ruling party, and last month the US secretary of state urged Cubans to work with US intelligence services.
Among the companies sanctioned on Thursday was Cyprus-registered Caroil, which operates three oil tankers, and Panama-registered Tentacool.
Also added to the sanctions list was Any Rodriguez Lastres, the daughter of the already-designated chief of Grupo De Administracion Empresarial SA (GAESA), a military conglomerate.
GAESA is Cuba's largest business conglomerate, with interests in all sectors of the country's economy, and it was already sanctioned in May of this year.
The new sanctions also listed two Cuban state-owned companies, CubaElectronica and Tecnosime.
The Chinese companies sanctioned on Thursday include state-owned China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and private firm Beijing H&C Technologies.

36428461fcaa3a4e: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Malaysians who pay for ChatGPT or other AI apps will be able to claim the cost as tax relief under Budget 2027, one of several measures proposed to get more people and businesses using artificial intelligence (AI).

The budget also adds 100,000 free AI subscriptions for young people and sets aside RM30 million to help small businesses adopt the technology, alongside longer-term spending on skills, research and a sovereign AI cloud, as part of the government’s goal of making Malaysia an AI nation by 2030.
Who gets the additional 100,000 free AI subscriptions?
The existing AI Untuk Rakyat programme offers 100,000 Malaysians aged 18 to 30 three months’ free access to selected AI apps once they pass six learning modules on the Rakyat Digital portal.
Current providers are YTL AI Labs, Alibaba and Google.
Budget 2027 adds another 100,000 places and brings in more apps, including ChatGPT.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the expansion followed a strong response to the first round.
What support is available for businesses adopting AI?
The government has allocated RM30 million through the Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation (MDEC) to help 4,000 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) adopt AI and automate their operations.
MDEC is a government agency responsible for driving Malaysia’s digital economy.
Its work includes helping businesses adopt digital technologies, supporting digital start-ups and attracting investments into the country’s digital sector.
For smaller businesses, adopting AI can involve more than subscribing to a chatbot, while financial support could help businesses that lack the resources to implement these systems independently.
The programme will also train and certify 5,000 AI professionals, helping to develop the workforce needed to support wider adoption.
However, the RM30 million allocation should not be interpreted as a fixed grant for every business.
The amount available to individual applicants, qualifying expenses and application requirements will depend on the programme’s implementation details.
Businesses interested in participating should look out for further announcements from MDEC.
Can you claim tax relief for ChatGPT and other AI subscriptions?
Yes, Budget 2027 proposes expanding individual lifestyle tax relief to include subscriptions to AI software and applications.
As specified under the Finance Ministry’s tax measures, the relief will cover subscriptions for personal use, as well as those purchased for a spouse or child.
This means taxpayers who pay for eligible AI services, including subscription-based applications, could claim the expenses when filing their income tax returns.
However, this is not a separate tax relief ceiling for AI subscriptions.
The proposed expansion means taxpayers will be able to include eligible AI subscription fees alongside other qualifying expenses, subject to the overall RM2,500 ceiling.
This expansion is proposed to take effect from the 2027 year of assessment, meaning it will apply to eligible expenses incurred in 2027 when taxpayers file their returns in 2028.
The measure is intended to encourage digital literacy and wider adoption of AI technology by making subscription costs more affordable.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Budget 2027 proposes expanding the existing RM2,500 individual lifestyle tax relief to cover eligible AI software and application subscriptions from the 2027 year of assessment. — AFP pic
How much is being spent on AI skills and research?
The government is allocating almost RM15 million to AI Malaysia Berhad to strengthen a safe and ethical AI ecosystem, with a target of developing 200,000 AI-skilled workers.
AI Malaysia Berhad is Malaysia’s national lead agency for AI, established under the Digital Ministry to coordinate the country’s AI development and implementation.
The initiative reflects the need to equip Malaysians with skills relevant to industries increasingly using AI.
These capabilities could include understanding how AI systems work, applying them to business operations and developing technology responsibly.
Separately, RM6 billion will be allocated across ministries for research, development and commercialisation of innovations.
This is a broader allocation rather than funding exclusively for AI, intended to support research and technological development that contribute to Malaysia’s wider innovation ecosystem.
Safeguards for data
Under Budget 2027, the government is planning a sovereign AI cloud to ensure the public’s data and the country’s strategic information remain under Malaysian control.
AI systems rely on computing infrastructure to process information, run applications and, in some cases, train models.
Cloud services allow organisations to access this computing capacity remotely rather than maintaining all the necessary equipment themselves.
A sovereign AI cloud aims to give Malaysia greater control over the infrastructure and data used in these operations.
This is particularly relevant when government agencies and businesses handle sensitive information, including personal records and confidential commercial data.
Protection will also depend on access controls, cybersecurity measures and rules governing how information can be used.
According to Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, the initiative would be managed by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) and the Communications Ministry.
bd1bc85d93760e11: NEW YORK, Nov 6 — Voters in dozens of American cities approved restrictions or outright bans on data centres during Tuesday’s midterm elections, in one of the clearest signals that a groundswell of anger over the AI boom has cut across political divides.
“Democrat, Republican, that didn’t matter,” said Alisha Lange, a farmer from Piqua, Ohio. “People want their town back.”

She was one of the driving forces behind the grassroots group Save Piqua, which advocated for a ban on data centres with a capacity of more than 25 megawatts, effectively ruling out any large-scale project.

The ban passed in a ballot measure on Tuesday and now jeopardises the construction of a data centre worth more than US$1 billion (RM4.04 billion) planned by Meta, even though the project had already been approved.
The 42-year-old farmer wept with joy when she learned that two-thirds of voters approved the measure.

“We’re just a little farm town, and we would much rather just have a cornfield or have some sort of industry that provides an income to a larger amount of people,” she said, referring to the relatively small number of jobs that data centres tend to create after they’re built.

While ballots are still being counted around the country, more than three dozen local measures have already passed that resulted in tighter regulations for data centres, according to consulting firm Redbud Consulting.
The outcomes add to restrictions already imposed by nearly 600 jurisdictions across the country, according to Electric Choice, including entire states in some cases, like New York and Texas.

Meta isn’t the only big tech company spending billions on data center construction — Google, Microsoft and Amazon are also investing heavily in an effort to meet growing demand for their AI products and services.
Last straw
In Ottawa, a small town near Kansas City, residents also overwhelmingly approved a ban on large data centres.
“We’re not for sale,” Michael Lewis said.
Lewis is a member of a grassroots organization called Ottawa United, and ran for Congress this cycle as a Democrat, though he lost on Tuesday to the incumbent Republican.
“You can dangle some money in our face, it doesn’t mean we’re going to give away our resources and deal with the environmental issues that stem from” data centres, he said.

In Janesville, Wisconsin, a majority of city council members were initially open to a proposal from developer Viridian, which was ready to put US$8 billion on the table to build a data center on a former General Motors site that closed in 2008.
But communities are starting to ask for more than job creation potential and total investment when scrutinising new construction projects.
“What we’re seeing now is that there is a much broader range of indicators that indicates a good project or a bad one,” Cathy Erdman, a member of Janesville for Responsible Development, said.

A project’s impacts on local tax streams, broader infrastructure, quality of life and other land uses “can be equal to or greater in importance than the number of jobs or just the dollar amount in capital investment,” Erdman said.
Under pressure, the city council ultimately rejected the Viridian project in June, then adopted a one-year moratorium, before a majority of voters on Tuesday backed new restrictions.
Any large-scale project on the former General Motors site must now be approved by referendum.
While some in Janesville went to the polls to express their outright opposition to data centres, others simply wanted “more transparency,” Erdman said.
“I believe that is the general consensus community-wide: that that project, in particular, was very poorly handled by the powers that be,” the 45-year-old activist said.
In Piqua, the Meta project was the last straw, Lange said, leading to the removal of two city council members and the mayor.
In Ottawa, Lewis will remember the data center protest joining forces across the political aisle with a Republican official to win a court order for a referendum.
“It was wonderful,” he said. “That was the true meaning of community right there.” — AFP
0c3961ad353536bb: BANGKOK, Nov 6 — A giant rodent weighing around 30 kilograms roamed what is now southern Thailand 33 to 35 million years ago, scientists said, after identifying a previously unknown species from two fossilised teeth.
The ancient animal, which one geologist on the team called a “giant rat”, was among the largest known from the Paleogene period, offering new clues about how early rodents evolved to enormous sizes.
The findings, published yesterday in the journal Scientific Reports, were based on a molar and an incisor discovered in 2004 at a coal mine in southern Krabi province.
Pannipa Tian, a geologist with Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources who found the incisor, said she initially misidentified the fossil because of its “unusually large size”.
“At first, I thought it was a bone. I showed it to my supervisor, who told me it was a giant rat’s tooth,” Pannipa, 51, told AFP today.
The cream-coloured fossil stood out against the dark coal deposits, while another expedition member found the dark-coloured molar the same day.
The Krabi basin has previously yielded fossils of ancient primates, carnivores and hoofed mammals.
But at the time of the discovery, the team lacked sufficient evidence and technology to identify the species.
More than two decades later, researchers from Thailand, France and Canada were able to do so through detailed analysis of the teeth.
The animal weighed around 30 kilograms — an estimated half as much as a large capybara, the world’s largest living rodent, they said.
Unlike the South American capybara, however, the prehistoric rodent belonged to the now-extinct Ischyromyidae family, one of the earliest major groups of rodents.
“It tells a lot about the diversity of life in the past,” Pannipa said, suggesting that ancient rodents may have evolved in what is now Thailand before spreading to other parts of the world.
But with only two teeth recovered, the animal’s appearance, diet and behaviour remain unknown.
The species was named Yakamys sirindhornae in honour of Thailand’s Princess Sirindhorn, a supporter of scientific and palaeontological research. — AFP
43ef69f1a502b004: KHARTOUM, Nov 5 — Nearly three and a half years into Sudan’s unrelenting war, soaring costs and a nosediving currency have left people like Sawsan Mahmoud struggling to afford even the most basic staple — bread.
Most bakeries in the capital Khartoum have shut their doors because of surging wheat prices and fuel shortages.
Mahmoud, 44, says she and her husband now spend their combined salaries on bread alone.
“The situation has become unbearable,” the mother of three said. “We’ve reduced the amount of bread we eat and now only have it with one meal a day.”
“We have to set aside 900,000 pounds (RM356) a month to buy it. That’s almost my salary and my husband’s combined.”
The price of a loaf in Khartoum has doubled from 250 to 500 Sudanese pounds over the past week.

International organisations have been sounding the alarm over the possible spread of famine, already declared in parts of the country, while around 20 million people suffer from severe food insecurity.
In one of the few bakeries still operating in the capital, Abir Mohammed complained that “we used to eat bread with all our daily meals; now we can’t do that”.
Sudan imports most of its wheat, making prices vulnerable to the deterioration of the local currency.

Over the past month, the Sudanese pound has lost about 25 per cent of its value against the dollar, hitting a record low of more than 10,500 pounds to the dollar before recovering slightly to around 10,200 on Wednesday.
The dollar was worth 500 Sudanese pounds in 2023, when the war broke out between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the army.
‘No flour’
Inside Mohammed al-Fateh’s bakery in Khartoum, workers mixed flour, water and yeast into a thick dough, which they divided into round discs and slid into the oven on long wooden paddles.
Within minutes, the dough turns into the traditional flatbread that forms an essential part of Sudanese meals.
“Many bakeries have closed because there is no flour in the market,” Fateh said, adding: “You can spend a whole day or two at the distribution centre and still come back empty-handed.”
In Khartoum’s southern Al-Azhari neighbourhood, Mutawakil Ahmed Babiker is struggling to keep his bakery afloat after the price of flour doubled.
He also pointed to “power cuts that have forced us to buy fuel for the generator”.
“Most likely I will close the bakery,” he said.
“We sell a loaf of bread for 500 pounds, which is less than its cost, but I can’t raise the price because of people’s circumstances.”
Khartoum and parts of eastern Sudan are suffering widespread power outages after repeated drone attacks on power stations.
Across the capital, Sudanese have returned to lining up outside public kitchens, waiting for free meals.
Many of these kitchens had stopped operating when the army retook control of the capital and expelled the RSF in March 2025.
The Ombada Emergency Room in Omdurman, which coordinates community kitchens in the area, has warned that “the circle of need is expanding to include thousands of families and displaced people”.
It cautioned of “a shortage of food supplies and soaring prices, making access to even a single daily meal a dream”.
Poverty rates in Sudan have soared to 80 per cent, according to data from the central bureau of statistics, while inflation registered an astounding 99 per cent last year.
‘No fuel’
Outside Khartoum, most wheat supplies arrive in the form of aid, but fuel shortages and spiralling prices, along with road closures due to the fighting, prevent deliveries.
The war has divided the country into rival zones of influence: the army holds Khartoum and central and eastern Sudan, while the RSF controls the vast Darfur region in the west and parts of the south.
More than 200,000 people in South Kordofan and North Darfur states are experiencing famine, according to UN-backed reports that also warn it could spread to eight cities by 2027.
The falling currency has further weakened the government’s ability to buy fuel, most of which the country imports.
Speaking to AFP from his car outside a petrol station, civil servant Yasser Mohammed said: “I’ve been here since six in the morning.”
By 4pm, he said he still had not obtained any petrol and had missed a day of work.
In an Omdurman market, where business was slow, Al-Muradi Awad complained of poor living conditions as he shopped for groceries.
“The nutritional value of each meal has declined,” Awad said.
“The price of a kilogram of meat ranges between 50,000 and 70,000 pounds. If you could previously afford to buy two kilograms of meat, today you will buy 125 grams.” — AFP
6e91f7aa3ad01462: KHAN YUNIS, Nov 6 — Above a maze of tents in a crowded displacement camp in Gaza, homemade wind turbines made from scrap metal and salvaged debris spin in the sea breeze, bringing electricity to struggling Palestinians.

In the southern Khan Yunis camp, Kamal Al-Dabary, a former engineering student, has put his skills to work for families who, like most Gazans, live in displacement with no direct access to the tiny territory’s shattered power grid.

According to the World Bank, more than 90 per cent of Gaza’s power generation and distribution capacity was destroyed in April 2026, much of it in Israeli strikes that devastated homes and infrastructure.
Sitting on the ground, Dabary tinkered with electrical wires, metal parts and basic tools on a plastic table.
After carefully twisting cables together and testing them with a multimeter, a small bulb flickered on, then another, signalling that the current was flowing.
“When solar panels were still relatively affordable, we bought one and kept moving it around to follow the sun,” the 60-year-old, displaced by the fighting between Israel and Hamas, told AFP.
The war was triggered by the Palestinian Islamist movement’s deadly October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
But after three years of war, prices have soared as aid and commercial supplies trickled into Gaza through crossings tightly controlled by Israel.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Kamel al-Dabbari, (right) who developed a wind turbine that generates electricity using scraps, points to mobile phones charging inside a camp for displaced Palestinians in Khan Yunis, in the southern Gaza Strip on November 3, 2026. — AFP pic
A single solar panel now costs at least 15,000 shekels (nearly MR20,235), putting it out of reach for most Gazans, Dabary said.
‘Changed everything’
“We haven’t had work or income for three years,” he added.
“That’s when the idea of a wind turbine came to mind. Why not harness the wind? So we salvaged parts from the rubble.”
The turbines are built from scooter motors and old water tanks cut into blades.

As the wind turns the blades, they drive a motor that generates electricity. The power then passes through circuits assembled from parts recovered from destroyed homes before being stored in batteries.
This provides enough electricity to charge phones and run lights, fans and even electric razors, small comforts that have become a luxury for families still living in tents and shelters.
