Kamel al-Dabbari, who developed a wind turbine that generates electricity using scraps, works in his makesfhift workshop inside a camp for displaced Palestinians in Khan Yunis, on the southern Gaza Strip on November 3, 2026. Al-Dabary, a former engineering student, put his skills to work for families who, like about 85 per cent of Gaza’s population, lives in displacement with no direct access to the heavily damaged electric grid. — AFP pic

Nearly all of Gaza’s residents were displaced at least once during the war, and most now live in a small area still under Hamas rule, while Israel controls more than 60 percent of the territory along its perimeter.
“They help us hold on... until God delivers us from this ordeal and we can return home,” said Dabary, known locally as Abu Ayman.
The output remains modest. But in a camp where shortages are constant, every watt counts.
The system “has changed everything,” said 50-year-old Saleh ben Hasan.
With healthcare and medication hard to access in Gaza, the power can also help keep medical equipment running.
“If a child needs a nebuliser (a device used to inhale medicine) in the middle of the night, who else can we turn to?” he said.
“Electricity is needed... So we turn to our brother Abu Ayman.” — AFP
f87ca9d921a68dd3: Is China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries—including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods—are the envy of the world, and its tech and AI industries are second only to the US, with Europe trailing far behind.
On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time?

In a recent Brookings paper, the International Monetary Fund’s Yuanchen Yang and I explore the striking parallels between today’s China and Japan in the 1990s, especially in residential and commercial real estate as well as related infrastructure.
In both cases, the collapse of the speculative frenzy left a massive construction overhang that can take years to work off. China is still in the middle of that process.

Stunningly, China has built more square metres of residential property per capita than either the UK or France, despite still being a much poorer country. Its road and railway networks are on par with those of the world’s most advanced economies and, in many ways, far superior to America’s.
But the Chinese economy is also deeply unbalanced, like a bodybuilder who has bulked up only his torso. Consumption, the primary growth engine in advanced economies, remains weak.

Eastern China has marquee cities that are well on their way to rivaling their Western counterparts, yet in many smaller cities and rural areas, home to at least half of China’s population, living standards fall somewhere between those of Latin America and South Asia.

The fear now is that, with its housing bubble having collapsed, China may never escape the so-called middle-income trap. When Japan’s real-estate crisis hit, it was already a very wealthy country, with per-capita income rivaling that of the US.

Thirty years later, its per-capita income is closer to Italy’s, which in turn is below that of Mississippi, the poorest US state. And China today is nowhere near as rich as Japan was in the early 1990s.

Between automation and AI, the most dynamic parts of China’s most dynamic sectors are not creating enough jobs. Youth unemployment has gotten so bad that authorities no longer publish the figures regularly.

Even under the best of circumstances, it would be difficult to replace the sagging real-estate and infrastructure sector, which, as Yang and I show, accounts for nearly one-third of demand once both direct and indirect effects are included.

Still, it would be wrong to assume that China’s real-estate crisis necessarily constrains its ability to compete geopolitically or economically. If you speak to businesspeople or attend tech conferences, you will hear that China’s economy is dominant and innovative.
China is not a democracy, and its leaders can allow the dynamic tech and export sectors to flourish even as the rest of the domestic economy takes decades to work off the overbuilding binge.

It is entirely possible to imagine 450 million Chinese people flourishing in a dynamic economy dominated by tech and manufacturing, while the other 950 million get by at a much lower standard of living.
Faced with such a divide, most Western democracies would be overwhelmed by pressure for redistribution, as European countries already know well.

But that need not be the case in China, particularly if the government believes that national security and the country’s global role depend on bolstering its frontier sectors. And 450 million people is still more than the US population and on par with that of the European Union.
Whether such an outcome is possible, of course, remains to be seen. Since Xi Jinping became president in 2013, the Communist Party has paid considerable attention to regional disparities.
But the economic forces that concentrate activity in major hubs, together with the strong desire to assert power internationally, may ultimately trump the pressure to reduce inequality.

The great economic historian Angus Maddison, writing in the late 1960s, argued that—contrary to the views of many economists, including Paul Samuelson—the Soviet Union would never fully catch up with the US. Nevertheless, thanks to its rich scientific tradition, the USSR could still compete at the technological frontier and achieve military parity.
One major difference between the Soviet Union and China is that China has bent over backwards to integrate with the US, both in trade and in science.
Despite US president Donald Trump’s trade war, it is clear that today’s challenges, from climate change to rogue AI, cannot be solved without extensive cooperation between the two superpowers.

So, as paralysing as China’s real-estate crisis has been, and even though excess construction will likely hold down growth for years to come, the dynamic core of its economy will keep thriving, so long as the country remains politically stable—and does not succumb to the temptations of imperial overreach.

Kenneth Rogoff, a former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund, is professor of economics and public policy at Harvard University and the recipient of the 2011 Deutsche Bank Prize in Financial Economics.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
63384c889714efb9: KUALA LUMPUR: Growing up in Kampung Alor Limbat in Marang, Terengganu, Nurul Asmaa' Akmal Din knew education was key for a better future.
Her father, a rubber tapper, and mother, a midwife and masseuse, made sure their children understood this.
“My mother always said she had no assets to leave us, but she could give us an education so we could stand on our own,” Asmaa' told FMT Lifestyle.

Her parents set aside a study space between the living room and kitchen for Asmaa' and her siblings to do their homework. She also attended tuition classes from Standard 2 and religious classes on weekends.

Today, Asmaa' holds a PhD and is a senior lecturer at Universiti Malaya’s (UM) Academy of Malay Studies. Behind those achievements are years of working as a cleaner to fund her studies, juggling long working days with classes, assignments and exams.

After completing her degree in 2018, Asmaa' was eager to keep learning. She applied for a master’s programme at UM, but when she got accepted, excitement gave way to worry. “I didn’t have the money,” recalled Asmaa'.
So, she began looking for work. But some jobs required several rounds of interviews, and she needed to start earning. One night, she spotted a Facebook advertisement for cleaners.
She applied. After all, the advertised pay was better than the other jobs she was considering.

She endured a demanding routine, riding across the Klang Valley with her cleaning supplies. “I would leave home at 7am and start work at 8am. Once I learnt to manage the jobs, I would work until 10pm,” the 30-year-old shared.

Rain made some journeys harder, and she recalled even falling from her motorcycle once during bad weather. Classes filled her weekends, followed by more cleaning jobs. She shared that she often worked seven days a week, taking time off only when she needed to rest or prepare for an exam.
“I didn’t feel like giving up. I knew I had to work hard so I wouldn’t burden my parents,” she added.

Asmaa' encountered kindness from others along the way. Customers who learnt she was working to pay for her studies offered food and cash tips. “One customer paid me double. She said, ‘Use this to pay your fees’,” she recalled.
As she worked towards her master’s, a new ambition began to take shape. Inspired by the academics around her, she imagined a future as a lecturer herself.
At her convocation ceremony, her professor asked whether she wanted to pursue a PhD. She was keen - and her years as a cleaner had given her a research idea.
“I had so many experiences working as a cleaner, but nobody knew the stories behind the life of one. I wanted to study that,” she shared.

A scholarship helped her begin her PhD in October 2020, researching the quality of life of Malay cleaners in the Klang Valley. She continued cleaning part-time to earn extra money and gather insights for her research.
She also interviewed other cleaners, economists, academics and representatives of large cleaning companies.
Among her interviewees was former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad, whose remarks about the attitude of Malays towards work prompted her to seek his views.

After years of hard work and determination, Asmaa' completed her PhD in 2024. The first person she called to share the news with was her mother. It was May, her mother’s birthday month, making the news a special gift for the woman who had always believed in the value of an education.
With that long-awaited achievement came a sense of relief. “That was the first time I felt I could sleep soundly,” Asmaa' recalled with a smile.

A new chapter followed that October, when Asmaa' became a senior lecturer at UM, making her the youngest member of her faculty, she shared. By then, she and her husband had also started a cleaning business.

For anyone whose circumstances seem to stand between them and their dreams, she offers this encouragement: “Don’t think that because life is difficult now, it will always be difficult. Keep finding ways to improve yourself."
3673982a251d9806: PETALING JAYA: Pertelingkahan DAP dan MCA mungkin tidak banyak mengubah sokongan pengundi Cina terhadap kedua-dua parti pada PRN Melaka, namun berpotensi menyebabkan peralihan sokongan kepada Bersama yang boleh menjadi pemecah undi, kata penganalisis.

Merujuk PRN Johor, Lau Zhe Wei daripada Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia (UIAM) berkata walaupun semua calon Bersama hilang deposit, pola pengundian menunjukkan ada undi memihak kepada parti itu yang menjejaskan DAP.

DAP gagal mempertahankan enam kerusi pada pilihan raya Julai lalu, termasuk di Perling yang menyaksikan calon Bersama memperoleh 2,996 undi, lebih tinggi berbanding majoriti 1,611 undi dimenangi Barisan Nasional (BN).
Pada PRN Melaka, Bersama dan DAP bertembung di enam DUN iaitu Gadek, Kota Laksamana, Bandar Hilir, Ayer Keroh, Kesidang dan Pengkalan Batu.

Bercakap kepada FMT, Lau berkata risiko berulangnya keadaan itu tetap ada walaupun DAP dilihat akan terus menguasai undi pengundi Cina di sebalik pertembungan dengan MCA, menyaksikannya saling mencabar antara satu sama lain untuk berdebat.
"Telah wujud pola undi memihak kepada Bersama tetapi peratusan masih tidak besar (berdasarkan keputusan PRN Johor).
"Namun, cukup menyebabkan parti lain kalah seperti dialami DAP," katanya.

Pemimpin MCA dan DAP dilihat berbalas kritikan dengan terbaru Setiausaha Agung DAP Loke Siew Fook mencabar Presiden MCA Wee Ka Siong berdebat mengenai pencapaian masing-masing ketika menerajui Kementerian Pengangkutan.

Pengerusi DAP Melaka, Khoo Poay Tiong, pula mencabar empat calon MCA yang bertanding pada PRN berdebat secara terbuka dengan empat calon Pakatan Harapan (PH) di Kota Laksamana, Bandar Hilir, Kelebang dan Machap Jaya.
Lau berpandangan, majoriti pengundi Cina masih berpihak kepada DAP berbanding MCA, mengambil kira kerjasama Umno dan PAS yang dilihat boleh menolak pengundi kaum itu condong kepada PH.
“Biarpun DAP kalah di banyak kerusi di Negeri Sembilan, di Johor tapi jangan lupa peratusan pengundi Cina kepada DAP masih tinggi," katanya.

Sementara itu, Anbumani Balan berkata DAP tidak boleh terlalu bergantung kepada serangan terhadap MCA untuk mempertahankan keyakinan pengundi Cina, sebaliknya perlu membuktikan pencapaian sendiri melalui prestasi yang boleh dinilai.
Pemerhati politik itu berkata, komuniti Cina lazimnya bersikap pragmatik dan menilai parti berdasarkan tiga prinsip yang dirumuskannya sebagai 3P – prestasi, pelaksanaan dan pemantauan.
"Jika terlalu banyak tenaga dihabiskan untuk menyerang lawan tanpa disertai penjelasan tentang pencapaian sendiri, ia boleh menimbulkan persoalan tentang keutamaan sebenar kepimpinan parti," katanya.
Anbumani berkata, DAP juga perlu memberi perhatian kepada hubungan dengan pengundi Melayu ketika menilai langkah seterusnya selepas prestasinya merudum dalam beberapa PRN.
“Sudah tiba masa DAP juga perlu membaca, menilai dan memperkasakan hubungan bersama pengundi Melayu," katanya.
ff574cd4a13cf3ed: PARIS: Carlos Alcaraz moved into the quarter-finals of the Paris Masters on Thursday after his last 16 opponent Matteo Berrettini withdrew.

f43303c0b1b6a0f4: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump lashed out at "crooked" elections on Thursday as the Democrats' midterm steamroller powered ahead, with another potential Senate upset in Mississippi threatening to deepen Republicans' historic defeat.
"Our elections are so crooked, you have no idea," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, as he denounced the "disgraceful" victory of a democratic socialist in the Los Angeles mayoral race.

His outburst came just two days after Americans handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in a sweeping rejection of Trump's presidency and the Republican Party he has remade in his image.

Although Trump initially accepted the midterm results, he has since demanded that votes cast for two minor candidates in Alaska's still-undecided Senate race be handed to the trailing Republican incumbent.
The president's renewed attacks on the electoral process contrast with a political landscape transformed by Tuesday's Democratic landslide.
Democrats are already set to hold at least 54 Senate seats to the Republicans' 44. Their House majority surged past 250 seats on Thursday, the party's biggest in almost two decades.
After Trump warned that he would use his veto power to block Democratic legislation, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer issued a warning of his own.

"If Donald Trump does spend the next year vetoing common sense legislation to lower costs and end corruption, this election — this absolute Republican catastrophe on election night 2026 — will look like a good day compared to what will come down on Republicans in the 2028 election," Schumer said.
Mississippi, Alaska nail-biters

The biggest remaining midterm nail-biter was in Mississippi, one of the most solidly Republican states in the nation, where, against all expectations, a 43-year-old Black candidate, Scott Colom, appeared to be on the cusp of winning a US Senate seat.
By afternoon, Colom's lead over incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith had increased to 1,724 votes, with only a handful of ballots left to count. The final result could take days to come.
Colom would be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat from the southern state since 1982 — and the first African American to do so since 1874.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola was also just ahead of the pack with 48.17 per cent of the vote, followed by Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with 47.88 per cent.

Trump's Truth Social outburst referred to a fringe candidate also named Dan Sullivan, whom Republicans accuse of being a "decoy" aimed at siphoning votes from their candidate, and another minor contender, Gerald Heikes, who is registered as a Republican.
Trump posted that all the votes for the "Fake" Sullivan and Heikes "should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan".
"There is no other fair solution!"
Making history
If Colom wins in Mississippi, he would join a host of other new faces smashing racial and cultural barriers in the midterms.
Keisha Lance Bottoms, the great-great-granddaughter of a slave, became the first Black female governor of Georgia — and in the country.
And Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed beat a Trump ally to become the first Muslim to enter the US Senate.
Tuesday's midterms also featured wins for Democrats in political territory where Trump had previously been so dominant that it was all but written off by the left.
James Talarico broke a 38-year hoodoo by winning a Senate seat in ultra-Republican Texas, and Adam Hamilton did even better, becoming the first Democratic senator from Kansas in 94 years.
Republican congressman Warren Davidson, in Ohio, said Trump's months-long war against Iran and global trade wars had lost the election for the party.
Young voters in particular, he said, felt "betrayed".

1c7d0f146926e0c6: LOS ANGELES: California governor Gavin Newsom said Thursday he was commuting all death sentences across the state to life imprisonment, in a move that will affect over 500 prisoners.
Newsom, who is widely expected to make a run for the White House in 2028, said capital punishment was "incompatible" with the values of the most populous state in the US.

"Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing," he wrote in a letter addressed "to all Californians".
With 548 people awaiting execution in California, the state has one of the largest death row populations in the world.
However, it has not carried out a death sentence for two decades, even as courts continue to impose the penalty on those convicted of murder and other serious crimes.

"Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," he said, calling the decision "among the most difficult of my career".

"I do, however, pray that this action will finally separate the memories of the victims of these crimes from the fate of those who harmed them. We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims."
The announcement comes with a renewed spotlight on the death penalty in the US, one of the few wealthy countries to retain capital punishment.
In September, the state of Tennessee failed twice to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike with a lethal injection before rushing her to hospital. The drama made headlines around the world.
Last month defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the firing squad execution of a man who went on a shooting rampage at a US Army base would be livestreamed.

Days later and after an outcry from both sides of the political aisle, as well as from the Catholic Church and the UN, President Donald Trump cancelled the plan, saying Nidal Hasan would still die, but that the sentence would not be broadcast.
'Not by our hand'
In a lengthy letter Thursday, Newsom appeared to be walking the public through his thought process and the discussions he said he has had on the issue.
He said the decision to issue a blanket commutation for all death row inmates came down to not differentiating among those affected by heinous acts.

"I have concluded that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims -- those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest," Newsom said.
"I will therefore issue the same commutation to every condemned person -- life without the possibility of parole," he added.
"These offenders will die in prison, but not by our hand."
Jess Nichol, whose sister's killer is on death row in California, said she had previously wanted the culprit to die for his crime.
"But over time I've realised that whether he's executed has absolutely nothing to do with my recovery or with real public safety," she said.
"The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn't. It's a distraction from what we actually need."
The American Civil Liberties Union applauded the move over a practice it said conlifted with "human dignity, fairness, and the values enshrined in our Constitution".
The commutations "reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long."

581771537c149e57: LONDON: The Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in over three years on Thursday and warned that at least one more increase was likely if the US-Iran conflict continues, as it started on a path already begun by its main peers.

British inflation is likely to rise to around 5% in the middle of next year, the BoE said, more than double the central bank's target and a blow to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has sought to ease cost of living pressures.

The BoE found little evidence so far of faster inflation outside sectors directly hit by higher energy costs. However, policymakers said that the amount of inflation pressure coming down the road after months of high energy prices required a rate rise now, even though that will increase borrowing costs for businesses and many home owners.

"Today's increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. That is not inevitable. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase," Governor Andrew Bailey said in his opening remarks at a press conference.

Sterling strengthened against the US dollar after the decision. Two-year British government bond yields which are sensitive to expectations of future rate moves — rose while yields fell elsewhere, as investors increased bets on a back-to-back rate hike next month.
"December's meeting now looks like a coin flip, with the path of oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor," said Andrew Goodwin, chief UK economist at Oxford Economics.

The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to raise rates to 4% from 3.75%, the first rise since August 2023. In contrast to expectations in a Reuters poll, the dissent came not from a policymaker seeking to keep rates on hold but one seeking a bigger hike.
Catherine Mann, who said last month that the BoE had been slow to reassure markets that it had a grip on inflation, voted for a half-point interest rate increase to 4.25%.

Until now, the BoE had not followed the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and other central banks in raising rates in response to inflation pressures from the Iran war, arguing that the higher starting level of BoE rates made a hike less urgent.

Bailey said a big fall in oil prices over the last 48 hours — a move largely driven by the results of US midterm elections — was "encouraging news" but said previous falls in oil prices and of easing Middle East tensions had proven to be false dawns.
Moreover, he said a further rate hike was likely to be needed even if oil prices stayed at current levels as there was "already a significant amount of inflationary pressure in the pipeline".
British household energy bills are regulated under a formula which follows wholesale prices with around a three-month lag.
BOE predicts faster growth, higher inflation

In its central forecast for growth and inflation, the BoE revised up its expectations for growth this year and next to 1.6% and 1.3% respectively — notably stronger than the government's Office for Budget Responsibility predicted last week.

The upgrade follows strong official data this year, and the BoE attributed some of the strength to spending on artificial intelligence and a small, temporary boost from finance minister John Healey's annual budget last week.
However, after the effect of inflation and taxes, the average British household's income from work is set to fall both this year and next, the BoE said.

Under the BoE's central scenario, inflation does not return to its 2% target until the third quarter of 2028, six months later than the BoE predicted in July after a lull in the US-Iran conflict which had lowered energy costs.
The BoE now sees inflation peaking at 4.8% in the second quarter of next year, and said it would have been on course to top 5% without measures in Healey's budget.

In a more adverse scenario where oil prices peak near $130 a barrel, up from around US$100 currently, inflation hits 6.2% in the third quarter of 2027 – just under half the rate it hit in 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
b6e2c3db44ded8c2: BRUSSELS: Nato on Thursday said it had launched a new platform to help its 32 member countries buy tried-and-tested anti-drone equipment faster, as incursions have fuelled fears about Russia.

The products -- made by firms from Britain, France, Germany, and the US -- are available for purchase or long-term rental by Nato countries.

The equipment -- which costs up to US$28 million -- is aimed at protecting borders and strategic sites, and includes a raft of different technologies including electronic jamming and interceptor drones.
Nato nations including the Baltic states, Romania and Poland have faced a series of drone incursions as part of the spillover from Russia's war on Ukraine.

1092b95f98283f0b: SAO PAULO: Lewis Hamilton will celebrate the 400th Formula One start of a glittering career at this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with rivals hailing the seven-time world champion's longevity, speed and enduring hunger for success.

The 41-year-old Briton, Formula One's most successful driver with a record 106 race wins and 105 pole positions, reaches the milestone still competing at the front and showing little sign of slowing down.
"It's kind of crazy. I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," Hamilton told reporters on Thursday.

"I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week (in Mexico). I still have the pace, I still have the speed, I still have the dedication, which is most important, and the focus."

Hamilton is third in the drivers' championship, two points behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen. He claimed his record-extending 105th pole position in Mexico last week but finished second after a clash with Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc.
Hamilton made his Formula One debut with McLaren in 2007 and won his first championship a year later.

He secured six more titles with Mercedes between 2014 and 2020 before joining Ferrari last season. Only Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso, 45, has made more grand prix starts, with the double world champion closing in on 450 races.

While Hamilton said the round number itself was not especially meaningful to him, he acknowledged the significance of reaching it in Brazil, a country where he enjoys enormous popularity and was made an honorary citizen in 2022.
"For me, that number is kind of irrelevant. But it's beautiful to be able to have that here in Brazil," he said.

McLaren's Lando Norris said Hamilton's career remained a benchmark for younger drivers hoping to build similar longevity, while adding performances this season had dispelled any doubts about his competitiveness.
"I think it's a pretty incredible achievement for him to fight for this long. He's a good inspiration for many of us," said the 2025 world champion.
"When I look at Lewis, he makes me not very happy to have only won one championship.

"But that's in a good way that I can look at him and see him and his age, his form, and makes me believe more than ever that I could fight for many, many more years, and that's something I look forward to doing."
Audi's Nico Hulkenberg also praised Hamilton's determination to continue competing despite having already surpassed nearly every major record in the sport.
"He could have easily retired many times and said, 'that's enough'," Hulkenberg, 39, said. "Fair play and respect to him that he still puts in the work, still wants this, and still does this."

112ca14e104a5b9a: LONDON: King Charles is "a secret weapon" increasingly being thrust by the British government into dealing with challenging political situations, a senior royal aide has said following a diplomatically challenging trip by the monarch to the Caribbean.

The trip, which also included a meeting of the Commonwealth of Nations, which Charles heads, was dominated by the issue of slavery, and specifically whether Britain and the king should apologise for the transatlantic slave trade and offer to pay reparations.

The king did neither in speeches he made, in line with British government policy, but his expression of personal sorrow about the horrors of slavery was broadly welcomed by leaders of the 56-nation Commonwealth as a positive step forward.
Statecraft by word and deed
In unusually frank remarks, the senior aide described the tour as complex and challenging, but said the king "had demonstrated his statecraft both by word and deed".

"It's a great secret weapon to send the king," the aide told reporters on condition of anonymity, adding that the monarch was "able to reach the parts that, dare I say, politicians probably couldn't quite have reached".
The monarch is Britain's symbolic head of state but is constitutionally required to stay out of politics.
In recent times, as Britain's influence over world affairs has diminished, the government has often turned to the monarch to lead its diplomatic strategies.

Amid tensions with US President Donald Trump, most recently over the Iran war, the government enlisted Charles — who became king in September 2022 following the death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth — to help smooth relations. The king hosted Trump on a state visit and then paid a reciprocal state visit to the US.

"We're just in the fifth year of the reign and I think what we're seeing is a very clear pattern emerging of the government asking the king to head into quite politically charged situations, quite challenging situations," the senior aide said.

Dealing with the tough part of the job was what he relished, the aide said, adding that "refreshing and reinvigorating relationships with nations where there have been some complex political issues at play, that is what he lives and breathes for".
Difficult year for monarchy

The tour marks a high point in what has been another difficult year for the monarchy, with the release of a biography of Charles' first wife, Princess Diana, written by her brother, which featured criticisms of Charles' reaction to her death.

Charles' younger brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, continues to make negative headlines as he remains under police investigation. Andrew denies any wrongdoing, while the return to Britain of the king's younger son, Prince Harry, has also brought complications.

While Charles remains head of the Commonwealth and is still the head of state of 15 nations, including Canada and Australia, the aide acknowledged that the situation could also change, with Barbados the latest nation to ditch the monarchy in 2021.
The aide said it was for nations and the Commonwealth to decide what to do in future.
"The (royal) family serves when it's wanted and if not, then a new arrangement can be found," the aide added.

Charles, who turns 78 this month, is still recovering from cancer, but the aide said concerns about his age and health were best answered by the sight of Charles waving cowbells as he danced down a street in the Bahamas in 40°C heat and the humour he showed after being caught in a tropical rainstorm.
"This is literally what he was born to do. He's very good at it, and he enjoys the reaction he gets from people," the aide said.

c039ef1b2e561dc4: BRUSSELS: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has criticised Europe's "disorderly" approach to negotiations on Ukraine and called on the European Union to decide who speaks on its behalf, in a letter seen by AFP on Thursday.

In the message to European Council president Antonio Costa, who chairs summits of EU leaders, Meloni complained about the recent proliferation of meetings in different formats to discuss Russia's war on Ukraine.
"All this is making us look utterly lacking in credibility in handling one of the most complicated dossiers our nations are facing," the Italian leader wrote.
"I am convinced that we all realise how, by giving the image of a Europe that is proceeding in disarray, we are doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue."
She cited recent talks in Miami and Oslo, as well as meetings this week in Brussels between representatives of Ukraine, the United States, several European countries, Nato and the EU.
She also mentioned a call between the leaders of Norway and Finland and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I want it on record that I will not go along with this dynamic, nor do I intend to stand by and watch it unfold," Meloni wrote.
"Proceeding in disarray, with initiatives that chase and overlap one another, will not help us, neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to stop a senseless aggression."
The Italian leader said she wanted EU leaders to decide "once and for all who sits at the negotiating table on behalf of the European Union, and with what mandate".
Leaders to discuss

3f447f2fbf4f296f: NEW YORK: Google, Meta Platforms and TikTok sued California to block enforcement of a new state law intended to limit the risk of addicting children under age 16 to social media platforms.

The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits such platforms from offering underage children "psychologically exploitative features" that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children's accounts with those features.

In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok said the law wrongly compels them to honour California's preferred means of presenting content to children, and substitutes the state's judgment for that of parents.

They said the law violates the US Constitution's First Amendment free speech protections, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.

The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who enforces the state's laws and is the only defendant, said on Thursday it is reviewing the lawsuits. "Our office is committed to defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online," it added.
Google owns YouTube and is a unit of Alphabet, while Meta owns Facebook and Instagram. TikTok is a unit of China's ByteDance.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on Sept 10, saying children's safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California "will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk."
The law takes effect on Jan 1, 2027, unless a judge voids it or puts it on hold.

"Parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda said on Thursday. "Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”

In its lawsuit, Meta said California cannot override its editorial judgments about how to curate and display billions of posts, while leaving children free to spend unlimited time on other online platforms that offer similar services.
TikTok, meanwhile, said protected speech "cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable."
Other critics also accused California of overreaching. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group, called the law "a massive privacy and free speech nightmare."
Many US states regulate children's ​access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social ​media for children under 16.

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to US$18 billion and limit teenagers' use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all US states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws.
Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in Los Angeles.

The companies and Snapchat parent Snap still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

ac5b663d87bdec96: JERUSALEM: Israeli president Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday whom he will task with trying to form a new government, after the opposition's Gadi Eisenkot secured a commanding number of recommendations to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Herzog will make his choice, but traditionally the mandate is given to the person recommended by more parliament members. Sixty-seven picked Eisenkot, 46 opted for Netanyahu, while seven abstained.

"The results of the consultations may appear clear, but the authority vested in me by law is to determine who has the ability to form a government, and that is not entirely clear, given the mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves," Herzog said on Thursday.
"I will try to determine this directly and quickly, in personal talks with some of the party leaders."

Eisenkot's Yashar party said on Thursday that "the citizens of Israel have chosen change and expressed a complete lack of confidence in outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his government", and called for the "immediate establishment of a national emergency government that will begin working for all citizens of Israel".
Two Arab-majority lists won an unprecedented 19 seats in the election, making them potential kingmakers if Eisenkot's opposition chooses to work with them, which remains unclear.
Both Arab lists on Thursday said they were backing Eisenkot.
However, another party in Eisenkot's camp, right-wing Israel Beiteinu, has repeatedly indicated it will not sit in a government that relies on support from Arab parties.

Party leader Avigdor Liberman, a former Netanyahu ally turned critic, cited as a reason the refusal by Arab parties to explicitly define Hamas as a "terror group" -- even though they have repeatedly condemned the organisation's attack on Israel on Oct 7, 2023.
Ultra-Orthodox exemptions

Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which backed Netanyahu after the previous five elections, in its meeting with Herzog declined to recommend Netanyahu again as premier, although it also did not side with Eisenkot.

Alongside Shas, another ultra-Orthodox party, they have pushed to maintain the exemption from military service for religious students.

Netanyahu has preserved the exemption but stopped short of enshrining it in law, in the face of major resentment from many other Israelis, as reservists serve multiple tours due to the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
"In whatever government is next formed, our immediate item is sorting out the status of Torah students," United Torah Judaism lawmaker Isaac Pindrus said.
Eisenkot, who has tried to appeal to secular Israelis from left to right, has been adamant about ending exemptions for military service.
Some of his opposition allies have criticised the ultra-Orthodox -- who make up about 14 percent of the population but have far higher birthrates than secular Israelis -- as a drain on the state.

Observers say United Torah Judaism's tactic is likely aimed mostly at punishing Netanyahu and showing that their votes cannot be taken for granted, while they would still serve in a government if he were to form one.
Arab parties play key role
Once Herzog gives his mandate to a lawmaker, the person will have 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension. If the lawmaker fails, Herzog will then task someone else.
Netanyahu's bloc, including United Torah Judaism, has 53 seats in the new parliament, compared to 48 for Eisenkot's bloc.

Arab-majority parties scored historic gains on the back of anger over Netanyahu's hard-right government and longstanding complaints about racism from some ministers and discriminatory treatment of Arab Israelis.

ff430ec6d234ec4f: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Following widespread backlash, Meta announced earlier this week it’s putting a planned update of its commercial terms of use on pause. The terms would have required business accounts to allow Meta to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

The new terms were initially set to go into effect on October 30, but after outcry from journalists and users who didn’t want Meta reaching far beyond Instagram and Facebook and into their websites to suck up their work as training data for its generative AI products, Meta announced it was pushing the change to November 20. Now, it’s on hold entirely.

“We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms,” Meta says on the page where the commercial terms announcement used to be. “These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”
If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training
In light of Meta's new terms that will allow it to scrape users' data for AI, people in the EU and UK have the option to "object" to certain uses of their information, for now.

The Los Angeles Times, which first reported the change, notes that following a case supported by the Norwegian Media Businesses’ Association and 180 Norwegian media companies, a court in Norway granted a temporary injunction suspending Meta’s new terms, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority said it would do its own investigation into the terms.

After pushing the update to November, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products.
2cd0d025ccf2b230: Whether through malware or other means, devices associated with the White House network appear to be serving as residential proxy exit nodes, potentially posing security risks to one of the world's most sensitive networks.

News of the security snafu comes from security firm Layer3 Intel, which reported this week that it discovered the likely illicit activity thanks to its recently launched Residential Proxy Observatory. According to Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk, the White House residential proxy activity might have gone unnoticed if not for the new tool.
“The observatory is just a public interface to explore the data we've been collecting for the past year,” Usatyuk told The Register in an email.

For those unfamiliar with residential proxies, they're like any old proxy network that obfuscates the location of a user, except in this case their exit nodes use IP addresses associated with residential internet connections, as opposed to datacenters. While many are legitimate, others are exploited by threat actors and used in the commission of cybercrimes, as the FBI warned earlier this year.

The FBI bulletin, put out in March, warns users to protect their systems against hijacking via malware, illicit SDK partnerships, VPNs with hidden service terms that repurpose user computers as exit nodes, and other threats used to turn victims into nodes without their consent.

Residential proxies are commonly used by threat actors to conceal command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, conduct phishing attacks, send spam, disguise malicious traffic, and the like, the FBI explained.

According to Layer3, its data shows 28 distinct residential proxy services exiting into the White House network nearly every day between October 5 and November 3, with 236 separate exits in that period. Other residential proxy detection services logged the same information, Layer3 said.

Most of the activity was happening in the evening, White House time, between 5 pm and midnight. That, Layer3 said, suggests someone at the White House - not a guest - has an infected device that’s serving as an exit, likely via an infected proxy SDK. If correct, that’s a problem.

“Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement,” Layer3 explained. “If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.”
In other words, this is a serious security risk, and one Usatyuk tells us could have been a problem for a while.

“Our data retention period goes back to July 10,” the Layer3 founder explained. “Given that there was continuous activity for a matter of months and other res proxy detection services independently verified the data, it's likely that White House IPs have been used by res proxy networks for all sorts of activity for some time now.”

Usatyuk said his firm’s data isn’t detailed enough to know how many machines are being used as exit nodes inside the White House network. He pointed us to an X post from security firm Synthient, which said it believes there are multiple Windows 10 and 11 devices on the White House network that likely have the Infatica SDK installed on them.

Infatica offers a software development kit (SDK) that allows app developers to monetize users' internet connections by turning their devices into residential proxy exit nodes. The possibility that this software is running on devices associated with the White House network raises serious security concerns: Vulnerable proxy software could potentially provide attackers with a route into internal systems.

Usatyuk told us that the most recent residential proxy activity on the White House network occurred Wednesday night, “hours after the blog went live,” but has since stopped. The US State Department contacted Layer3 Thursday morning to request a copy of the company’s logs, which Usatyuk tells us he’s sent over.
“Hopefully they've figured out the situation,” Usatyuk added - and hopefully before any government secrets have been exposed.
The White House didn't respond to questions for this story.®

d4e31870e3fc049e: When BMW debuted the new 7 Series in 2022, it set a new standard for large luxury sedans, increasingly irrelevant though that class is. Rather than siloing off an electric alternative like Mercedes, with its EQS alongside the normal S-Class, BMW simply made the powertrain an option. b2a9c85dded5b523: With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet.

While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star's light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope's configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets.

Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.

16f01f55a4865d25: Power is draining away at home, but the US president will see a chance to make his mark through foreign policy Kim Darroch was Britain’s ambassador to the US between January 2016 and December 2019 Election nights are party time in Washington. The bars and restaurants fill up and the city rocks. For diplomats, it’s an opportunity – but it’s also a long night, as you trek across the party scene in search of insight and illumination. Invariably, it has its moments. I recall being at the Washington Post party on the night of the presidential election on 8 November 2016. Washington is an overwhelmingly Democrat city and the atmosphere was raucously optimistic, reflecting Hillary Clinton’s small but consistent lead in the polls. As the first results came in a shocked hush fell across the room. People gathered in small, murmuring groups. Within 30 minutes, half the guests had left. In contrast, I recall speaking to Nancy Pelosi, the queen of the Democrats, at a watch party on 6 November 2018, for the midterms during Trump’s first presidency. I asked her what I should put in my overnight report to London, given that most results wouldn’t be in. She said, with striking confidence, that I should predict that the Democrats would retake the House of Representatives. She was right: the Democrats flipped 41 Republican seats. It gave Pelosi a second term as speaker of the House and gave the world the enjoyable theatre of her sitting directly behind Trump at his State of the Union speeches, rolling her eyes at the bombast. Kim Darroch was British ambassador to the US from 2016 to 2019, and is author of Collateral Damage: Britain, America and Europe in the Age of Trump Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? c61645b48e45a038: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Archaeologists have discovered the oldest direct evidence of psychoactive cannabis use in a Siberian tomb that dates back 2,800 years and was the site of human and horse sacrifices, according to a study published on Thursday in Science.

During excavations of the tomb, a team found more than 1,400 cannabis seeds scattered around the remains of several Iron Age individuals, and even identified cannabinoids—including the active compound tetrahydrocannabinol (THC)—in a person’s preserved hair.

Though humans cultivated cannabis for many millennia before the Iron Age, this is by far the earliest clear-cut proof that the plant was consumed for its psychoactive effects, which have made it one of the most widely used drugs in the world today.

The discovery is “absolutely crazy,” said Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology and the University of Bern who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. “People have been speculating a lot about psychoactive use of cannabis in the past, but to actually pin it down and prove it with soft tissue evidence of the humans involved—that is something very special.
“That is an absolutely unique and extremely rare combination of evidence,” he added.

Cannabis has a multifaceted history as a recreational drug and a pop cultural touchstone, as well as a traditional medicine that has been used for millennia by many cultures, including in China, Russia, and around the Mediterranean Basin. Humans began cultivating the plant as early as 10,000 years ago for its oil and fiber, but the origins of its specific consumption as a psychoactive substance is unclear.

Cannabis was important to the Scythian culture, a horse-riding people that emerged on the Eurasian steppes in the 9th century BCE and became a major force in the subsequent centuries. The historian Herodotus described Scythian rituals that involved ceremonial burning of cannabis in enclosed spaces, and their cannabis residues and products have been found at Scythian archaeological sites.

“Herodotus speaks about the Scythians being quite fond of cannabis in the first place, so this has always been in the back of our minds,” Caspari said. “But it is so incredibly rare to find well-preserved plant remains that this is not really something you can hope for or look for. This is ultimately complete luck and chance.”

Now, Caspari and his colleagues have hit an archaeological jackpot at a tomb known as Tunnug 1, located in Siberia’s Uyuk River Valley. Six elite individuals are interred in the interior of the royal mound inside several tree-trunk coffins and wooden structures. They are mostly men, though one woman is also present. The mound is lined with remains of sacrificed humans, as well as dozens of sacrificed horses, close to the surface.

As the team carefully worked through the layers of the burial, they found hundreds of cannabis seeds distributed around the bodies that were dated to the 8th century BCE. However, the real smoking blunt was the detection of cannabinols in preserved hair samples, including traces of THC, the most important mind-altering compound in cannabis.

The results confirm contemporaneous accounts of Scythians as cannabis consumers who used the plant for purification and mortuary rituals. It’s possible that the people selected as human sacrifice consumed the drug to prepare them for their unenviable fate.

“It being in a burial context, of course, there's a ritual aspect to it,” Caspari explained. “It might be a little bit more sinister, but this is speculation. We do have a lot of horse sacrifices and also some human sacrifices on the surface of the mound. And if you imagine humans being sacrificed, they usually don't like that very much. It might be advantageous to have them dosed a little bit, at least, to make the procedure a bit more humane, if you will.”
“Of course, that is speculation,” he cautioned. “We don't have any written sources about that particular area, but that's at least one way we could go with our interpretation.”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The researchers hope to learn more about the context and meaning of the cannabis use at Tunnug 1 through continued excavations and an analysis of more hair samples. What’s more, the team plans to conduct DNA analysis on the seeds, an approach that could yield new insights about the murky history of cannabis domestication and its early use as a psychoactive substance. This line of research could also shed light on modern cannabis strains, and may even be revived for new medicinal or recreational purposes.

“We've already sequenced part of the seeds to unravel and disentangle the domestication history,” Caspari said. “Funnily enough, we don't even know what wild cannabis actually looks like because there has been so much intermixing and interbreeding since the 70s, when people started experimenting and trying to get more potent drug variants. Some of the initial landraces and the actual wild cannabis has been lost.”

“Now, having DNA that's almost 3,000 years old, we will be able to take that step back into the past and see what an unaltered cannabis would have looked like,” he said. “In the ideal case, we might even be able to work together with the medical industry and bring some of these very ancient genetics back into cannabis production to potentially help people with very interesting and distinctive cannabinoid combinations.”

Put that in your pipe and smoke it. Regardless of where future research into this ancient plant leads, this long-sought evidence of cannabis use thousands of years ago confirms the rich cultural legacy of the plant across time and space.

“As an archeologist, I might be a bit biased here, but I think the history and cultural practices really do matter,” Caspari concluded. “I think our findings do indeed inform current discussions on legalization, on usage of medical cannabis—which is very much an ongoing discourse—and I think what we've been able to do with this study is provide an anchor, and show that there is this deep cultural history to the use of cannabis as a psychoactive drug.”

9db2ee442db69062: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions.

The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled.

If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration.
That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not.

Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration.
The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually.

In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account.

Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out.

The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk.

Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going.

In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times.

On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack.

Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set.

There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

9bfc288acd5354c8: Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens.

In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time.

In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company.

Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials.

Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials.
In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work."

These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page.

Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."
The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5).

Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords.

"We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary.
"We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely."

Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks."

"This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30.
"Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems."

In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed.
Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base.
It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations.

Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews.
It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

49b4025f4149468c: openSUSE Leap 16.1 lets users choose between a conventional Linux installation and an immutable system from the same installer, bringing the previously separate Leap Micro into the fold.
It's the first point release after Leap 16.0, which we looked at last year when it reached the release candidate stage.

Leap 16.1 has arrived ahead of its paid enterprise sibling, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1, which is expected later this month. Its release notes are already available, and IBM discussed the release in September.

The big change in the 16.1 release cycle of both the free and commercial products is that SUSE is merging its conventional Linux with its immutable version, a change the company announced back in February.

SUSE previously offered a commercial stripped-down immutable OS, aimed mainly at hosting containers, called SLE Micro. To correspond with that, there was a free community OS called Leap Micro – the final release was Leap Micro 6.2.

Leap Micro is being discontinued as a separate community distribution. The Leap 16.1 announcement says: "Immutable Mode with transactionally updating a system with a read-only root filesystem is a big change for this release. Users who know Leap Micro will recognize it right away, because it is the same approach, now integrated directly into Leap. Leap 16.1 in Immutable Mode replaces Leap Micro, and there will be no Leap Micro 6.3 or 7.0. Users simply boot the regular Leap 16.1 install image and select Immutable Mode in Agama."

Both Red Hat and Canonical offer immutable distros, but both use different architectures from their conventional package-based distros. Ubuntu Core is built entirely from snap packages, while Red Hat's "Atomic" immutable distros are built from bootable containers, running on top of OStree, which works a little like a local Git server. Immutable distros built on Arch, such as SteamOS 3 or KDE Linux, resemble ChromeOS at filesystem level, with dual root filesystems that update one another.

Leap belongs to the openSUSE family of distros, backed by enterprise Linux vendor SUSE. Its commercial sibling is SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES). Leap is the free, community-supported version, and they are based on the same core packages and release schedule. openSUSE also has a rolling-release version, called Tumbleweed.

To rephrase this in terms of slightly more familiar Red Hat equivalents, SLES is SUSE's equivalent of RHEL. Leap is the free openSUSE equivalent of the late lamented CentOS Linux. Leap shares a common core with SUSE's enterprise products while offering a broader community package selection. SLES and openSUSE began sharing enterprise binaries in 2021. Red Hat, meanwhile, announced the end of CentOS Linux in 2020, shifting its focus to CentOS Stream.

To continue the Red Hat comparisons, openSUSE Tumbleweed is loosely equivalent to Fedora Rawhide, but with automated testing and rollback of problematic updates. Unlike the best-known rolling distro, the entirely community-built Arch Linux, Tumbleweed uses SUSE's Snapper technology to offer snapshots. If an update breaks something, Tumbleweed users can boot into a snapshot of an older version of the OS, before the offending update was installed, and keep on working. If dozens of updated packages a day prove too much, then openSUSE also offers an experimental slower-moving rolling release called Slowroll.

Despite the modest version-number bump, Leap 16.1 is a substantial annual update. Its release cycle sits between Fedora and interim Ubuntu releases on one side, and Debian and Ubuntu LTS on the other. Along with its other updates, it brings GNOME 48.8, KDE Plasma 6.6.4, and LXQt 2.4.
We tried its Xfce desktop, which surprisingly defaulted to X.org rather than the Wayland-based setup using labwc that we saw in 16.0 last year.

Immutable distros look to be the future of Linux for non-technical users. Android is an immutable OS based on the Linux kernel, and sells in the billions – which is why, as we reported last year, Google is replacing ChromeOS with Android. The result is the AI-festooned GooglebookOS, on sale in Mountain View's new high-end GoogleBook kit.

The Reg FOSS desk isn't aware of any other Linux OS in which you're able to choose, at the point of installation, whether you wish it to be immutable or not. For now, in the commercial Linux OS space, only SUSE has anything like this flexibility. It's marketing its immutable versions as being ideal hosts for containers, and as suitable for "edge" devices, meaning that they are expected to be provisioned remotely, update themselves automatically, and recover from faults on their own.
SUSE is a much smaller company than Red Hat, and unfortunately, as we reported earlier this week, it is getting smaller.
This vulture is both a former SUSE Linux user and a former SUSE employee, and we hope it and its unique distribution survive and thrive. ®
