<!--kg-card-end: html--> “I adore breath play. I love being strangled, suffocated and drowned, and I love strangling and suffocating others. Waterboarding: that’s my favourite,” Melissa Todd, a UK-based writer and sex worker, told me. “Many women do: it really isn’t only horrid men forcing us to do these dreadful depraved acts. Interrupting oxygen supply produces the most intense sensation of euphoria. I enjoy it in my private life, and I offer it in sessions too.”

Starting tomorrow, she and anyone else in the UK distributing or possessing this type of content, even if it’s just recorded in the privacy of their homes and not for sale on a porn site, could face up to five years in prison. The maximum penalty for possession is “two years’ imprisonment for pornography that depicts strangulation or suffocation, or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives,” according to the law, and “three years’ imprisonment for pornography depicting sexual activity involving a person who is, or is pretending to be, under 16,” with five years as the maximum penalty for publication of all of the above.

Updates to the Crime and Policing Act go into force on November 6. The law criminalizes a list of sexual acts, including downloading or making choking and incest roleplay porn. According to the law, it will be a criminal offense in England and Wales to possess or publish porn that “explicitly and realistically” depicts strangulation or suffocation, penetrative sexual activity between people who “a reasonable person would think are related, or pretending to be related, in a certain way” and sexual activity between people where “a reasonable person would think at least one person is, or is pretending to be, under 16.” Sixteen is the age of consent in the UK.
“You have to speak up for porn you don’t like, as well as the porn you do, because otherwise the government will keep censoring more and more depictions of acts they don’t fancy."
“The offences only capture pornography that shows people which appear, to a reasonable person, to be real,” the law states — whatever that means.

The rest of the law is similarly vague in defining what’s criminalized. The “guidance” on the law says: “We consider that strangulation generally means one person applying pressure to another person’s neck,” and “We consider that suffocation will generally mean depriving a person of air in a way that affects their ability to breathe. Unlike strangulation, this does not require pressure to the neck. It could, for example, involve covering someone’s mouth and nose or compressing their chest.” This could mean anything from relatively common acts like face sitting or pushing someone’s face into a mattress, to gagging and more extreme breathplay generally left to professionals. The law says it’ll be left to the courts to decide.
As the adult industry advocacy group Free Speech Coalition notes in its guide for performers and platforms, the government has said this content doesn’t need to appear life-threatening to count.

“This isn’t just about my personal preferences,” Todd said. “You have to speak up for porn you don’t like, as well as the porn you do, because otherwise the government will keep censoring more and more depictions of acts they don’t fancy. Even if you think strangulation is disgusting, immoral, dangerous, that is no reason to ban it. In a liberal democracy people must be allowed to behave in ways you think ridiculous and disgusting, in the hope that they in turn will extend the same courtesy to you. I don’t understand why people go skiing, or camping, or abseiling, but I’m happy for them to crack on with it. Consenting adults must be allowed to do whatever they want with their own bodies. It is illiberal and dangerous for the government to interfere."

The effect of the law’s vagueness — as it has been in the US when legislators, payment processors and platforms similarly inflict poorly-defined terms on sex workers — is censorship and has a chilling effect on otherwise consensual legal activity between adults. It’s already happening: Adult clip site iWantClips warned, according to content creators using its platform, that in light of the law it’s banning a list of genres and acts: “iWantClips is required to remove certain categories of content from the platform for Artists located in the UK,” the message said, followed by a list including every kind of “smother” imaginable (including ass, foot, and breast smothering), plastic fetishes, all face sitting and specifically, face sitting in jeans, “butt drops,” and trampling fantasies. This isn’t the first time iWantClips has complied in advance of a threat to free speech: In October 2021, following new, strict moderation and documentation regulations set by Mastercard, the platform told creators they’d need to review their archives of content and make sure it was in compliance or risk a permanent ban.

Kinky sex has long drawn the ire of UK officials. In 2014, the British Board of Film Classification attempted to ban a litany of erotic acts from video on demand and streaming services under the The Audiovisual Media Services Regulation. Many protesters doing face-sit-ins in front of Parliament pointed out at the time that the ban was focused on acts that prioritize women’s pleasure. The ban was overturned in 2019.

UK based porn performer and producer Vex Ashley, who owns the independent studio Four Chambers, told me that when the Crime and Policing Bill went through Parliament earlier this year, she examined her back catalog and found that the work she considers her “magnum opus,” which explores the sexual archetype of the mother, could contain criminal content under this law.

“I had to go back and gut the film from the inside out,” Ashley told me. “It exists now in a very different form than it did when before. And obviously the law not only makes it illegal for me to publish it, but it also technically makes it illegal for me to possess the original cut of my film now, which just seems completely wild, considering that it’s me who is in it, and it's me talking about my own experience of my own sexuality.”

Ashley noted that attacks on sexual freedoms always come for non-normative sex first: “kink, fetish, queer and trans bodies, anything a compliance team can’t file under vanilla,” she said. This, she believes, is part of an ongoing swing toward conservatism, authoritarianism, and control.

"Even if you're somebody who doesn't care about porn, who doesn't care about sex, but you do care about this rollout of conservatism that's being force-fed to us, you can defend people's right to fuck and be fucked, and to explore that through media"

“The underlying message here is that actually, it's people's faults for being too horny, and that you should just control yourself,” she said. “That if you see this rollback in our sexual freedoms and this criminalisation of our sexual imaginations as wrong, you are just dangerous and perverted. Which is, I think, a swing back to old conservative and fascist ways of thinking about sex and freedom and bodily autonomy.” The “save the children” narratives that brought us harmful laws like FOSTA/SESTA in the US and an ongoing age verification nightmare around the world are at play with the Crime and Policing Act. In the UK, the Online Safety Act has forced people to verify their ages to use even non-sexually explicit parts of the internet. Looking at Pornhub from a UK-based IP address today, for example, you’d think it was a platform for podcasters and influencers; only once you log in and verify your age with a government ID and/or facial scan does the actual porn become visible.

Independent creators and people dependent on online sex work in the UK will be the hardest hit by this new law. Dominatrixes have reported that they’re expecting to take a financial hit. And even people and platforms outside of the UK may need to block users based in the UK from accessing their content to remain compliant. Many performers focus on specific niches to cater to audiences that seek out fetish content. But a lot of what’s being banned is already either banned by platforms or difficult to monetize, due to the extra-legal morality restrictions imposed by payment processors. Todd told me that while she enjoys the kind of content that’s now banned in the UK in her private life, she doesn’t bother uploading it to platforms where she could monetize it, because their terms of use have restricted most of it already.

Those trying to comply with the law and avoid the threat of jail time face a task. The law's guidance makes it clear that possession and publication apply retroactively. “It's easy to talk about pornography as though it's a constantly replenished stream of disposable content, but for many performers it represents years of work and a significant investment of time and money,” Todd said. “A back catalogue can be an important source of continuing income. If material has to be removed, that isn't simply a matter of changing what you film next week; it can mean losing an asset you've spent years creating.”

“Sex is a vital part of the human experience and it deserves exploration through storytelling, through media, through creation, in the same way that any other part of our experiences is,” Ashley said. “And that is not going to always be super comfortable. Sex is this very complicated, very vulnerable, very powerful thing, and it brings up a lot of things for different people.”

Deciding, as a society, that it’s not worth defending or thinking deeply about is doing us all a disservice, she said — and comes at the cost of sex workers’ safety and freedom. Faced with potential prison sentences for having a face sitting video stored on a hard drive, the freedom in this case is very literal. “Even if you're somebody who doesn't care about porn, who doesn't care about sex, but you do care about this rollout of conservatism that's being force-fed to us, you can defend people's right to fuck and be fucked, and to explore that through media... I think you can defend it even if you think it's complicated.”

23a6d17cc28a2920: OpenAI, on Thursday, released its latest cybersecurity-tuned model, GPT-6 Cyber, which the House of Altman says combines "stronger cybersecurity capabilities with better adherence to researchers’ rules of engagement."
The new model, we’re told, is much better at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, compared to GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra.

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in early September, and less than a month later, killed off the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after the model got better at pursuing tasks but worse at staying within the boundaries of what it had actually been authorized to do.
The model maker said the latest cyber model was "trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions and report results accurately."
In OpenAI's ExploitGym training evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1 percent on these same benchmark tests.

"In a separate evaluation of whether the model respects the boundaries of an assigned task, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time," Open AI said. Only 0.07 percent of cases went beyond the intended scope of the training exercise.

OpenAI declined to provide additional details about what happened in that 0.07 percent of cases and whether they involved any real-life safety or security incidents - like hacking companies or carrying out supply chain attacks as its earlier models have done during training. We do know, however, that OpenAI recently began denying internet access to the frontier models it is training to help prevent its models from doing bad things.

The latest cyber model is also really good at finding and exploiting serious security vulnerabilities, OpenAI claimed. Its researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has started fixing. The model also helped researchers develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown bugs. The Linux findings are being reported with potential patches for maintainer review.

OpenAI classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” under its Preparedness Framework. This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute end-to-end cyberattacks.

As such, it’s initially only available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers - these are customers who are authorized to use OpenAI’s models for offensive security actions such as proof-of-concept exploit development, exploit-chain validation, penetration testing, and red teaming.
Over the coming weeks, OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers, and is also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to this group, as well.
The model release comes as OpenAI makes a concerted push to improve the security of its products.
Earlier this week, OpenAI raised its bug bounty reward payments, and added new bonuses for independent researchers.

This includes quadrupling reward-range midpoints, on average, for medium, high and critical findings, so a critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000 - or up to or $51,577 after bonuses - compared to the previous $6,500 payout.
Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses.®

3d075c233b1a9144: Microsoft is applying usage limits to more Copilot Chat features for commercial users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, and it won't publish the numerical caps.

Copilot Chat comes with qualifying Microsoft 365 business and enterprise subscriptions. Without the Copilot add-on, it can reason over web information and uploaded files. The paid license adds broader access to work data, including emails, meetings, chats, and documents.
Tasks already in progress won't be interrupted. Once a limit is reached, users will receive an in-product notice explaining when to retry the affected feature.
Administrators can't adjust these limits; Microsoft sets them. The Windows behemoth says it "doesn't publish specific limits because they're subject to change."
Microsoft also suggests that hitting a limit "might indicate interest in additional Copilot capabilities." The remedy it proposes for administrators to consider is, conveniently, another license.

Users may also be offered an upgrade route – although buying a license themselves depends on whether their organization permits self-service purchases. Microsoft explained: "In most organizations, the limit notification includes an option to upgrade.

"Users can select it to request a Microsoft 365 Copilot license from their admin, who can approve or deny requests in the Microsoft 365 admin center. If the organization allows users to buy licenses directly, users might also see an option to purchase a license."
Microsoft concluded: "Admins can turn off direct purchases for each product."

The rollout began on November 2 for organizations with 2,000 or fewer Microsoft 365 seats and is due to start on November 9 for larger organizations. It also applies only to users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license in commercial tenants. Web, desktop, and mobile apps are all affected.
The change could be Microsoft's latest wheeze to turn included Copilot Chat access into paid add-on sales. Users who hit an unpublished ceiling may well start pestering administrators for an upgrade.
The alternative is that admins decide tighter controls are preferable to unpredictable feature availability. Not necessarily the sales outcome Microsoft had in mind. ®
480e162e103a09f1: October’s Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Gerd Altmann on Pixabay.

Fifteen years ago I wrote an article about “networked authoritarianism,” describing China as “exhibit A” for how an authoritarian state adapts to the internet and then adapts digital technologies to increase its own power. I sought to counter prevailing narratives of the time that the internet and tech companies were intrinsically a liberating, democratizing force. While such narratives were eventually discredited, we must not give up on our ability to use technology to defend and exercise our rights. Nor can we simply demand that governments and companies solve the problems they jointly continue to create.

October’s spotlight on Big Tech and Authoritarianism explored a range of relationships between tech companies and political actors across the global majority. Power is wielded through digital technologies in many ways. There are no quick fixes or easy solutions to stop abuses.

But we are not helpless: our Global Voices community has a role to play in strengthening solidarity and cooperation among people fighting to defend their rights, hold abusers accountable, and claim agency over our information environments.

Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts: from Brazil to Hong Kong, Kenya, Myanmar, Palestine, Venezuela, Xinjiang and beyond. They’ve told stories of how different types of governments (or sometimes political insurgents) leverage geopolitical alliances, relationships with tech companies, regulatory power, or other advantages in order to expand political or military dominance, manipulate public opinion, or exercise direct control over citizens. Meanwhile, companies use their own technologies, resources, and government relationships to expand market access and profit.

Tech power is often wielded in ways that make it harder for ordinary people to fight back against abuses. In some cases it is difficult, if not impossible, to prove who has committed what abuse and whether it was intentional — even while harm to individuals or communities has clearly occurred. In other cases, companies discover abuse of their systems to threaten, silence, surveil, or mislead users only after the damage has been done. In Brazil, one expert warns of “governance washing.” An NGO leader working in West Asia and North Africa warns of the rise of a cottage industry of organizations focused on tech accountability without measurably preventing harms.
The dangers of regulation without accountability and public oversight

In North America and Europe, government regulation of Big Tech is often touted as a silver bullet for protecting citizens from harm. But stories from Bangladesh, Kenya and the DRC illustrate different ways that without rigorous safeguards, regulation and enforcement in the name of holding Big Tech accountable can be abused by governments to threaten, track, or discredit critics and political rivals.

Our contributors pointed to conditions that must be met if we are to prevent government abuse of regulations. Laws and regulations need to be evaluated for their compatibility with human rights standards, and reformed or rejected if they fall short. Citizens — through the free press, watchdog NGOs, whistleblower protections and grievance mechanisms — need to be able to monitor and document harms and abuses with clear process for redress and remedy. Sadly, most democracies fail to hold governments — let alone companies — accountable for protecting human rights.

Then there is the even harder problem of what multinational companies should do after a coup or military takeover, leaving users’ data exposed with deadly consequences. Such cases underscore the vital importance of encryption, data security training for civil society, and corporate data minimization practices.
Rejecting techno-imperialism and great power competition

A number of stories describe how global powers leverage their national tech companies to advance strategic and economic interests well beyond their own borders. The companies in turn benefit from such relationships to expand their own global market access, serving as opaque information intermediaries and channels of digital infrastructure.

There has been much media reporting on China’s global tech strategy as a form of its growing soft power. (At the same time, at least one Chinese company insists it is operating independently and should not be treated as an agent of its home government.) But China is not acting alone: It is actually part of a network of authoritarian states, including Russia, Iran, and North Korea, building an international market for digital surveillance. Customers include many countries often described as democracies.

This eye-opening piece points out that, before the U.S. removal of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro, then vice president and now interim president Delcy Rodrígues negotiated a deal with the Chinese company iFlytek to jointly develop artificial intelligence. That company has been under U.S. sanctions since 2019, but Australian researchers identified layers of Chinese technology deployed across Venezuela. A UN fact finding mission confirmed that they remain in use despite the interim government’s close relationship with the current U.S. presidential administration.

Meanwhile, this article delves into the consequences of global market competition between the U.S. and China. While highly subsidized Chinese ICT infrastructure brings extra benefits to governments that fear their own people, in many cases Chinese tech is the only affordable option. U.S. reciprocal trade agreements that compel countries to restrict purchases of non-U.S. approved infrastructure may make it harder for signatory countries to bridge their own digital divides — which is another way of disempowering their own citizens by keeping digital services out of reach. The piece raises important questions about how countries can assert digital sovereignty to control their own digital infrastructure.
A call for global solidarity

The Chinese government exercises techno-imperialism against its own citizens. Putin’s regime does the same not only at home but in states the Kremlin views as “near abroad.” The articles in October’s spotlight cover events and harms in the global majority. But as I write from San Francisco on the day after U.S. midterm elections, the people of the U.S. are waking up to how the current occupant of the White House and his allies in Silicon Valley have been practicing techno-imperialism on them.

Tech billionaires and trillionaires have been given free rein to maximize profits at the expense of many Americans’ rights and livelihoods, while hyperscaling the government’s ability to surveil, intimidate and imprison. As this chilling piece from Palestine points out, digital surveillance technologies that are first tested in contexts of military occupation, conquest, and even genocide can be — and are — sold and deployed everywhere that governments can get away with doing so.

Several pieces in the series point to open source, decentralized, and community governed technologies as an antidote to Big Tech, exploitation and weaponization. The challenge lies with finding resources and solid legal footing to build out such technologies and systems — especially when so many governments prefer corporate partners as convenient instruments of control and influence. The good news is that cross-border networks of technologists and grassroots organizations are increasingly collaborating around an alternative vision in which communities have agency over their own information environments.

Networked authoritarianism is a global problem. We will only defeat it with global solidarity. As the African-American voting rights activist Fanny Lou Hamer said in 1971: Nobody’s free until everyone’s free.
Written by Rebecca MacKinnon

1e627e63424b095e: PARIS: French lender Credit Mutuel Arkea said on Thursday hackers had stolen around €100 million (US$112.61 million) in a cyber heist and it was working to try to recover the money, in a rare case of cybercriminals successfully stealing from a mainstream bank.

The cyberattack, which was made public on Wednesday, follows the theft last week of US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance and a wave of cyberattacks targeting internet-connected fridges in Europe. French prosecutors said they were investigating the heist.

The attackers used an account belonging to Credit Mutuel Arkea to carry out "fraudulent transactions", Credit Mutuel Arkea said in a statement on Wednesday. The funds were not in the form of cryptocurrency, the bank said, but could have been converted to crypto after being stolen.
Credit Mutuel Arkea temporarily suspended some transactions as a precaution, resulting in delays to some transfers, but said customer assets were not affected.
A spokesperson rejected media reports that its online banking subsidiary Fortuneo was the entry point for the attack, saying that neither the division nor its customers' accounts were involved.
Cyber experts told Reuters that while cyberattacks are common, it was unusual for money to be stolen virtually from a bank.
Rafay Baloch, CEO of cybersecurity and security engineering firm RedSecLabs, said the Credit Mutuel attack was unprecedented in Europe.
"We're seeing a lot of these sophisticated attacks targeted at the application layer and sophisticated social engineering attacks being targeted at banking institutions," he said.
The Paris prosecutor's office said its cybercrime unit received a complaint from Credit Mutuel Arkea on Wednesday and immediately opened an investigation, led by France's cybercrime police.

Credit Mutuel Arkea's spokesperson declined to identify the third-party service provider whose platform was used in the attack and said it had informed the European Central Bank, French banking supervisors and prosecutors. France's banking regulator, the ACPR, declined to comment.
While successful hacks of large financial institutions are rare, financial regulators globally have stepped up warnings about the risk of cyberattacks, particularly with the growth of AI.
"Any time you have a hit in the financial system, it's a big deal," said Puneet Kakkar, Managing Director at Nardello & Co in Paris.

Brittany-based Credit Mutuel Arkea is a French co-operative banking group with more than 5.8 million customers and €211.5 billion in assets. It is part of the wider Credit Mutuel banking network and is affiliated with its central body, while retaining significant strategic autonomy.
French banks typically have strong cybersecurity, due to regulatory requirements, said Kakkar. Still, he said, "cybercriminals are becoming more opportunistic and more creative."

In 2016, attackers stole US$81 million from the Bangladesh central bank account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Millions of dollars' worth of funds have also previously been stolen from banks in Russia and India during cyberattacks, Reuters has reported.--REUTERS
573fc05e2da4d43b: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture.

Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets.

Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it.

"I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here."
Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client.

"My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes."

Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company.

He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside.
The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share."
“I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file.
Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated.

But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all.

He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all.

"And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe."

He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it.

"The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

600826703541818f: The big memory manufacturers continue to print money at the expense of long-suffering buyers, with industry DRAM revenue approaching five times its level a year ago.
Demand for datacenter capacity and AI accelerators drove the 369 percent year-over-year surge in Q3 2026, Counterpoint Research reports.
"Bit shipments rose only about 4 percent this quarter, yet DRAM revenue reached nearly $200 billion, close to 5x a year ago," says Counterpoint senior analyst Jeongku Choi.

"AI has turned memory from a commodity into a valuable scarce resource, and buyers are now competing for supply rather than negotiating on price. With prices still rising, suppliers are on track to set new earnings records again next quarter."

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, the AI infrastructure boom has sent demand for server memory soaring. Manufacturers have prioritized more lucrative products for that market, squeezing supplies for PCs, smartphones, and other devices.

The consequences have been a sharp increase in memory costs, leading to higher prices of products that use it. The average price tag for a laptop or desktop was up by double-digit percentages across Europe this summer, resulting in falling PC shipments as vendors struggled to secure supplies and buyers were put off by the expense.

A similar effect has been seen in the smartphone arena, with shipments down by at least a fifth as rising memory costs squeezed budget models out of the market, leaving vendors to focus on high-end devices instead.

Price increases slowed from the steep rises seen in the first half of the year, Counterpoint says, but average DRAM selling prices still reached $1.90 per gigabit and remained the main driver of revenue growth.

Of the big three memory makers – the DRAMvirate, if you like – Samsung led with a 38 percent share of DRAM revenue. Separately, it forecast company-wide operating profit of about $80 billion for Q3, up from $9 billion a year earlier.

SK hynix posted stronger sequential growth, helping it recover some of the share it lost earlier this year, according to Counterpoint. The firm made a $62.8 billion profit, and predicts that memory shortages will persist until at least 2030.

Micron's DRAM revenue grew more slowly than rivals', but its wider business hardly suffered: fiscal fourth-quarter net profit reached $37.7 billion, exceeding its entire second-quarter revenue of $23.8 billion.

89ff999c8cc5689c: At The Money: How Do Financial Professionals Invest Their Own Money? (November 4, 2026)

Most investment authors tell you what to do with your money – but they never tell you what they do with their money. Brian Portnoy holds a PhD from the University of Chicago. His latest book is “How I Invest My Money,” foreworded by my partner, Josh Brown (CEO of Ritholtz Wealth).
Full transcript below.
About this week’s guest:

Brian Portnoy is founder and CEO of Shaping Wealth, which helps advisors and their clients to achieve “funded contentment,” and operates as an outsourced Chief Behavioral Officer. Portnoy has held senior investment roles throughout the hedge fund and mutual fund industries.
For more info, see:
Shaping Wealth Bio
LinkedIn
Twitter
At the Money: How Much Money Is Too Much?

Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here, and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts, YouTube, Spotify, and Bloomberg. And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify
TRANSCRIPT:
Bloomberg · Barry Ritholtz with Brian Portnoy, CEO of Shaping Wealth · Transcript

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Most investment authors tell you what to do with your money, but they never reveal what they do with their own money. That bothered Brian Portnoy. He spent more than 20 years in the mutual fund and hedge fund industries. He holds a PhD from the University of Chicago, and he is the CEO of Shaping Wealth. His 2018 book, The Geometry of Wealth, was really a fascinating exploration of behavioral finance and emotional intelligence. He has co-edited two editions of How I Invest My Money with my partner Josh Brown—full disclosure, Josh is at Ritholtz Wealth Management. So let’s talk a little bit about both of these books. They’re really very different from the usual investment tomes. Tell me a little bit about their genesis.

BRIAN PORTNOY: Thanks, Barry. Appreciate it. The genesis is a fun little story. It was 2019, and Josh, who you know and I know is a very sharp and good writer, published a blog with the title “How I Invest My Money,” and he made the simple observation that in all the years that he’s been in the market, no one’s really ever asked him for investment advice or financial planning advice. So he decided to write a blog that walked through how he builds his portfolio, venture investments in friends’ companies, a variety of things. And it got great feedback. It was very well done. I read it, I texted him, I said, “This was great, and hey, what do you think about getting a bunch of our friends together to write similar short blogs or chapters, and we could put it together as a volume?” And he loved the idea. I called our friend Craig Pierce at Harriman House and said, “Craig, what do you think?” I’ll say, from me texting Josh to us having a book contract was about 72 hours. Harriman House was very into it. Josh and I proceeded to build a volume of 25 contributors, and that volume was published in 2020 and really received wonderful reviews. And as you indicated, we’ve followed up with a second volume very recently.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So the really interesting thing about this is, with some people who are free to share their advice, the question comes up: Hey, might they be a little reluctant to open the kimono about how they run their own books, their own portfolios, their own household finances? Did you get any pushback from people who were a little reluctant to drop their professional personas and speak honestly about what they do with their own money?
BRIAN PORTNOY: The short answer is no. For the first volume, 25 phone calls, 25 chapters.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really?
BRIAN PORTNOY: Yeah, 25 for 25.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: That’s amazing. Second one, no hesitation? Nobody tapped out? Nobody said, “Not for me”?

BRIAN PORTNOY: Second volume, 25 for 25. But your word—hesitation. So here’s the thing, and a word that has surfaced with the publishing of these two volumes that I think is so important to being successful financially, which is permission. Effectively, we gave permission to people. They happen to be financial experts, financial advisors, portfolio managers, economists, and the like. But we gave permission to, quote unquote, go there—talk about how you invest your money. Because think about an equity fund manager. Well, they might run a large-cap equity sleeve and be very good at that, but when they think about running their money, well, they’re going to have lots of equities, lots of bonds, they’re going to have real estate, they’re going to be doing a lot of different things with their money beyond the portfolio. Charitable giving and insuring and risk management, on and on. And so the stories ended up being this unbelievable kaleidoscope of different journeys. And Barry, it’s the part that I’m proudest of in this ongoing project. Now 50 chapters, 50 completely distinct life stories from people who all know, quote unquote, the right answer. But then when invited to—and again, given their permission—to really talk about how they invest, how they allocate to the things that are important to them, they went in their own direction and expressed it in a very unique way.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m really curious about both the first 25 people in the first book and the second 25 people—or I should say the other 24 people, because I’m one of them in the second book.
BRIAN PORTNOY: Yep.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: How did you put that list together? Did you just go through the contacts on your phone, or was there a “Hey, let’s have a few of these and a few of those”? What did that look like?

BRIAN PORTNOY: It was important for me to have a diverse set of voices. One of the outcomes that I want from this ongoing project is for readers—just regular folks, friends and neighbors—to pick up the volume. You’ve now got 50 four-page chapters, very easy bite-size insights. I want people to find voices that resonate with them. And so it was important for me that we have people further along in their career, we have people who are relatively young, we have men, we have women, we have people of color. We’ve just got sort of a differentiated set of perspectives that tie into individual journeys, and those are what they are. The feedback that we’ve gotten from so many readers is exactly that: One, I was able to find some voices that really synced with my life experience, and then secondly, I read chapters from other contributors and I would’ve never thought about that particular perspective or journey. So I think it was important in both volumes to have a mix of people so that everyone can appreciate the diversity of experiences that we have with our money stories.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Did contributors get a brief—“Hey, we want you to talk about this or that”—or was it just a blank page without any structure and, “Hey, we want a thousand words. Knock yourself out”?

BRIAN PORTNOY: Completely blank page. There was a one-line instruction: Answer the question, how do you invest your money? You contributed, you saw that firsthand. In the second volume, people could look back and see what folks did in the first volume. But with the first volume, this being just a total greenfield experiment, what was really neat was to see that we gave that simple instruction and people tended not to answer the question “how I invest my money.” They leaned into why I invest my money, because we got all these wonderful stories about families and priorities and hopes and dreams and fears. So it really isn’t sort of a bullet-point list of, “Hey, I have a 75% allocation to equity and a 20% allocation to bonds and 5% allocation to real estate.” That’s not the way these turned out. Some people went into more detail on their specific investments, but without asking, what the contributors did across all 50 chapters was basically say: This is my life. This is what’s important to me, and this is how I allocate my capital. I mean, you in particular, Barry, were one of a handful of people in the two volumes who pointed out that when we’re talking about money, we’re actually talking about our capital—our financial capital, our temporal capital, our social capital, our human capital. And we’re all making decisions about what those are and how we want to invest them in order to live the life that we want.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m curious about the use of proceeds. I should have asked you this earlier, but let’s talk about the royalties on this book. This isn’t just a money grab for the authors. Tell us a little bit about that.

BRIAN PORTNOY: Anyone who publishes a book outside of someone like our friend Morgan Housel knows there’s not a lot of money in this. There really isn’t. So no, this was a labor of love. Everybody contributed their chapters without any expectation of compensation. And as I said to several of the contributors to the two volumes, if you want one twenty-fifth of the proceeds, I’m happy to send that to you. Or I could just send you a Starbucks gift card so that you can get maybe a large coffee.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m curious as to the biggest surprises in each edition. What chapters kind of leapt out at you and said, “Hey, I’ve never really thought about this aspect of money and investing quite this way before”?

BRIAN PORTNOY: It’s a good question, and I think back—volume one was published six years ago, so I’ll have to rack my brain a little bit. It was really the stories that people surfaced, and how well they were able to articulate things in their lives that brought them joy, that were important to them. So in the first volume, a couple or three people. I mean, Bob Seawright wrote a beautiful chapter about a cottage, a vacation home that his family has had for a couple of generations. And his chapter on how I invest my money was really about how do they maintain that house as a place where grandparents, parents, and grandkids can come together and enjoy life. At the same time, Dasarte Yarnway in volume one wrote a beautiful chapter—it was sort of an immigrant’s tale about how his family came from Africa, built a life in America, and how that influenced the way Dasarte thinks about his portfolio and supporting his family and community. Leighann Miko, writing about growing up in pretty intense scarcity and how that impacted her perspective on becoming a financial advisor who could help people really come along. So volume one—you asked about surprising. I wouldn’t say that I was terribly surprised. I thought I knew most of these people reasonably well. It was a delight to read their life story and learn something new about them. And the same experience carried over to volume two. Heather Robertson Fortner wrote a very personal tale about some intense childhood struggles she had that established and changed her lens on money. Samantha Russell, who many in the industry know well—tragically, at a very young age, she lost her husband to cancer and has three small children, and asked some very profound questions about what does any of this matter? Basically, like, how do I invest my money? Like, who gives a flip? I’ve had this tragedy and it has made it so clear what’s truly important. And so the money questions, which are real—because you need the portfolio, you need the insurance, you need to have the estate plan, and thankfully they had that in place before her husband passed—all of that is in this broader context of navigating life’s ups and downs, uncertainties, happiness, tragedy, and so forth. The surprise with someone’s financial strategy, not so much. The surprise is usually delightful in terms of, wow, I didn’t know that about this person—on almost every page.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. So the underlying thesis is, hey, people always tell you what to do, but they don’t tell you what they do. I’m curious: Where were the biggest gaps between the typical investment recommendations and the sort of things people either actually do or think about and talk about as part of their approach to investing?

BRIAN PORTNOY: I think across all 50 chapters, you see a pretty subjective approach to risk. We know technically that risk can be measured and managed in some quantitative ways that tell us whether or not we’re taking too much, too little, or the right amount of risk. I think what we saw across many of the chapters were narratives about how attitudes toward risk, which tended to come from childhood and adolescent experiences, then later influenced an approach to managing the family finances. A couple of specific examples. Mortgages, I think—and we could talk about whether there’s a sample bias in who came along for this journey. But on the mortgage front, there are a number of people who indicated that they paid off their mortgage early. You can run the math and you could say, well, if I don’t pay off my mortgage early and I take that extra cash flow and I invest it in the market, there’s probably going to be—depending on your rate—a delta between the rate of return in the market and your mortgage rate, and hopefully that’s a positive delta. And so it’s, quote unquote, rational to not pay off your mortgage—forget about it. A number of people, including me, have paid off their mortgage at one point or another because it just feels good to know that, leaving aside taxes, you own your home and you’re safe and you’re secure. The number one question with our money lives, with financial planning across the board, is simply: Am I going to be okay? You saw lots of these financial experts in their own way answer the question, am I going to be okay? Paying off the mortgage is one thing. Establishing that safety, holding a lot of cash—another theme that came up multiple times across both volumes. There’s a, quote unquote, optimal level of cash that you want to have in your portfolio relative to the risk you’re taking, relative to your monthly expenses, and whether you set aside six months of living expenses, whatever rule you choose. Lo and behold, we saw a number of people hold what the theory would say is too much cash. But in the same vein as paying off mortgages early, there’s a certain element of safety that comes through that, and you forsake maybe higher long-term returns for that feeling of safety now.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: We’ve all had this conversation with people, and I believe the question that we often ask is wrong. It’s not, which is mathematically the optimum solution. The question is, for you and your personality and your risk tolerance and your just sense of wellbeing, are you willing to do what is suboptimal mathematically for something that is going to be—I don’t want to say optimal, but much better psychologically, much better in terms of your comfort level? A lot of—I don’t want to say left-brain people, but a lot of the math people. And just as an aside, my CFO, Bill Sweet, and I have this ongoing discussion about, do you take the cash back on your credit card or do you take the points? And Bill, who is a CFO, says, “Well, of course you take the cash back.” And me, who has been married for nearly 35 years, says, “No, I want the points,” because $43.72 dropping into my checking account will kind of sneak by unnoticed. But when I want to buy that really stupid cappuccino maker for two grand and my wife is going to make me sleep in the backyard—“Honey, I’m getting it with points.” “Oh, go ahead then.” So sometimes the optimal mathematical solution may not be the optimal human solution.

BRIAN PORTNOY: So Daniel Crosby, who is a good friend and an expert in behavioral finance, wrote exactly about this and used the line that there’s a difference between spreadsheet optimal and behaviorally optimal. So in a sense, How I Invest My Money, both volumes one and two, are sort of masterclasses in applied behavioral finance, because we’re asking the experts to reflect on which version of optimal are you going to choose. And across the board, it was the behaviorally optimal path that they took. We know that the best financial plan is the plan that you can stick with. And so if you build the perfect plan according to modern portfolio theory, but it introduces behavioral risks that the client can’t manage, well, then you don’t have a good portfolio. So unfortunately for the ultra-left-brain folks among us, it’s life. It’s a mess. But this is what we do. This is the good stuff.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Wes Gray of Alpha Architect wrote a white paper a couple of years ago where the highest-returning combination of factors was something like deep value and momentum, but it was so volatile and the drawdowns were so fierce that he titled the paper “Even God Would Get Fired as an Active Manager.” Just to give you an idea.
BRIAN PORTNOY: I love that piece.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: The difference between mathematically and behaviorally optimum. Second to last question: Any conflicting approaches? Are there, throughout the books, different chapters that sort of lie in opposition to each other? Or are they really more, listen, we kind of forget personal finance is personal, and what’s right for one person may not be right for another?

BRIAN PORTNOY: Tim Maurer has that great line that personal finance is more personal than finance. So based on risk tolerances or approach to risk, mapping it up to goals, short-term and long-term, you see a pretty wide range of people who have more aggressive portfolios versus more conservative portfolios. The key is to understand the why. So what is it about who you are now and what you want to achieve, but also your experiences that got you here, that led you to have a portfolio that’s more balanced between stocks and bonds versus one that’s entirely in equities, where you’re okay with taking what’s likely to be more volatility in the hopes that that portfolio returns more over time? So I’d say that there are disagreements across the chapters if you put them in the same room in terms of how to invest. But the point is that all of these folks, all 50 of them, are saying, well, this is the way I invest, and it’s not in conflict with how I might manage client assets. It’s just that what I do for them isn’t perfectly mapping to my life and my constraints—taking care of kids, supporting parents as they age, things you want to do in the community. Imagine the full range of choices that we have. Even if you’re a seasoned portfolio manager with an outstanding track record or a financial advisor who’s been taking care of families for the last 20 or 30 years, your life circumstances are yours. Everybody is quite unique. So that’s what makes these chapters so fun and colorful. You could just find different smart people doing it differently.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: And last question: Did editing the book change how you invest your own money, or what you wanted to accomplish with that money?

BRIAN PORTNOY: No. No, because I think good financial planning starts by looking in the mirror. And that’s something that I’ve done a lot. I think I’ve been reasonably thoughtful about who I am and my money journey. I write about this and do this for a living. I have what I think is a healthy, ongoing dialogue with my wife about this. Increasingly we’re folding our adult children into more mature conversations about finances and legacy and things like that. So I was delighted to see the range of perspectives, the way folks wrote about answering, well, how much is enough? What risks should I take? How do I navigate this complex relationship? I learned a lot, but in terms of the way that we’ve managed our own financial assets and my philosophy, which is really based around simplicity, diversification, and compounding—I would say that those have been some anchor principles for me for a very long time. And those did not change based on editing these chapters.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”

BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.

The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
This is what they stole from us pic.twitter.com/q1GnpjF394
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026

The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.

This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.

It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.

“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a research assistant at the Anti-Defamation League who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.

In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.

During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.

"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.

“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.

Asmongold (@Asmongold) realizing in real time that he's a total fucking moron who got duped by the most cartoonishly obvious con-man of all time and ragequitting his election night coverage pic.twitter.com/XgtnqNjAaf
— kilo (@kilotonics) November 4, 2026

Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.

“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
"I see through the lies of the Democrats."
VOTE STRAIGHT TICKET REPUBLICAN pic.twitter.com/i1HjdHdAn7
— Utah College Republicans (@UtahCollegeReps) November 1, 2026

The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.

As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”

Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”

Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
It cannot be overstated how culturally significant Anakin poasting is. I dont think you could engineer a better anti-progressive memetic virus in lab if you tried.
— Max (@minordissent) October 31, 2026

Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.

“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”

Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.

In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”

It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.

She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”

“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”

Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

189779f0923d5df3: For months I’ve been speaking to an AI fraud kingpin. You might remember in 2024 we revealed the existence of OnlyFake, an underground site that let anyone generate realistic photos of fake IDs using ‘neural networks’. The creator of that site went by the handle John Wick. A while later, the creator was arrested.

Turns out there was a lot more to that story. Yuriy Nazarenko, the creator of OnlyFake, told me his side of it. How when I published my initial article he panicked, and destroyed his laptop and emails and got a new phone, paranoid that authorities were about to bust down his door. How the pressure of a growing fraud empire pushed him to drugs. And how North Korean fake IT workers used his site. Read below for his story.
The Confessions of an AI Fraud Kingpin

A few years ago, Yuriy Nazarenko sat at a desk in his grandfather’s apartment in Ukraine and, on a diet of cigarettes, Lay’s chips, and beer, painstakingly made digital copies of fake identity documents. One of his four computer screens had the messaging app Telegram open. Another displayed a scan of a passport in Photoshop filling the entire monitor.

Pixel by pixel, with rap music blaring, Nazarenko edited each part of the passport. That included the MRZ codes, the block of text printed at the bottom of identity documents; the photographs to superimpose someone else’s face into the document; and the overall dimensions and quirks of each different type of passport. Nazarenko would sometimes sit for more than 12 hours at his computer, obsessively tinkering away, with a single, high-quality fake identity document taking up to a week of work.

When someone thinks of fake IDs, maybe they imagine a spotty underage teen buying a physical counterfeit drivers’ license so they can score some beer. But in the global criminal underworld, digital copies or scans of IDs are like a skeleton key. A convincing scan of an ID or utility bill, loaded with a bogus name or someone else’s identity, can unlock the ability to make bank accounts, bypass checks on cryptocurrency exchanges to buy or sell more Bitcoin, or rent a safehouse, all while keeping the criminal’s real identity hidden. The digitally altered IDs need to fool both human reviewers and automated systems that scan them for inconsistencies. Making fake IDs requires exquisite attention to detail.

All of that manual labor doesn’t really scale, Nazarenko thought to himself as he meticulously edited passport after passport. He went on to make templates of fake identity documents that sped up the process, but it was still slow.

After many of these quiet nights, he had an idea. He built a website to automate the process that autopopulated a fake ID with the personal data a customer wanted, rather than having him do it by hand. Then, when generative AI became mainstream a short while later, he incorporated that too.
“That gradually became OnlyFake,” Nazarenko told me.

OnlyFake, the underground website Nazarenko made, landed like a bomb in the fraud world. It allowed anyone to generate not only convincing scans of drivers’ licenses or passports, but also realistic looking photos of those fake identity documents laying on a sofa, carpet, or desk, as if someone had taken the ID out of their wallet and snapped a picture of it on their phone. Needed a convincing looking photo of a California drivers’ license to open a cryptocurrency account in someone else’s name? Or a British passport to incorporate a company overseas? Or a Social Security card? No problem. The results were photos of identity documents that didn’t really exist, of people who may not be real, but yet could trick the sorts of people and companies that verify documents.

With OnlyFake, you didn’t have to be a master forger like Nazarenko to make fake documents. Now, anyone could churn out fake IDs at scale, sometimes even hundreds or thousands at a time. OnlyFake threatened the entire idea of know-your-customer, or KYC, where financial institutions take steps to know who exactly are using its services. When anyone can make a photo of a fake ID for just a few dollars in Bitcoin, is anyone really who they say they are?

Nazarenko didn’t know it then, hunched over his desk, but OnlyFake would soon become so influential that it would spawn copy cats, and the FBI would eventually arrest Nazarenko and shut down some of its competitors. The Department of Justice said in an announcement about Nazarenko’s guilty plea that OnlyFake made more than a million dollars selling fake IDs for just $15 a pop.

Now for the first time, Nazarenko, 28, free after a year in prison and living in Asia, is telling his story: how North Korean fake IT workers used his creation, how he ended up in ICE detention for months after serving his sentence in the U.S., and how OnlyFake unleashed a new age of AI-powered fraud. Nazarenko said he wanted to talk to me because I was the first journalist to reveal that OnlyFake existed. This article is based on interviews with Nazarenko and his lawyer; court records; and my own reporting in the online world of fraud that OnlyFake inhabited.

“OnlyFake was the first time I saw how quickly a small internet project could turn into something global. Unfortunately, it also taught me, in a very painful way, what can happen when the scale of something grows faster than your understanding of its consequences,” Nazarenko told me.

Growing up, Nazarenko’s parents questioned whether Nazarenko would ever find a job. His father worked for the Security Service of Ukraine. Raised in a suburb outside of Odesa, Nazarenko jumped between a few different gigs. He worked as a cook, a waiter, at a supermarket, and as a cameraman at a local Ukrainian TV station.
