a4a80543c2ee181d: PARIS, Nov 5 — Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to take to the streets across France on Thursday, as unions hold strikes alongside student-led demonstrations that have gripped the country for weeks.

The protests come as the eurozone’s second largest economy battles to redress its finances, six months ahead of elections to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in opinion polls.

The high school student movement that began with youth protesting dismal learning conditions has coincided with widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, which culminated on October 17 in the worst rioting France has seen in years.
“We should be able to make a decent living from our jobs,” CFDT union secretary general Marylise Leon said on the BFM television channel, addressing both the state and employers.

The unions are calling for an increase in the minimum wage, which has not received any discretionary boost since 2012, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.
Authorities estimate some 500,000 to 700,000 people will protest across the country on Thursday, while as many as 80,000 people are expected to march from 2pm (1300 GMT) in the capital Paris.
Unions hope for a turnout comparable to France’s pension reform protests in 2023 that saw over one million people march.
‘Firm response’
Public and private education unions have called for strike action, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.
Train travel experienced some disruption on Monday morning.
At the capital’s Montparnasse train station, a psychologist who gave her name as Jeanne said her trip had been delayed.
“It’s tedious to get up early, wait, and then see your train cancelled, but it’s understandable there’s a strike,” she said.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country, promising “an extremely firm response” to any “acts of violence” or disorder.
Dozens of high-schoolers protested in several cities.
In Paris, police used tear gas to try to prevent students from blocking access to the Helene-Boucher high school, an AFP reporter said.
The protests have been largely peaceful, with some disintegrating into clashes with police, with tear gas and water cannon fired to disperse crowds.
An attempted murder investigation has been launched after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces in Paris on Saturday.
‘Wake-up call’
The police response has been criticised as heavy-handed and internal police investigations have been launched over allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
Several teenage protesters have been seriously wounded and thousands arrested.
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes, large-scale looting and vandalism of public property that erupted on October 17.
On Wednesday, the Paris prefecture banned a major protest route, instead replacing it with an authorised route moving eastward away from the centre.
Several unions have denounced route bans as a move to repress freedom of demonstration.
A union source in the southern city of Toulouse said they would be protesting in its centre, despite a court upholding a police ban on the route.

“We can feel a cumulative effect: public sympathy for the high school and university students’ movement is not waning, and people are questioning restrictions on liberties, especially bans on demonstrations,” Fabrice Fort of the CGT union explained.
“This has sparked a wake-up call among people who usually don’t speak out much,” he added.
Similar protests have sparked in other European countries in recent weeks with youth-led demonstrations seen in Denmark, Germany and Italy. — AFP
9a88e9ef40dec43a: MUNICH, Nov 5 — Harry Kane said he felt “right at home” after he signed a two-year extension at Bayern Munich, keeping the Ballon d’Or winner at the club until 2029, the German champions announced on Thursday.
The 33-year-old England captain joined Bayern from Tottenham in 2023 and has scored 156 goals in 161 games in all competitions.
“I feel right at home at FC Bayern. I love the club, the fans and the city of Munich. We have a fantastic team and, in Vincent Kompany, a fantastic manager,” Kane said in a statement.
“It makes me very proud to be part of this club. My whole family is very happy here. I was keen to stay. I’m now looking forward to the future.”

Famously without a team trophy after over 10 years spent at boyhood club Spurs, Kane has won two Bundesliga titles and one German Cup since joining Bayern, although the Champions League has proved elusive — reaching the semi-finals twice in three campaigns.
Kane achieved the ultimate personal accolade for a footballer when he was voted the men’s player of the year at the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London last month.
He became the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 and the first Bayern player since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981 to win the award, beating France captain Kylian Mbappe into second place.
In September, Kane became the fastest player in German history to reach 100 Bundesliga goals, doing so in 98 games to shatter the previous record set by Dieter Mueller in 1977 by 31 games.

Bayern sporting director Christoph Freund said the club were “absolutely delighted” to extend Kane’s deal, adding: “With Harry Kane we have the Ballon d’Or winner on the pitch — a team player, a leader, the best all-round striker in the world.
“We all benefit from his qualities as a player and as a person, day in, day out.”
Bayern and Kane were in negotiations about the extension since August, with the duration of the deal the main sticking point, according to German media.
‘Best place possible’
Much as Premier League sides might have dreamed of luring him back to England, Kane’s longer-term Bayern future has never been in doubt.
He has repeatedly thanked the city, the club and its fans for warmly welcoming him to southern Bavaria.
Last season, Kane said contract talks would take place after the World Cup in which England bowed out in the semi-finals to Argentina.
In August, he told FourFourTwo magazine his desire to return to the Premier League had waned.
“When I first left, for sure it was something that I thought I’d definitely be coming back. That itch isn’t there as much anymore.
“I’m extremely happy here in Munich. It’s opened my eyes to a totally different world of football outside of England. It’s made me appreciate European football even more.
“With the team we have here, with the manager. My family are really settled here. It’s just about being in the best place possible.
“I never say never but, for now, I’m concentrating on Bayern Munich, and we’ll see what the future holds.”

Kane scored 61 goals for Bayern last campaign and 12 for England, bringing him to an incredible 73. That mark was bettered only once this century, by Lionel Messi in 2011-12, who scored 82 in a Ballon d’Or-winning season.
Kane reserved special praise for the club in his Ballon d’Or acceptance speech.

“Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn’t be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much,” he said after collecting the award.
Bayern won the league and cup double last season while pushing eventual winners Paris Saint-Germain all the way in a wild semi-final, with the French side triumphing 6-5 on aggregate over two legs.

This season, Bayern are the only remaining undefeated club in Europe’s top five leagues. The Bavarians sit atop the Bundesliga table, ahead of Dortmund on goal difference, and are 13th in the Champions League table after four of eight league phase matches. — AFP
c0b233248cc7b0fc: PARIS: Shares in Air France-KLM climbed over 12% Thursday after the carrier surprised investors with higher operating profit in the third quarter (Q3) despite a soaring jet fuel bill.
Like other airlines, Air France-KLM has raised ticket prices to cope with the surge in fuel costs as the US-Israeli war on Iran keeps global energy costs high.
Operating profit in the July to September period, one of the busiest for airlines, increased 10% to €1.35 billion (US$1.5 billion), the company said, with passenger traffic up 1.8%.
Unit revenue per available seat kilometres (ASK), a key profitability measure for the industry, rose 6.6% to €9.70 cents.
Higher ticket prices helped cushion the blow from fuel costs, which were €436 million higher in the third quarter compared to the period last year.
"Strong unit revenues fully offset the impact of higher fuel prices amid the Middle East crisis," the airline said.
For the full year it expects total fuel costs to hit €9.3 billion, up €2.3 billion from last year.
"This performance reflects the benefits of the strategic choices we have made in recent years, starting with Air France's move upmarket," group chief executive Benjamin Smith said in a statement.
The airline said it would also pursue "additional structural measures" to improve profitability at KLM, its Dutch unit whose margins have lagged behind Air France's.
In a separate statement, KLM said the restructuring would include a further 15% cut in overall jobs, with around 5,000 posts "reorganised".
It aims to eventually boost earnings by €1 billion a year.
Air France-KLM shares were up 12.5% at €12.69 on the Paris stock exchange.
830af81e3142292d: KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit extended its gains against the US dollar and other major currencies on Thursday after Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) kept the overnight policy rate (OPR) unchanged at 2.75%.
The decision was made during the central bank’s final monetary policy committee meeting of the year today.
At 6pm, the local note rose to 4.0445/4.0490 versus the greenback from Wednesday’s close of 4.0610/4.0660.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the decision to keep the OPR unchanged at 2.75% was in line with estimates.
He said BNM is seen to be positive about the current state of the economy, with the 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) growth expected to settle above 5%.
“At the same time, the balance of risks is seen to be stable although concerns on higher inflation going forward warrant a cautious stance.

“On that note, the case for a 25-basis point hike in OPR during 2027 should not be ruled out and perhaps it could happen in the first quarter of 2027. As such, this could provide further support to the ringgit,” he told Bernama.

Afzanizam also said the US midterm elections were a key driver of market sentiment today as a Democrats-controlled Congress could mean more scrutiny on President Donald Trump administration's policies.
“Consequently, Brent crude oil fell below US$100 to US$95.12 per barrel currently, while the US Dollar Index (DXY) fell by 0.14% to 101.423 points,” he said.

Meanwhile, SPI Asset Management managing partner Stephen Innes said market sentiment was also supported by a decline in US Treasury yields following the sharp overnight drop in crude oil prices, as the geopolitical risk premium was effectively stripped from the oil market.
He said traders were increasingly convinced that a return to conflict with Iran was unlikely, easing inflationary concerns in the US bond market.

“The currency is taking its cues from external developments rather than domestic monetary policy. That said, the US dollar has not weakened significantly, and I expect that's because the US Federal Reserve (Fed) is still expected to raise rates in December.

“Until those expectations begin to unwind, there's probably a limit to how far the ringgit can appreciate. For now, the direction of crude oil prices and the Fed's reaction function as the two big moving parts for Asian currencies, including the ringgit,” he added.
The ringgit traded higher against a basket of major currencies.

It strengthened versus the Japanese yen to 2.5548/2.5578 from 2.5636/2.5669 at Wednesday’s close, appreciated against the euro to 4.5428/4.5478 from 4.5723/4.5779 yesterday, and edged up vis-a-vis the British pound to 5.4455/5.4516 from 5.4783/5.4850 previously.
However, the ringgit performed mostly lower against its Asean peers.

The local currency gained versus the Singapore dollar to 3.1679/3.1717 from the previous close of 3.1771/3.1813, but slipped against the Thai baht to 12.1013/12.1199 from 12.0673/12.0868 yesterday, inched down versus the Indonesian rupiah to 223.6/224.0 from 223.5/223.8, and fell vis-a-vis the Philippine peso to 6.42/6.43 from 6.39/6.40.
2911d8bf4e68a2bc: SAP has taken meaningful steps in opening its data to bidrectional sharing across the enterprise, and in decoupling the advanced analytics needed for AI from its ERP upgrade path.

During a technical conference last week, the German software giant adopted native support for Apache Iceberg, the open table format, and extended its partnership with Databricks to bring data from legacy ERP systems into its modern cloud analytics platform.

"By putting [a] stake in the ground with Iceberg, we now have SAP moving from a very closed application storage model to an open lakehouse model," said Aaron Rosenbaum, Gartner senior director analyst, referring to the concept which brings together data lakes and warehouses.

Also important was the bridge between modern analytics in the cloud and on-prem or hosted legacy systems such as ECC, the ERP system broadly adopted by global companies. "SAP made a pretty big move in saying we're going to open this up, not just to S/4HANA Cloud [the latest ERP system], but ECC users. That coupling — leveraging of AI, leveraging a lakehouse for AI to the ERP upgrade lifecycle — was a problem," said Rosenbaum.

In May this year, SAP bought Dremio, a lakehouse platform built around Apache Iceberg, ending its previous preference for Databricks' Delta Sharing to bring together SAP data products with existing lakehouses bi-directionally.

At SAP's TedEd conference last week, SAP said its Business Data Cloud (BDC) – the "trusted data foundation for SAP Business AI Platform" – would now support native Apache Iceberg and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris, "providing an open and governed data foundation for users and [AI agent platform] Joule to consume data."

Together with SAP BDC Connect, the new tech policy will support platform interoperability with "zero-copy data sharing" across platforms from Databricks, Snowflake, Google, AWS, and Microsoft. The system would also continue to support Delta Lake, the alternative open table format from Databricks, SAP said.
With the integration of Dremio's SQL query engine, BDC users will also get access to relational databases including SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without moving data, the vendor said.

During the same conference, Databricks – the lakehouse company born out of an Apache Spark platform – extended its partnership with SAP based on the previously announced SAP Databricks, which embeds the Databricks Data + AI Platform in BDC.

That "expanded scope" promises to make data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. The vendor said that a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, for example, could use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring historic order data into SAP Databricks, combining it with third-party data, and allowing data engineers to build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines. They can keep that work as they move to the cloud, Databricks suggested.

This being 2026, the hoped-for output from all of this data engineering is not just business insight, but automated action, by way of AI agents. SAP has its Joule AI assistant and agentic platform, while Databricks has Genie, and the two companies have promised to bring them together.

The increasing openness is good for users who will get more options in plotting a strategy to bring together enterprise data, leaving them pondering over where to put the business context layer, which vendors will no doubt fight to control, Rosenbaum said.

"You have the comment that they're going to bring Joule and Genie together in the future. This is pointing to a struggle that's going on throughout enterprises and throughout all the vendors about the context layer. I don't necessarily see that there's one winner. You do have different points of context within the transaction system and across the whole business, and they have been points of tension.
"Lack of single vendor lock-in is important. It's something that all the customers are struggling with: how do we build these context layers and deliver sort of consistent answers?"

SAP's shift in the direction of openness is likely to help users in this struggle, whether they choose to build the context layer within the ERP vendor's data platform using its semantic layer, or outside of it using tools from other vendors – there are plenty of companies offering help for those opening their wallets.
Nonetheless, whichever path users choose, a lot of work lies ahead. ®

b968e4ad148f7ea9: The young men and Hispanic and Latino voters who helped propel Donald Trump to his presidential victory in 2024 swung sharply towards the Democrats in the midterm elections, contributing to the historic defeat for Republicans. Charles Hunt, an associate professor of political science at Boise State University in Idaho, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast that the results suggest weakened support for Trump and his MAGA movement among these key groups of voters. Hispanic and Latino voters “swung heavily towards Trump in 2024”, Hunt says. But midterm results in Florida, Texas and elsewhere “are showing these voters just slingshotting completely in the other direction,” he explains, citing early exit polls and analysis by The New York Times. Not just back towards where they were in, say, 2018 or 2020 in terms of support for Democrats, but past that – being more supportive of folks like James Talarico in Texas than they have been of any Democrat in the last 20 years. That’s really, really significant, especially since that’s a growing part of the electorate. The New York Times’ analysis of voting trends reveals young voters swung back toward the Democratic Party by more than 30 percentage points – the largest shift of any age group. Young men, in particular, swung strongly back towards the Democrats. The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of voters across all 50 states, shows Democrats regaining ground among young and Hispanic voters, too. The scale of the Republicans’ defeat goes beyond the usual midterm backlash against a sitting president, Hunt says. He draws a comparison with the 1974 midterm elections following the Watergate scandal and then-President Richard Nixon’s resignation: This is a level of […] midterm blowback against an incumbent president of the sort that we haven’t seen since 1974. […] It’s really pretty historic and in a completely different league than 2018. So what drove voters towards the Democrats? Economic pressures are one reason, Hunt says. He points to the effects of the Iran war and tariffs, particularly on highly visible costs such as petrol: A lot of political science tells us that economic issues are almost always front of mind for voters. But those pressures also gave force to Democratic messaging about corruption and an economy favouring billionaires. He adds: I think those issues tie together with a lot of Democratic messaging around things like corruption, and the influence of billionaires, and Elon Musk spending half a billion dollars in this election probably did not help, at the end of the day. aa77b635d887aeb9: A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.
ada58846ea285577: TOKYO, Nov 5 — Japanese gaming giant Nintendo reported a drop in quarterly net profit today as unit sales slowed for its Switch 2 console, but maintained its annual forecasts.
A remake of 1990s action-adventure classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which comes out today has sparked nostalgic fan excitement.
But market analysts will be watching to see how much the title can boost sales of the Switch 2, which became the world’s fastest-selling games console on its 2025 release.
Nintendo reported an 11 per cent year-on-year rise in net profit for the first half of 2026-27.
But in the second quarter, from July-September, net profit was down 29 per cent to 73.5 billion yen (US$465.3 million) -- missing estimates of 82.2 billion yen in a Bloomberg survey of analysts.
The company maintained its annual net profit forecast of 310 billion yen.

“Although sales declined year-on-year due to lower hardware unit sales, operating profit rose” nearly 50 per cent in the first six months, due to steady sales of games and a windfall connected to US tariff refunds, Nintendo said.
The company sold nearly 6.5 million Switch 2 consoles in the first half, down from nearly 10.4 million the previous year, when the gadget was new.
This year Nintendo raised the price of Switch 2, as the global artificial intelligence boom causes the price of memory chips used in everyday electronics to soar.
Memory chip shortage
Some analysts have also said the lack of any blockbuster title to boost Switch 2 adoption among gamers has led to sluggish sales of the console.

“While working to bring Nintendo Switch 2 to more consumers, we will also leverage the Nintendo Switch hardware installed base and rich software lineup to expand software sales and maintain engagement,” the company said Thursday.
Nintendo’s latest addition to its long-running Zelda series, “Ocarina of Time”, is being released gradually across the world as part of the 40th anniversary of the saga.
It has already garnered widespread praise with a score of 96 out of 100 on aggregator site Metacritic by the eve of its release, putting it among the best-reviewed titles of the year so far.
Sony raises forecast
Sony upgraded its annual earnings forecast for the current fiscal year today thanks to robust sales of its games, music and movies.
The firm now expects to earn 1.33 trillion yen for the year to March, up from the previous upgraded forecast of 1.21 trillion issued in July.
The Japanese tech-entertainment conglomerate said second-quarter net profit jumped 44 percent to 449.6 billion yen, driven largely by games and films.
For the game operations, sales were helped by favourable foreign exchange rates but also strong sales of new titles.
In the movie segment, it noted an “increase in theatrical revenues primarily due to the contribution of ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’”.
The film was released in July and was a blockbuster success.
The game segment is also expected to benefit from the eagerly awaited November launch of “Grand Theft Auto VI”, which is predicted to be the biggest release in gaming for years. — AFP
904c44b6cf569f5f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 5 — Maritime Network Sdn Bhd has issued a letter of demand (LOD) to Singapore-based Olam Global Agri Pte Ltd seeking clarification over the alleged commingling of Indonesian and Malaysian palm oil cargoes before they were shipped to Egypt.

The LOD, dated October 29 and served through law firm Jaya Prem Chambers, disputes an assertion allegedly made by Olam Global Agri that Maritime Network had prior knowledge of, and consented to, the cargo arrangements before it issued three bills of lading dated September 30, 2026.
According to the LOD, Maritime Network was appointed by the vessel’s owner as port agent for its call at Port Klang and signed the bills of lading on behalf of the vessel’s master.

The letter said the vessel had loaded about 35,432 tonnes of palm oil products at Dumai, Indonesia, before taking on a further 4,999.715 tonnes of Malaysian crude palm olein at Port Klang for shipment to Adabiya, Egypt.

It said the Indonesian outward manifest and accompanying documents described the cargo as refined palm oil products, including refined palm olein, refined, bleached and deodorised (RBD) palm oil, RBD palm stearin and RBD palm kernel oil.

However, Maritime Network said it later received information raising questions over whether the Malaysian crude palm olein had been commingled with the Indonesian cargo, and whether the actual grade of certain Indonesian products matched their descriptions in the shipping documents.
The LOD acknowledged that the precise nature, composition, timing and extent of any alleged commingling remained subject to documentary verification.

It also referred to WhatsApp correspondence dated October 16, in which an Olam Global Agri representative allegedly claimed to have previously spoken to Maritime Network and informed it that the cargo was crude.

The law firm said its client disputed that the correspondence established prior notification or informed consent, adding that no contemporaneous written notification or documentary evidence of such consent had been produced.
The LOD sought details of the alleged communication, including the persons involved, the date and time, the information disclosed and the terms of any purported agreement or approval.

It also referred to emails dated October 19 and 23, in which Olam Global Agri’s representative reportedly said the company had bought the Malaysian cargo from Mewah Oils Sdn Bhd on free-on-board (FOB) terms and was not the exporter of record.
The law firm said its client was not suggesting that Olam Global Agri had automatically assumed the exporter’s statutory obligations by buying the cargo on FOB terms.
However, it maintained that the company’s involvement in the vessel’s chartering arrangements, and any instructions on loading, stowage, commingling and documentation, required clarification.

Among the documents sought were cargo quality certificates, certificates of analysis, stowage plans, quantity measurement records, surveyor reports and communications involving the vessel’s master, owner, terminal operators and shipping agents.

The LOD also cited Regulation 12 of the Malaysian Palm Oil Board (Quality) Regulations 2005, including Regulation 12(3)©, which concerns the disclosure of the ingredients and composition of blended oil palm products in relevant commercial and shipping documents, where applicable.

The law firm said its client was not making a final determination on whether any regulatory breach had occurred, adding that the matter would have to be assessed by the competent authorities based on the evidence.

Olam Global Agri was given seven days from receipt of the LOD to provide documentary evidence supporting its position on prior notification and consent, or to withdraw the allegation if it could not be substantiated.
The LOD also sought an indemnity against specified claims and losses to the extent they are attributable to the company’s conduct, and reserved Maritime Network’s right to pursue legal remedies.
7711a7fecc8d4aa9: PETALING JAYA: AirAsia Group Bhd shares surged today as crude oil prices dropped sharply on growing hopes for an end to the Iran war following the US midterm elections where president Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered a drubbing.
AirAsia shares jumped as much as 25% or 11.5 sen to 57 sen this morning as Brent crude fell below US$100 per barrel yesterday, the first time since Oct 7.

The stock pared some of its gains in the afternoon session, and was trading at 54 sen, an 8.5 sen or 18.7% increase, at the time of writing. At this price, AirAsia has a market capitalisation of RM1.81 billion. A total of 81 million shares were traded.

Brent oil traded as high as US$118 per barrel last Friday but was at around US$95, and WTI crude at US$88, earlier today. Despite the drop, the price of oil remains 60% higher compared with the start of the year. The war, which erupted in February, sent the price of crude oil and diesel skyrocketing.
Energy experts are watching closely for a sign that Tuesday’s midterm election results would pressure Trump into ending the Iran war without further escalation.

High jet fuel costs have weighed on airline stocks since the war began, even though equity markets have been performing strongly. In the case of AirAsia, its share price had plummeted by 70% year to date.
Research analysts say a further decline in fuel prices and easing of Middle East geopolitical tensions are needed for a sustained recovery in airline stocks.
AirAsia, which employs about 17,000 people regionally, is reported to be seeking fresh funding to counter headwinds from rising jet fuel prices and foreign exchange losses.
The Edge reported on Oct 1 that the fundraising effort was backed by the ministry of finance, which has highlighted AirAsia’s significant role in the country’s aviation sector.
In 2025, the airline accounted for about 41% of the 104.5 million passenger movements recorded at airports operated by Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd, and nearly 60% of domestic passenger movements.
AirAsia saw its net loss widen to RM527.16 million for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, from RM154.88 million a year ago while revenue fell 14.5% to RM5.09 billion.
As of June 30, the group had net debt of RM2.27 billion, with cash reserves of RM953.67 million against total borrowings of RM3.13 billion. The group also has RM13.3 billion in lease liabilities.

116a664aec224964: Royal London plans to cut hundreds of IT jobs and shift work to India under an outsourcing deal with IBM, according to sources, with redundancies expected by the end of December.

Sources said Royal London's chief technology officer, James Sandell, told IT staff in September that the insurance and pensions giant was partnering with IBM to outsource a substantial portion of its technology operations. A consultation process was expected to follow.

A Royal London spokesperson told The Register: "Royal London has appointed IBM as its strategic technology infrastructure partner as it continues to develop its technology strategy. The partnership will give Royal London access to IBM’s specialist capability, scale and experience. Royal London will remain accountable for service delivery and regulatory requirements and continues to focus on ensuring continuity and quality of service for customers."
We asked Royal London how many UK IT roles it would retain and whether IBM would move work to India.

The exact number of jobs at risk remains unclear, although one Glassdoor review posted on October 6 claims that hundreds of positions in the company's technology operations division are being eliminated.
"A vast amount of knowledge is being lost by the business, a lot that is not yet documented due to constant years of recruitment freeze and workload volume," they wrote.

The reviewer also questioned whether management had grasped just how much work would be involved in handing operations over to IBM, particularly with already stretched teams being cut to a fraction of their former size.
Royal London replied to the Glassdoor review, acknowledging staff concerns about the changes, though it didn't comment on the claims about outsourcing and redundancies.

"We recognise that as Royal London is going through a period of transformation, this has raised questions and concerns for some colleagues," the company wrote. "We have established channels for colleagues to raise these, including through People Leaders and Colleague Representatives, and I encourage colleagues to use these routes to discuss their concerns."
Other October reviews questioned the handling of the outsourcing and Royal London's commitment to its mutual values.
An October 12 reviewer identifying themselves as an IT infrastructure employee said the company had historically offered good career prospects, before criticizing its new direction.

cecdb40ec5b3ec06: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 5 — Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has decided to maintain the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) at 2.75 per cent following its final Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting of the year today.
In a statement, the central bank said the latest indicators pointed to continued resilience in global growth, supported by strong global technology investment and stable labour markets.
“At the current OPR level, the MPC considers the monetary policy stance to be consistent with the outlook of continued price stability and sustainable economic growth,” it said.
BNM said the MPC would remain vigilant to evolving conditions and assess their implications for the balance of risks surrounding the outlook for domestic inflation and economic growth.
Year-to-date, headline and core inflation averaged 1.8 per cent and 1.9 per cent, respectively, the central bank said.
Looking ahead to 2027, geopolitical developments, elevated global commodity prices and adverse weather conditions are expected to exert upward pressure on inflation.
Both headline and core inflation are therefore expected to edge higher, although they are likely to remain contained amid continued domestic policy measures and stable demand conditions.
“The MPC will remain vigilant to cost pressures and domestic demand conditions given their impact on the inflation outlook,” BNM said.
Inflation has edged higher following an increase in energy costs and is expected to remain elevated as higher costs continue to be passed through to consumer prices.

On the global outlook, BNM said uncertainties surrounding geopolitical developments would continue to weigh on growth and fuel inflationary pressures. However, the impact is expected to be cushioned by sustained technology-related spending and continued adaptation to supply constraints.

Downside risks to global growth include prolonged geopolitical tensions, tighter global financial conditions arising from monetary policy adjustments, concerns over financial market valuations and fiscal vulnerabilities.
“Upside potential could come from stronger technology spending and a faster-than-expected recovery in supply chain conditions,” the central bank said.
On the domestic front, recent indicators point to continued strength in economic growth in the third quarter of 2026, underpinned by robust exports and sustained domestic demand.
The solid momentum is expected to lift full-year growth in 2026 to above five per cent.
“Looking ahead, the economy’s sound fundamentals are expected to keep growth resilient in 2027.
“The external sector is expected to remain a major driver of growth, supported by the ongoing global technology upcycle and firm tourist spending,” BNM said.
Stable labour market conditions and continued investment activity are also expected to support domestic demand, while measures under Budget 2027 will provide further impetus to private consumption.
However, the growth outlook remains subject to downside risks, including a prolonged conflict in the Middle East and lower commodity production.
On the upside, stronger-than-expected global growth, firmer technology-related export demand and higher tourism activity could provide additional support to economic expansion, BNM added. — Bernama
22b3559c44474108: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 5 — Malaysia stood out in Southeast Asia’s initial public offering (IPO) market in the first nine months of 2026, accounting for 38 of the 56 listings recorded across the region, according to Ernst & Young (EY).

The 38 IPOs raised US$1.62 billion (RM6.56 billion, based on US$1=RM4.05), compared with US$992 million (RM4.02 billion) raised through 37 listings in the corresponding period last year, stated EY in a factsheet today.

In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026), Malaysia recorded nine IPOs raising US$167.2 million (RM677.2 million), compared with eight IPOs that raised US$94 million (RM380.7 million) in the same quarter last year.

Among other Southeast Asian markets, Singapore recorded eight IPOs raising US$1.28 billion (RM5.18 billion), followed by Indonesia with seven IPOs raising US$121.3 million (RM491.3 million) and Thailand with three IPOs raising US$21.3 million (RM86.3 million).
Southeast Asia recorded 56 IPOs raising US$3 billion (RM12.15 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, a decline of 26 per cent in volume and 13 per cent in value year-on-year.

EY Capital Markets representative Nghia Trung Nguyen said Malaysia exceeded both the number of listings and proceeds recorded over the same period last year.
“The stronger proceeds are encouraging and point to continued investor appetite for quality companies with compelling growth prospects.

“This momentum also reflects the role of the capital market in supporting companies as they pursue their next phase of growth, providing access to capital while broadening their investor base and market profile,” he said in a statement.
Nghia said issuers needed to be well-prepared and realistic about market timing and investor expectations amid an uncertain global environment, as investors became increasingly selective.

He added that a compelling business proposition, supported by strong fundamentals, good governance and a clear growth strategy, remained crucial to securing a successful listing and sustaining investor confidence beyond the IPO.

EY Asean IPO leader Chan Yew Kiang said regulatory reforms, a muted economic outlook and geopolitical uncertainties had dampened listing sentiment across the region, prompting IPO aspirants to adopt a more cautious approach.

“Hence, in 3Q 2026, except Malaysia, IPO transaction counts across Southeast Asia slowed compared with the same period last year. Exchanges in the region also began to focus on unlocking shareholders’ value through different initiatives.

“For example, in Singapore, while the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) that was introduced in February 2025 had injected liquidity and vibrancy into the local exchanges, more needs to be done by corporates to improve liquidity and post-IPO performance,” he said.

Globally, EY said there were 908 IPOs that raised US$290 billion (RM1.17 trillion) in the first nine months of 2026, representing a two per cent decline in deal volume but a 153 per cent increase in proceeds compared with the corresponding period in 2025.
It said for 3Q 2026, there were 387 IPOs that raised US$95.6 billion (RM387.2 billion), compared with 374 IPOs that raised US$52 billion (RM210.6 billion) over the same period in 2025.

In terms of regional performance, EY said Asia-Pacific recorded 399 IPOs raising US$93.2 billion (RM377.5 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 14 per cent in volume and 79 per cent in proceeds year-on-year.

Meanwhile, the Europe, Middle East, India and Africa (EMEIA) region recorded 389 IPOs raising US$30.2 billion (RM122.3 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, representing a one per cent increase in volume and six per cent in proceeds year-on-year.

669a0c8f4c667cce: Google Cloud has revealed that the cause of the October 20 outage in its europe-west-2-b availability zone was a ‘misconfiguration’ of its systems that meant its emergency generators didn’t start.
The outage at the London facility caused service interruptions at outfits including Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and Revolut.
In a November 4 update to its service status page, Google explained what went wrong.

“The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture — where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load — backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC),” Google revealed.

The facility gets its juice from two independent utility feeders, which Google calls “A” and “B”. There’s also a “standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events.”
Google says the root cause of the incident was failure in an external underground cable through which its power supplier brings ‘leccy to its bit barns.
That cable connects to primary feeder A and it broke at a time when feeder B wasn’t working.

“Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026,” Google admitted. “Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.”
That shouldn’t be a problem for a top-tier operator like Google, which knows it needs to install backup sources of electricity like uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and on-site generators.
Indeed, europe-west-2-b employs UPSes that Google says can keep things up and running for five minutes if the availability zone loses its connection to the grid.
The UPSes worked, but a “voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load.”
Google’s UPSes therefore ran out of juice, but its generators didn’t start. The rest is history.
The search giant has figured out that its PLCs weren’t set up to handle the conditions it faced on this fateful day.

“PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant,” the status update reveals.
Once Google was able to reconnect to its power utility, it reprogrammed the PLC so it wouldn’t make the same mistake again.
The Big G has since made many changes to the electrical setup at europe-west-2-b and says it’s tested them and that they all work.

It’s also given itself two action items, one of which it describes as a “Communications Enhancement” that will see it “bolster notification speed by developing an automated alert-to-communication mechanism for location-impacting incidents.”
The other is to “expand platform-wide testing outcomes for infrastructure-level events.”
Once Google gets that done, perhaps it will be able to handle outages better – and if not, at least advise customers about its troubles more quickly. ®
cf403874a276142d: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?

e8bf6269fd8b236d: Anna Moneymaker/Getty The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections puts them in a stronger position to interfere with President Donald Trump’s agenda. This includes his deeply unpopular and costly war against Iran, which could be among their first priorities. As president, Trump will be able to veto any legislation aimed at ending the war. But the Democrats still have another powerful card up their sleeves: cutting off funding for the war. There are caveats, however. History suggests exercising this power could trigger a political confrontation that may backfire. And even if the Democrats succeed in ending the war, they may not be able to reverse the damage it has done to the US’ global standing. The limits of legislation Democrats will have three main options to try to force the war against Iran to a close. Two of these, however, face significant limitations. The first – and perhaps most obvious – option is through legislation. There are a few different ways to do this. One approach is to pass a resolution calling for an end to the war. Congress already attempted this in June, passing a concurrent resolution (with the support of some Republicans) that directed the president to either withdraw US forces from hostilities against Iran or seek the approval of Congress before continuing. This was done under the War Powers Resolution of 1973. These so-called concurrent resolutions are, however, widely seen as non-binding. Intended to express the opinion or will of Congress, they are generally used to deal with internal matters within Congress. Trump ignored it. A similar resolution then failed in the Senate in September. For such a resolution to be binding, it would need the force of a law passed by Congress, which the president would likely veto. To overcome that veto, the Democrats would need the support of a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This would require a significant number of Republicans to cross the aisle. Exercising oversight A second option for the Democrats is to launch a series of congressional investigations into the way the war has been conducted. This would likely include public hearings, subpoenas and demands for documents from the Trump administration. The Democrats may also attempt to impeach senior officials in the Trump administration. If Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat tipped to become the next speaker of the House, wants to appease some of the more progressive voices in his party – or the hardline voices on the Iran war or against Trump – Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be targeted for impeachment. But the grounds for such proceedings are unclear at this stage, and even with the Democrats’ new Senate majority, he would be unlikely to be convicted unless a significant number of Republicans crossed the aisle. More pertinently, congressional investigations are a protracted process, and unlikely to bring the war to a swift end. The ‘power of the purse’ The more immediate power that Congress has to end the war swiftly is in Article I, Section 9 of the US Constitution, which states: No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law […] This is known as the “power of the purse”. Once the new Congress is sworn in in January, every new dollar that Trump’s Department of War wants to spend needs to be approved by the House and the Senate. A Democrat-controlled Congress could put a clause into the defence budget, prohibiting funds from being used for hostilities against Iran. Trump could veto this, but this would mean blocking the paycheck for everyone in the military, as well. The Democrats tried this very approach in 2007, attempting to force a timetable for a US withdrawal from Iraq. Then-President George W. Bush vetoed it, but it became a political football, with both sides accusing the other of leaving US troops unfunded. The Democrats ultimately backed down due to the growing risk of backlash from voters. Today, this approach would carry a similar risk. Are the Democrats willing to put their political credibility on the line if the president accuses them of letting American soldiers down? Who blinks first? Republicans face a reckoning As the dust settled on Wednesday, Trump himself acknowledged the Iran war had played a role in the Republican Party’s crushing defeat. But he doubled down on the decision, saying he would do it all over again if necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Vice President JD Vance was less defensive. In a detailed statement posted to X, Vance bluntly declared the war was the reason the Republicans lost. He added, “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there”. Vance has long criticised US military involvement in overseas conflicts, but in his role as vice president has publicly backed Trump’s actions against Iran. 16de4ca3c25d3eed: In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device. This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifies entries in a robot’s memory that might be wrong and corrects the descriptions of mislabeled objects.  In the future, this method could make household or industrial robots better able to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as clearing a dining room table or working alongside human collaborators to assemble a piece of machinery.  Called UQ-DAAAM (which stands for Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), the system compares multiple descriptions of the same object, seen from different viewpoints, to quantify the robot’s uncertainty about what it saw.  It then selects additional views to reduce the uncertainty and combines these captions into a more accurate description of the object, which it saves to memory. The researchers also employed a special technique to streamline this process so a mobile robot can continually update uncertain memory entries in real time.  When compared to baseline methods, UQ-DAAAM boosted the robot’s confidence and improved the accuracy of its answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when it saw them.  “Contrary to ChatGPT, when we think about physical AI, it is not enough to simply put a disclaimer cautioning that sometimes the robot might be wrong. Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro), principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), director of the MIT SPARK Laboratory, and the senior author of the paper presenting UQ-DAAAM. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Harry Zhang and Nicolas Gorlo. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  Amending memory This new method builds on the researchers’ prior work, DAAAM, a robot memory system that uses a vision-language model (VLM) to richly describe objects in scenes a robot captures with its onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored as detailed captions in a 3D map-based representation of the robot’s environment that it can call upon later to answer questions.  But the robot sometimes sees objects only partially or from far away, or its camera might capture blurry or poorly lit images. In these cases, DAAAM might describe these objects incorrectly, such as by mistaking a gray chimney for a squirrel perched on a rooftop. “With no way to correct itself, this wrong memory would persist as the robot proceeds in its environment, which could impact downstream applications,” Zhang says. UQ-DAAAM integrates uncertainty quantification into the DAAAM framework. It allows the robot to measure its confidence in the accuracy of object descriptions and fix incorrect captions as it travels through an environment. While on the move, the robot constantly collects and stores images of the world around it. Many of these images show the same objects captured from different angles. UQ-DAAAM uses these additional viewpoints to identify and correct unreliable descriptions. First, it calculates the VLM’s confidence level in the words it generated to describe a potentially mislabeled object. Then, it measures consistency by comparing this description to captions of images that describe the same object from different vantage points. “We fuse both sources of uncertainty into a single number that captures how certain the VLM is in its overall understanding of the object,” Carlone explains. If that number exceeds a certain threshold, the uncertainty is too high, and UQ-DAAAM will refine the caption by using additional images of the object. It does this using a heuristic, or simple rule, that determines which additional viewpoints will reduce the robot’s uncertainty about the object. For instance, it might choose an image captured a few frames later that clearly shows smoke emanating from the chimney.  The researchers mathematically proved that this heuristic can identify the best frames to select without rerunning the VLM, dramatically reducing the amount of computation.  “The key challenge Nico and Harry had to overcome is how to combine VLMs with uncertainty quantification into something that is running in a fraction of a second on a robot that is moving,” Carlone says. Remembering with confidence Once it has identified additional captions that will reduce its uncertainty about the object, the system uses an LLM to fuse them into a single object description. To boost accuracy, the LLM puts more weight on new captions and those with less ambiguity. This refinement step is able to resolve ambiguities for about 92 percent of the objects in the robot’s environment, while only requiring two additional captions per object. It increased the accuracy of object descriptions by 5 percent compared to the state of the art. UQ-DAAAM also provided more accurate answers to questions about the objects it observed, where it saw them, and when it last encountered them than baseline methods. “Performing this uncertainty quantification procedure across the entire map the robot generates allows it to improve its understanding of what it has observed,” Gorlo says. Next, the researchers want to use UQ-DAAAM to guide different types of robots, like mobile robotic manipulators, and apply their uncertainty quantification techniques to other domains.  In addition, they are studying the use of UQ-DAAAM to identify areas of high uncertainty the robot could revisit to improve its understanding of the environment. They are also exploring uncertainty quantification in systems that predict the future state of a robot’s environment. This research is supported, in part, by the U.S. Army Research Laboratory and the U.S. Office of Naval Research. Carlone is currently on sabbatical as an Amazon Scholar; this article describes work performed at MIT and is not associated with Amazon.
2e0612d18143103c: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
449e386054c8faa3: VMware appears to have made a concession to European regulators by extending the life of its low-end vSphere Standard and Enterprise Plus products.
The virtualization pioneer quietly announced the extension in the November 4 blog post in which it announced a new low-end product called vSphere Express, which The Register reported yesterday.
We based our report about vSphere Express on an interview, and on material provided by VMware – which sent a version of the blog post linked to above.
The version we saw did not include the following paragraph, the contents of which were not mentioned in our interview:

“Furthermore, for customers in countries in the European Economic Area, vSphere Standard version 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus version 8 will remain available for sale until October 31, 2027, and will have Extended Support included in any active subscriptions to those offerings until the earlier of the applicable subscription end date or October 31, 2028.”
The latter date is more than a year past the October 11, 2027, end-of-general-support date for the more capable vSphere 8 and Cloud Foundation 5.x products.

“This has the potential to be a positive development for organisations within the European Economic Area,” independent analyst Michael Warrilow told The Register. “It could provide them up to an extra 12 months to transition vSphere 8 to VCF 9 and/or migrate workloads to another platform.”
Warrilow thinks European users should seek “absolute clarity” from VMware about the specifics of its offer.
“What level of extended support will be provided and what longer-term commitments will need to be made? I cannot find any of that detail,” he wrote.

A reminder: VMware has promised in the past to make patches available for users who choose to persist with perpetual licenses instead of moving to its preferred subscriptions. The Broadcom business unit later paused patch downloads for months, claiming it needed to adjust its website to make them possible.
Warrilow wonders why VMware will keep selling vSphere Standard only in Europe and suggested “regulatory muscle” is the reason.
Regulators around the world cleared Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware. In Europe, authorities have since revisited the matter.

Lobby group Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe (CISPE) has succeeded in having the European Commission open an antitrust investigation into whether VMware’s channel changes inappropriately shaped the cloud infrastructure provider market. The Register understands CISPE feels regulators are receptive to its arguments.
In the Netherlands, local courts enforced a VMware support contract of the sort that Broadcom has tried to walk away from at other users.
Warrilow wonders if VMware might now change its policy regarding vSphere Standard in other countries.

“The subsequent question is how can organisations in other regions get the same concessions from Broadcom? I would encourage them to amplify their voice by rallying industry associations and user groups to the cause whilst lobbying the regulators in their jurisdiction.”
Overall, however, he thinks VMware’s decision isn’t enormously impactful.
“Ultimately, all it does is buy a little more time to upgrade or migrate,” he wrote.
It may not even do that, as The Register often heard that VMware seldom issued quotes for vSphere Standard or Enterprise Plus.
Paul Turner, chief product officer for VMware’s Cloud Foundation Division, told The Register that inappropriate incentives for channel partners caused that situation, and that VMware later fixed it.
Continental users will be hoping VMware got that effort right. ®
b9b4a6a49c564e9c: When The Register writes about professional certifications offered by vendors, we often receive comments arguing that such credentials are nowhere near as valuable as real-world experience. Now, Microsoft has acknowledged there’s some merit in that argument.

Redmond revealed its stance last week in a post from general manager for content and insights Cameron Percy, who observed: “For years, people have asked for a simpler way to prove the skills they use in the flow of work, without stepping away to prepare for another test.”
Microsoft’s response is the “Pro Badge,” a new form of credential that Percy wrote “works alongside Microsoft Certifications.”

“Certifications show that you can solve problems in a role or field. Pro Badge shows how you use a specific product in your everyday work. Together, they give a more complete picture of what you can do.”

“Instead of capturing skills on a single test day, this approach keeps pace with your work and the products you use,” Percy added. “It gives you a current, verified signal of what you can do, at no cost and without a separate exam or study guide.”
The first Pro Badge is for GitHub Copilot. To earn it, users need only visit learn.github.com and sign in with their GitHub account.

Going through those steps fires up a “proficiency engine” that Microsoft says “gets to work analyzing relevant product usage signals and evaluating them against a defined proficiency framework.” Percy’s post says it “systematically uses evidence from everyday product use to calculate and automatically update your proficiency level.”
Microsoft offers five levels of proficiency: beginner, intermediate, proficient, advanced, and expert. To earn a Pro Badge, users must reach the proficient level.
A beginner has had “first contact” with GitHub and “understands what Copilot is, where it can be used, and how it might fit into everyday development workflows.”
An intermediate user is “familiar with web-based collaboration features, core IDE features, model management, agent configuration, customization options, and techniques for managing context.”

To score the Pro Badge, users will need to demonstrate “practical ability to work on projects” and use GitHub “across typical scenarios, demonstrated through consistent hands-on usage across multiple repositories and extended periods.”

“A Proficient user can use many web and IDE features, select appropriate models, and apply customizations to tailor Copilot for specific project needs. They have experimented with extended features and are aware of extensibility/integration options.”
At the time of writing, Redmond hasn’t defined expert or advanced proficiency. It has published more criteria for the first three levels here.
Microsoft has kindly integrated GitHub’s learning site with LinkedIn, which it owns, so users can add Pro Badges to their profiles.
Percy’s post suggests Microsoft has other Pro Badges in the works.
Elsewhere, Microsoft makes it plain that Pro Badges won’t replace its other credentials.

“GitHub Verified Proficiency is part of Microsoft Pro Badge, a new credential type designed to recognize skills as they are applied in the flow of work,” explains a page offering detail of the new cred. “It does not replace certifications or Microsoft Applied Skills. It adds a third signal: how skills show up through everyday product use.”
The Register welcomes comment on this new approach to professional credentials. ®

9ac961ed71311970: Google-owned autonomous cab company Waymo has revealed it will stop allowing Uber users to book its robo-cabs, hours before the OG rideshare giant made a case for all autonomous vehicle fleet operators to use its platform instead of creating their own.

This slow-motion fender bender played out across Wednesday, starting with Waymo Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana telling Bloomberg that her company would end a partnership that saw it work exclusively with Uber in Austin and Atlanta.
Mawakana said Waymo wasn’t happy about the fact that when users of Uber’s app requested a ride in one of its robo-cabs, they weren’t guaranteed to get one.

News of that break-up came on the same day that Uber announced its quarterly results. As is common on such occasions, the company published remarks [PDF] its execs intend to make during an earnings call.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi used those remarks to promote the idea that Uber is the natural home for robotaxi fleet operators, because it already delivers around 30 percent higher trips per vehicle per day compared to apps run by autonomous cab companies. He said that higher utilization rate, plus use of shared charging and maintenance infrastructure, can deliver “higher fleet profitability even after paying Uber’s marketplace fee.”

“As autonomous technology becomes more widely available, we believe this ability to commercialize vehicles profitably will become an increasingly important source of competitive advantage and value capture.”

The two events are deliciously ironic, because Uber is arguing the scale of its platform makes it the ideal host for third-party players – just as Google does with its search, app store, and YouTube services. Left unsaid is that the two companies hold concerningly dominant positions in their respective markets.

Khosrowshahi also outlined more ways Uber intends to strengthen its position, including by putting around 2,000 robo-cabs on the road in 2027, before “a much larger commercial ramp beginning in 2028.” That plan means Uber will run some cars itself and rely on third-party robo-cab operators who allow bookings on its app.

“Importantly, building a broad ecosystem does not mean spreading our resources evenly,” the CEO explained. “We intend to maintain an open platform while concentrating capital, integration resources, and hands-on deployment support behind a smaller group of partners with the clearest paths to commercial scale and attractive economics at maturity.”
Or in other words, as Uber uses more robo-cabs, it will try to maximize profits.
Uber users booked $59.8 billion worth of services in its third quarter, up 20 percent year-over-year. The company recognized $14.75 billion of that as revenue, a ten percent improvement.
Rideshare accounted for $29.5 billion of bookings and $7.5 billion of revenue. Delivery services brought in $5.5 billion of revenue on $28.5 billion of bookings.
No wonder Khosrowshahi wants more robo-cabs: they’ll boost Uber’s more lucrative business.

The company might need that boost because Australia’s High Court yesterday decided [PDF] that the company must pay AU$81 million ($57 million) in State payroll taxes because the fees paid to rideshare drivers are effectively wages. While the case considered Uber’s activities in one of Australia’s six States, all of them charge payroll tax. The case is one of many around the world in which courts have found gig workers should be treated as employees for legal and tax purposes. The High Court is Australia’s highest judicial authority and like-minded jurisdictions around the world are aware of its decisions, potentially making more trouble for Uber further down the road. ®
