0a73cffbe155abce: Repeated giving may give the impression that companies care more. useng/iStock via Getty Images PlusPeople tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount. This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people. The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team. Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts. Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies. To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal, a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke, a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations. This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder, a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. Yanyi Leng does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

416b7eba9f32ddf4: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

545726cbe77aae8a: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — The ringgit edged up against the US dollar and other Asean currencies at today’s closing ahead of Bank Negara Malaysia’s (BNM) Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) decision tomorrow.
BNM’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will hold its sixth and final policy meeting of 2026 on Nov 5.
At 6pm, the local note rose to 4.0610/0660 against the greenback from yesterday’s close of 4.0735/0775
According to reports, research firms expect BNM to maintain the OPR at 2.75 per cent tomorrow and throughout 2027, supported by resilient economic growth and a manageable inflation outlook.
It said headline inflation is expected to remain comfortably within BNM’s projected range of 1.5 to 2.5 per cent in the near term.
On the external front, SPI Asset Management managing partner Stephen Innes said the ringgit was on firmer footing following the Democratic Party’s gains in the US Mid-Term Elections.

He said a Democratic sweep of US Congress could provide modest support for Asian currencies, including the ringgit, as increased political gridlock in Washington could reduce the likelihood of further US fiscal expansion, potentially weighing on US Treasury yields and the US dollar.
“However, for the ringgit to make more meaningful gains, we would probably need to see markets start pricing out some of the odds of a December US Federal Reserve (Fed) interest rate hike.

“The complication is that President Donald Trump’s tariffs remain largely under presidential control, so the election result does not necessarily remove the inflation pressures that could prevent the Fed from shifting toward a more dovish stance. That may limit how far the US dollar can fall, at least initially,” he told Bernama.

Similarly, Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said market sentiment appeared to have improved following the US Mid-Term Elections result as the Trump administration could face greater legislative hurdles in passing new laws, although the US President retains veto powers.

“Consequently, the US Dollar Index (DXY) fell 0.46 per cent to 101.399 points. It is still too early to tell whether the elections result would see significant shift in US policies especially in relation to trade and the ongoing war in Iran.
“For now, markets are quite constructive which to some degree, may have resulted in improved risk appetite. Therefore, the ringgit was gaining by 0.20 per cent to RM4.06 today,” he said.
Against major currencies, the ringgit traded mostly lower.

The ringgit was higher against the Japanese yen to 2.5636/5669 from 2.5762/5789 at yesterday’s close but inched down versus the euro to 4.5723/5779 from 4.5587/5631, and edged down vis-a-vis the British pound to 5.4783/4850 from 5.4658/4712 previously.
However, the ringgit strengthened against its Asean peers.

It gained against the Singapore dollar to 3.1771/1813 from the previous close of 3.1807/1841, rose versus the Thai baht to 12.0673/0868 from 12.0696/0858 yesterday, inched up against the rupiah to 223.5/223.8 from 224.3/224.6, and climbed vis-a-vis the Philippine peso to 6.39/6.40 from 6.42/6.43 previously. — Bernama

c9a67bff41d827f7: 65 maritime workers certified, and 10 local companies recognised under the RM245.468 million Kuala Kedah RoRo Terminal project

KUALA KEDAH, Nov 4 — Technology Depository Agency Berhad (TDA), through the Industrial Collaboration Programme (ICP), has recorded a 100 per cent certification success rate for 65 maritime workers, while recognising the participation of 10 local companies in the Kuala Kedah Passenger, Cargo and Roll-on/Roll-off (RoRo) Terminal development project.

The achievement marks a milestone in TDA’s efforts to ensure that strategic government procurement generates long-term benefits through skills development, industry participation and the strengthening of local capabilities.

All 65 participants successfully obtained the Mate Domestic (Open) Certificate, with the certificates presented by Transport Minister Anthony Loke Siew Fook during the Maritime Competency Recognition and Local Company Empowerment Ceremony at the Kuala Kedah Passenger Jetty Terminal on November 2.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Transport Minister Anthony Loke Siew Fook during a site visit to review the upgrading works at the Kuala Kedah Passenger Jetty Terminal, accompanied by Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, Datuk Seri Jana Santhiran Muniayan and Mohamad Rafidi Mat Dahan. — Picture courtesy of Technology Depository Agency Berhad

The ceremony was also attended by Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, Ministry of Transport Secretary-General Datuk Seri Jana Santhiran Muniayan and TDA Chief Executive Officer Mohamad Rafidi Mat Dahan.

The certification represents the first milestone under the ICP initiative, “Future-Ready Seafarers Through Professional Certificates and Competency Programme for Domestic and International Maritime Standard”, implemented in collaboration with Sunissa Sdn Bhd, the ICP provider for the Kuala Kedah terminal project.
Transport Minister Loke said the development of skilled maritime personnel must progress alongside infrastructure improvements and greater participation by Malaysian companies.

“The maritime industry requires a competent workforce and a strong ecosystem of local companies capable of meeting operational standards. Through the ICP, government procurement can be translated into skills development, knowledge transfer and more meaningful industry participation,” he said.
In his officiating address, Loke also emphasised that infrastructure development alone was insufficient without a competent workforce, adherence to safety standards and operational discipline.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Transport Minister Anthony Loke Siew Fook receives a briefing from Sunissa Sdn Bhd on the upgrading works at the Kuala Kedah Passenger Jetty Terminal, together with Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, Datuk Seri Jana Santhiran Muniayan and Mohamad Rafidi Mat Dahan. — Picture courtesy of Technology Depository Agency Berhad

He highlighted the benefits of the Mate Domestic (Open) qualification, which provides a broader scope of competency than the Mate Domestic (Limited) certificate, allowing qualified operators to undertake maritime activities across Malaysian waters, subject to the Marine Department Malaysia’s regulations.
The qualification allows fishermen and boat operators to develop their skills, explore wider employment opportunities and potentially increase their income.
The 65 participants comprised members of the Kuala Muda Fishermen’s Association, Kuala Kedah Fishermen’s Association and Pantai Merdeka Boat Operators’ Association.

Training was conducted by Polaris Maritime Training Academy Sdn Bhd, a training centre recognised by the Marine Department Malaysia, across three sessions in Alor Setar in February, April and June 2026.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Technology Depository Agency Berhad CEO Mohamad Rafidi Mat Dahan delivers his remarks at the Maritime Competency Recognition and Local Company Empowerment Ceremony, held at the Kuala Kedah Passenger Jetty Terminal. — Picture courtesy of Technology Depository Agency Berhad

TDA Chief Executive Officer Mohamad Rafidi Mat Dahan said the achievement demonstrated how the ICP translates government procurement commitments into tangible outcomes for Malaysian industries and communities.

“This recognition signifies more than the completion of a training programme. It demonstrates how collaboration among the Government, implementing agencies, training providers, and industry can systematically build local capability. TDA will continue to ensure that strategic procurement delivers competencies, capacity and enduring value,” he said.
Beyond maritime competency development, the ICP also supports the participation of Malaysian companies in the Kuala Kedah terminal project’s supply chain.
Ten local companies were recognised during the ceremony, reflecting the programme’s focus on developing local industry.

Under the project’s localisation and subcontracting component, Malaysian companies participate in activities including machinery rental, soil investigation, marine and onshore piling, construction-material supply, building systems and electrical works.

Their involvement is intended to strengthen domestic capabilities, facilitate knowledge and technology transfer, and create opportunities for local businesses to participate in larger infrastructure projects.
The Kuala Kedah RoRo Terminal project, valued at RM245.468 million, commenced in April 2024 and has an implementation period extending to September 2027.
Upon completion, the upgraded terminal is expected to accommodate up to 3,000 passengers, compared with approximately 800 previously, and allow three large passenger vessels to berth simultaneously.

As an agency under the Minister of Finance Incorporated, TDA facilitates and monitors the implementation of Malaysia’s ICP, ensuring that strategic government procurement delivers measurable and sustainable value through industrial capacity building, human capital development and technology transfer.

The Kuala Kedah initiative demonstrates how infrastructure investment can be leveraged to develop a more capable maritime workforce while creating opportunities for Malaysian businesses to strengthen their participation in the national supply chain.
For further information on TDA and the Industrial Collaboration Programme, visit www.tda.my.

07e5df5b0b383c36: Donald Trump’s Republican Party has received a stunning rebuke in the US midterm elections. Republicans went into the evening hoping that the polls might be wrong and that they could at least cling on to control of the Senate. But by midnight in Washington, the GOP was staring down what looked like its worst defeat in 50 years. Republican losses were not just confined to the type of swing districts that parties usually worry about on election night. The scale of the losses was staggering. They lost Senate seats in deep red states such as Texas and South Carolina. They lost districts they had gerrymandered and in which they were supposed to be unbeatable. They lost seats that even the sharpest analysts thought were safe. Why? For months, surveys have shown that voters are fed up with high prices, with the war in Iran, and with what is increasingly being talked about as the Trump administration’s corruption. A president who was narrowly elected on the promise of a steady economic hand instead spent two years pursuing an extreme ideological agenda favoured only by a minority of Americans. He ignored what voters were saying, and now they have delivered a harsh verdict. Read more: What recent polling suggests will happen in the US midterm elections But these results have implications beyond just the remainder of Trump’s presidency. They break some of the patterns that have defined American politics for decades. Democrats are suddenly winning in places where they have been counted out for a generation. Suddenly, the American political map looks different. Take Texas. The last time a Democrat won election as a senator there was 1988. Democrats have not won a presidential election in Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. Yet last night, Democrat James Talarico powered to a convincing victory. If elections in Texas become politically competitive on a permanent basis, it will become much harder for Republicans to take the presidency in the future. The Republican Party will now be looking nervously towards the 2028 election. For the first time since 2016, there is likely to be a serious debate within the party about whether to move on from the aggressive nationalism and bigotry of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement. Democrats, meanwhile, face their own questions about how to capitalise on their victories. Foreign policy futures But for the rest of the world, change might not come so quickly. Despite the fact that his party has suffered this electoral setback, Trump remains president until 2028. And because despite its constitutional role in declaring war and ratifying treaties, Congress tends to be less involved in foreign policy, there is still a lot that he can do with that power. Indeed, US presidents whose parties perform badly in midterm elections often become more active in foreign policy than they had previously. With the chance of passing a significant domestic agenda mostly beyond their reach, they have a more time on their hands to think about America’s relations with the rest of the world. The same is likely to be true of Trump. The fact that the midterms are over also means that Trump no longer has to be so careful about the political consequences of his actions. As the midterm elections got closer, the president has backed down from major military confrontation with Iran and sought a truce in his tariff wars. Now, with political constraints lifted, he could become more erratic and unpredictable. Congress would not be completely powerless to stop him, at least in theory. But most actions it can take – such as cutting off funding for the war with Iran or seizing tariff power back from the president – require margins of control in both chambers that Democrats are unlikely to have, despite their formidable victories. They would need to have a two-thirds majority to override an almost certain presidential veto on any attempt to pass laws to achieve these outcomes. So a key question is whether this midterm drubbing was serious enough to make some Republican members of Congress get serious about joining Democrats in restraining Trump. Something that Democrats will definitely be able to do is launch all manner of investigations into the conduct of the Trump administration and some of its officials. Their efforts are likely to focus on the war with Iran, Trump’s personal financial dealings with foreign leaders, and the management of the Pentagon by secretary of defence Pete Hegseth. Hegseth, indeed, could be an early casualty of these efforts – there is speculation that he will resign or be fired rather than face possible impeachment. But ultimately a change of direction in US foreign policy depends on the decisions of Trump himself. A changing of the guard among his advisers, or in Congress, can only do so much to influence a president who has never willingly submitted to constraint. The world should prepare itself for the possibility that a politically wounded and angry Trump could now decide to vent his frustrations abroad. Andrew Gawthorpe is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Centre in London.

9771953a3bc61423: Supporters of South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews cheer during her election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Charleston, S.C. AP Photo/Mic SmithVoters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions, including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago. Democrats took control of the House and Senate, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed. The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections. It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida? There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win, and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought. It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats. Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district. What does that tell you? It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties. It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts. I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump. Voter numbers in some key areas were at levels typically seen only in presidential election years. That surge in turnout helps explain why Democrats outperformed expectations in the midterm elections,according to political scientist Charlie Hunt. I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections. That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years. Voters cast their ballots on Election Day at the Cross Insurance Center polling location on Nov. 3, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. Joe Raedle/Getty Images Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending? Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns. This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day. And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton. And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes. Any final thoughts? The territory that Democrats covered is unbelievable. The South Carolina Senate race went to Annie Andrews, the Democrat, which was unfathomable even a few months ago. Mississippi still appears to be somewhat in play. The blue wave turned into something approaching a tsunami. I think a lot of Democrats saw the polling and didn’t want to believe it or couldn’t bring themselves to believe it. But some of this late polling seems to have gotten things on the mark. What we’ve seen in these midterm elections is a massive rebuke of the last two years of the Trump administration, and a sort of blue wave of epic proportions toward the Democrats, the likes of which we haven’t seen in 20 or more years. It’s a huge confirmation of the approach that Democrats took in this election. d3140bfa455d8dce: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine. He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
A war that is running out of men

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries. Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.
Who is accepting this offer?

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted, while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy. Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds. Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.
The legal door and the missing agreement

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training (BMET) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).
Agents, agencies, and the price of a seat

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.
Counting the dead without a count

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.
No Justice for the victims

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.
Written by Zulker Naeen

914fe66fbaac1cb7: From Moaz Nair
When political parties ride on the back of religion, it is rarely the state that suffers the most – it is the faith itself.

Globally and domestically, the dangerous fusion of the spiritual and the secular has transformed religion from an immutable moral guide into a raw tool for worldly power. When the boundary between the house of worship and the polling booth dissolves, public perception shifts. Faith becomes tethered to the behaviour of opportunistic politicians and the inevitable failures of administration. To protect the sanctity of belief, we must separate religion from partisan politics.
When politicians weaponise faith to mobilise voters, they strip it of its deeper theological and moral complexities.

Religion ceases to be a path towards spiritual growth, universal compassion or ethical governance. Instead, it is flattened into a rigid, polarising political boundary. This exploitation fosters a destructive "us versus them" mentality, making a faith that should champion justice appear intolerant, exclusionary and tribal.
A dangerous paradox

Furthermore, when political parties base their core principles on a specific doctrine, they create a dangerous paradox. If a government aligned with religion becomes corrupt, incompetent or oppressive, the public does not simply blame the politicians – they blame the religion itself. The faith is unseated from its sacred pedestal and recast as a symbol of governance failure.
To prevent this decay, several developed nations have intentionally kept political parties free of religious tags.

Turkey stands as a foundational historical blueprint. Through its secular constitutional framework, it deliberately decoupled state affairs from religious identity to protect both governance and the sanctity of personal faith.

Conversely, where religion and politics aggressively intertwine, modern history offers cautionary tales of profound public disillusionment. In some countries, decades of administrative corruption and economic mismanagement by a clerical state have severely damaged the moral authority of the faith, driving massive waves of domestic secularisation.

In the US, the tight embrace between the Christian Right and partisan factions reduced faith to a few polarising "litmus test" issues, alienating millions of moderate believers and fuelling a rapid rise in the "unchurched" population.

In India, the rise of aggressive majoritarian religious nationalism has systematically reduced vast, ancient philosophical traditions into a rigid checklist for political loyalty, fracturing communities into hostile factions.

These global shifts resonate deeply with current Malaysian political dynamics. For decades, our local landscape has seen a creeping politicisation of faith, where theological monopoly is used as a shortcut to electoral legitimacy. Political actors increasingly reduce the rich ethics of faith to divisive rhetoric and identity policing.
This local trajectory manifests in three highly destructive ways.

First, it forces a reduction of public morality. To win elections, politicians narrow expansive spiritual traditions down to a few polarising, headline-grabbing issues. This allows unqualified figures to dictate what is considered "moral" purely to suit campaign agendas.

We see this tension play out vividly in modern policy gridlocks such as the intense debates over reforming historical university admission quotas. Critical socioeconomic solutions to address specialist medical shortages were immediately hijacked and framed as a zero-sum threat to communal identity.

Second, it leads to a profound distortion of sacred texts through bureaucratic overreach. Authoritarian and populist politics frequently weaponise scriptures to justify state-sanctioned exclusion or the restriction of basic freedoms.
Instead of elevating public morality through social justice, religion is too often co-opted by state machinery as a shallow marketing proxy.

This political co-optation was starkly highlighted by the public outcry over restrictive Selangor state planning guidelines. By attempting to ban non-Muslim places of worship from commercial shop lots – a policy born out of bureaucratised hyper-regulation – the state bureaucracy treated minority faith communities not as equal partners in society, but as administrative zoning headaches.

Finally, behavioural political science confirms that intense political-religious polarisation actively drives people away from religious institutions. When observers and moderate believers see faith used as a cynical business or a hypocritical political instrument, they distance themselves from it. By transforming a universal faith into a partisan weapon, politicians end up fracturing the very communities they claim to protect.
Preserve the integrity of faith

Faith can and should be a powerful personal motivator for ethical leadership and social justice. When it truly informs politics, it elevates the state, strengthens the rule of law and fosters community under shared moral instincts. But when politics co-opts religion, faith is debased, hypocrisy breeds and polarisation thrives.

When religion is used to chase votes, it loses its soul. If we wish to preserve the integrity of faith as a universal compass for justice and peace in Malaysia, we must insulate it from the corrosive arena of partisan politics.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

12feaf67ddae85b1: Running a modern research laboratory requires more than maintaining sophisticated instruments. Researchers need to complete training, obtain access, schedule and operate equipment, navigate billing, and more. For large, shared facilities, coordinating these activities across hundreds of instruments and thousands of users can be a significant undertaking. As research becomes increasingly interdisciplinary, another challenge is emerging: finding the right capability in the first place. Addressing these challenges was a central theme of the 2026 NEMO User Meeting, hosted by MIT.nano Oct. 5–6. The meeting brought together 65 representatives from 25 laboratories and organizations, including facility directors, laboratory managers, technical staff, software developers, industry representatives, and government researchers. Sponsored by the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition (NEMC) hub, the meeting focused on sharing approaches to lab management and building connections among facilities. At the center of the meeting was the NanoFab Equipment Management and Operations (NEMO) system, an open-source platform that provides tools for managing shared research facilities while allowing individual laboratories to adapt the system to their own needs. The meeting highlighted an important characteristic of the NEMO community: The same platform can serve a very diverse set of facilities, and while the scale or the scientific missions of the facilities may differ, their core operational challenges are often remarkably similar.  For Anna Osherov, associate director of Characterization.nano and organizer of the meeting, the collaborative model is one of the most compelling aspects of NEMO. “Open source changes the way we think about technology development,” she says. “We can build on what others have already developed, contribute improvements back to the community, and collectively create a platform that is more capable than what any one facility could develop on its own.” NEMO was originally released as open-source software by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2018. Its community edition (NEMO-CE), launched in 2023, allows facilities to develop and share extensions to the platform. At the October meeting, participants from organizations including MIT; Stanford, Columbia, and Princeton universities; the University of Pennsylvania; NIST; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; and Atlantis Labs presented tools to address challenges ranging from chemical management and user administration to equipment status, training, and workflow automation. The range of presentations illustrated how differently configured facilities are adapting a common platform to their own needs. Stanford, for example, presented real-time displays for equipment status and reservations, while Columbia shared its experience migrating to NEMO and extending the system for billing and facility workflows. Princeton demonstrated automated process charts for monitoring tool performance, and the University of Pennsylvania presented approaches to chemical management. Overall, the projects demonstrated the premise behind the NEMO community: a solution developed to address a problem at one facility can become a resource for others. “Together we can do way more than any one of us individually can,” said Vladimir Bulović, director of MIT.nano, during his opening remarks. “NEMO is the platform that gave us, finally, a streamlined way to do so.” From individual facilities to a connected research ecosystem As the NEMO community grows, another opportunity emerges. Universities and research organizations operate specialized facilities, each with unique equipment, expertise, and capabilities. But researchers cannot use a capability they are unaware of or cannot easily find. This is particularly important for microelectronics R&D, where progress often depends on moving quickly between specialized capabilities. A researcher may need fabrication at one facility, advanced characterization at another, specialized microscopy somewhere else, and a process or analysis capability available at only a handful of institutions. Finding those capabilities, and knowing where and when they can be accessed, can itself become a bottleneck.Traditionally, networks of facilities have relied on static webpages or databases to describe available resources. But as facilities evolve, this information can quickly become outdated. At the meeting, MIT.nano presented Hydra, a new open-source platform being developed with support from NEMC as a key component of the NEMC Technical Concierge, a program that aims to help researchers identify and access specialized capabilities across a network of facilities. Hydra is designed to connect multiple NEMO installations and draw information directly from the systems that facilities already use, rather than requiring someone to manually update a separate database. The result is a compilation built from the ground truths of actively-used facility management systems. “Hydra does not replace any lab management system,” Osherov explained. “It connects, synchronizes, and keeps data up to date across all connected systems in real time.” In this model, NEMO provides the operational source of information within an individual facility, while Hydra makes that information discoverable across facilities. For a researcher, that could mean finding a specialized capability without first needing to know which laboratory might have the relevant equipment.  “The focus is to make the distributed infrastructure supporting research more discoverable and usable,” Osherov said. Building infrastructure that can change The approach reflects a broader philosophy: Research infrastructure needs to evolve as research itself changes. “We need to build a flexible research space and a community-oriented space so that people feel empowered to go to it, use it, and then redefine it as the years progress, adapting it to the needs of the next generation of researchers,” said Bulović. That flexibility applies to operational systems as well as physical laboratories. New instruments and research methods emerge, user communities change, and facilities develop new requirements. An open-source platform allows individual facilities to respond to those changes while providing a mechanism for improvements to be shared. At MIT.nano alone, NEMO supports more than 1,600 active researchers using more than 200 tools, with approximately 160,000 hours of tool usage each year. For Jorg Scholvin, associate director of Fab.nano, operating at that scale makes the efficiency of everyday processes, and the ability to adapt and change quickly, important. “A small improvement in an administrative workflow can be multiplied across thousands of users and tens of thousands of equipment interactions,” he said. The NEMO wave The sense of community and positive outlook for the future of shared facilities was apparent throughout the two-day meeting. Closing discussions looked ahead to the role of data integration, automation, and artificial intelligence in lab operations. “The community is taking on a life of its own,” said Mathieu Rampant, CEO and co-founder of Atlantis Labs, describing a model in which facility managers can share ideas and solve problems together. “It’s more sustainable,” he added as he talked about having to do less as the NEMO-CE manager because the facilities managers are talking to each other — sharing ideas and solving problems as a network: “the NEMO wave,” Samantha Roberts, director of the City University of New York nanofabrication facility, called it. “Everyone is invested in it and cares about it. It takes a lot of effort to change your lab management system and if we keep this going, we can build out something that’s really cool and that works.” For Osherov, the purpose remains straightforward. “Ultimately, this is about enabling research. The better we can manage the operational side of our facilities, the more effectively we can make our instruments, expertise, and capabilities available to the research community.” In microelectronics, where innovation increasingly depends on access to specialized and distributed capabilities, that availability matters. The ability to find the right capability at the right facility, using information drawn directly from actively used systems, can help researchers move more quickly from an idea to an experiment to real-world application and impact.

434383af97f0d061: Egypt convicted Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations, and ordered it closed
Originally published on Global Voices
Lina Attalah. Photo from Mada Masr website, used with permission.
A crackdown on independent media in Egypt is escalating.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.

The six-person team was forcibly disappeared, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news. They remain in pretrial detention.

The crackdown then reached Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah. On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.

The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license, in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial. She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later. The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.

According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected. The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.

Mada Masr was founded in 2013 as an independent, critical, investigative outlet. In another decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region. It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.

Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
An attack on journalism
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism. At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday, October 30, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.” A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.

“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about. But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads. It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.” It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.
Solidarity and journalism

In an op-ed published on October 26, the Mada Masr team wrote that “in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday.”

They added: “There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism.”

And: “We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small us, Mada Masr, but a much bigger we.”

In Egypt, journalists who documented torture, political imprisonment, and security crackdowns now face courts that process them quickly and unfairly, under a licensing scheme that has left applicants without an answer for years.
For journalism to be free, that licensing scheme and its chilling effects on access to information, knowledge production, and critical voices in Egypt and beyond must be stopped.
Written by Walid El Houri

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.
Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.
Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.

The noise we make is hurting animals. Can we learn to shut up?

As human society has expanded, animals have started struggling to hear one another. For many birds, the noise has grown so loud that they’ve begun to sing with faster trills. Now, their mating calls aren’t as effective.

The growing hubbub can also increase bird-on-bird conflict, and entire species that can’t handle urban clamor simply leave town for good. But there are technological solutions to the noises hurting animals—and they could help humans, too.

d3f0528600d0917e: Since it’s election day, let’s discuss the polls. Specifically, why their track record has been so poor. I love this topic because it closely tracks prediction errors in market and economic forecasts.

In 2024, I discussed a major source of polling error: the pools pollsters use. Today, I want to discuss a more challenging failure: what is termed “respondent error,” but you are probably more familiar with as Human psychology.
The key respondent errors are Attitude, Intention, and Behavior. These three phenomena affect our ability to predict our own future decision-making and/or behavior.
I have made various arguments over the past twenty years; rather than reiterate these, consider three questions that confront pollsters:
1. What do people really believe?
2. How well do they know their own actual intentions?
3. How likely are they to act on those?
That is the challenging psychology of polling voters, and it has plenty of interesting wrinkles.

Note that I am not addressing whether pollsters reach a representative audience (they don’t) or whether they use unbiased polling questions (it varies). Instead, I suggest that the better pollsters understand the psychology, the more accurate their numbers will be.
Let’s discuss a few details.
1. What do people really believe?

A surprisingly challenging question. We assume people know what they believe; after all, we know our religion, partisan affiliation, favorite sports teams, hobbies, etc. But with so many complex, emotional, and conflicted issues, what people say and what they truly believe often don’t match.
We also assume they answer honestly; ask who they think will win, and you get a biased response based on who they prefer.

This tension creates problems for pollsters. People hold “non-attitudes” on many (most?) issues — ask about a policy they’ve never considered, and they’ll create a response on the spot that’s unstable.1 Answers can reflect weak opinions, conflicting values, and are impacted by the way a question is presented.

Ambivalent voters who like one candidate’s personality and the other’s policies will respond to pollster questions with a squishy answer they’ll likely revise. This is especially problematic for issue polling.2
Then there is expressive answering: some respondents use a poll to send a message rather than report voting preferences.
2. How well do they know their own actual intentions?
Humans declare their intentions to do a specific act with high confidence. After all, we wouldn’t say it if we didn’t think we’d do it (would we?).

What tends to happen is that we say what we either want to believe or what we think the listener wants to hear. This again creates a gap between stated intentions and future behavior. Expressing support costs the poll respondent nothing; their commitments to those responses may be conditional or aspirational.
Then there is the bandwagon effect: Some state their preference based on who they perceive will win. We don’t want to back a loser, and we often claim support for who we expect will win.
3. How likely are we to act on these?
This is the big one: Self-reported turnout intention overstates actual turnout by a large margin. Many people say they’ll vote, but don’t.

Pollsters try to model this from election to election with various degrees of success. But turnout shifts in ways past models can’t anticipate. The 2022 midterm “red wave” never materialized; 2024 showed the reverse. The low-propensity voters who show up only for a specific candidate (e.g., a Trump-only voter) are exactly the people a likely-voter model often excludes. The results of these model adjustments have been decidedly mixed.

People can state what they want to do, and then the world intervenes: bad weather on Election Day; breaking news that changes how we perceive one candidate or the other; geopolitics, the economy, markets, and inflation. The electorate consists of people who vote but whose composition is uncertain beforehand. Voting history and other evidence make turnout only partly predictable.

Pollsters mistakenly believe their core work is data analytics; history suggests it’s more similar to the work psychologists do when trying to predict future behavior. Failing to discern that distinction is why their track record ranges from not bad (2024) to abysmal (2016, 2020).

Endless things can happen between when a pollster gets an answer and when it’s time to vote. A respondent to a poll who says a) I like this candidate; b) I am a registered voter; and c) I intend to vote for that person — does not guarantee a ballot will be cast as stated, if at all.

We know that the earlier the polls are, the worse their predictive values are; we also know that all models are wrong, but some are useful. Models also presume the future looks like the past, and during periods of disruption, that assumption tends to be problematic.

In a nation where partisan lines are fairly well drawn, the middle 5-10% will decide many elections. Those independent undecideds are often equal to the margin of error.3 No wonder polling has had such a mixed track record.
Get out and vote!

a312adbc2b5e0af7: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.

Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”

Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.

During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”

One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)

Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.
